Conventional fault diagnosis method and its position in the diagnostic method system. There are many approaches to fault analysis of marine electrical equipment, among which the analysis methods for electronic equipment faults cover three commonly used means: the conventional fault diagnosis method, fault tree analysis and the expert system diagnostic method. The conventional fault diagnosis method, also called the empirical diagnostic method, is a marine electrical equipment diagnostic method that determines and eliminates equipment fault points through fault symptom analysis and past experience, and is one of the currently commonly used marine electrical equipment fault analysis methods. Its diagnostic accuracy mainly depends on the quality of the diagnostician, and its basis includes personal experience or past experience obtained from books; therefore maintenance personnel are required to master the equipment working principles and the fault characteristics of each component, which is especially important for offshore management and maintenance personnel.

The abbreviation of fault tree analysis is FTA; it uses a logical tree structure containing the top event, intermediate events and basic events, and is a reliability evaluation method that analyzes system faults through a logical tree structure, originating from graph theory. It was first used by Bell Labs in the United States in the design of the Minuteman missile control system to predict random failure probability, and was later successfully applied in the WASH-1400 report, quantitatively giving the risk of nuclear power plants for the first time and proving their safety. Fault tree analysis uses a fault tree; a fault tree is a connected logical tree containing no closed loops, using graphical symbols to represent the logical combination among various events that cause an undesired event of the system; its structure is a logical tree containing the top event, intermediate events and basic events, and the logical relationships are AND and OR. The fault tree develops downward from the tree root of the top event; the branches represent accident events and the nodes represent logical relationships, among which the most commonly used logical relationships are the "AND" and "OR" relationships.

The expert system diagnostic method is based on expert knowledge and contains a knowledge base and an inference mechanism; it uses a marine electrical equipment fault diagnosis expert system. An expert system is a computer model using expert reasoning methods to handle complex problems that require expert analysis and judgment; in the marine field it is used for fault diagnosis of highly automated electrical equipment, and its output results are consistent with the analysis results of human experts.

Implementation steps of the conventional fault diagnosis method. The conventional fault diagnosis method uses a series of steps such as interviewing the operator, observation, check the monitoring and indicating device, making the fault symptom reappear when conditions permit, inspection using the five senses, evaluating the inspection results, determining the system structure and test method, and system testing; these steps have a clear sequential relationship among them.

Interviewing the operator is the first step in fault analysis while keeping the site intact in the conventional fault diagnosis steps; the inquiry link conducted by maintenance personnel to the operator refers to this. The inquiry content includes the fault occurrence situation, time, equipment and operating duration; it is necessary to confirm whether abnormal phenomena such as sound, light alarm, smoke or peculiar smell have been noticed, to check whether there has been misoperation, and to pay attention to the inquiry manner; it is necessary to ask whether the control system operation is normal and whether the operating procedure has changed, and also to understand whether there were special difficulties or abnormal conditions during operation.

Interviewing the operator precedes observation. Observation belongs to a sub-link of the first step of conventional fault diagnosis, "conducting fault analysis while keeping the site intact"; its content includes abnormal phenomena, component status, conductor status and equipment operating parameters. Specifically, it is necessary to observe whether components are jammed or damaged, whether conductors are loose, broken, abraded or burnt, to observe changes in equipment operating parameters, and whether there are obvious interference signals or damage signals; when conditions permit, the equipment may be restarted to make the fault symptom reappear so as to observe carefully. Observation is the in-depth process of the sensory inspection means "looking" in the second step "inspection using the five senses". When identifying the type of transistor, it is necessary to observe the magnitude and direction of the multimeter pointer deflection; when testing the performance of a thermistor, it is inserted into hot water to observe how the resistance value changes with temperature.

Observation precedes check the monitoring and indicating device. Checking the monitoring and indicating device belongs to the inspection objects of the "observation" link in the conventional fault diagnosis steps; its inspection content includes instrument readings, alarm devices, interlock devices, print output or display. It is necessary to check whether all instrument readings are normal, such as voltage, frequency, current, etc.; to check whether the alarm devices and interlock devices are normal; and to check whether the print output or display is normal. Voltage is one of the instrument readings to be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis, and its voltage value can be measured with a multimeter or voltmeter; the generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when building a fault tree, overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, and no residual magnetism voltage will cause the generator to fail to build up voltage. Current is likewise a reading to be checked, and its current value can be measured with a multimeter, ammeter or clamp-on ammeter; the display is used to display radar images and is the display terminal of the ship's radar and monitoring system, used to present images, data and alarm information; it should be installed in the wheelhouse in a place free of strong electromagnetic radiation, away from heat sources and dry, fixed with a hardwood base, with the main radar display oriented so that the observer faces the bow, installed on the starboard side of the bridge. This step belongs to the observation link in the first step of conventional fault diagnosis, "conducting fault analysis while keeping the site intact"; the operation method is to restart the equipment when conditions permit, with the purpose of carefully observing the fault symptom, and during execution personal and equipment safety must be ensured and the fault result must strictly not be allowed to expand.

Making the fault symptom reappear when conditions permit precedes inspection using the five senses. Inspection using the five senses belongs to the second step of equipment inspection and is the process of continuing in-depth observation; its inspection methods are looking, touching, listening, smelling and checking. "Looking" includes checking plugs and sockets, motor operation, control positions and whether there are arcing and burning traces, and also includes disconnecting the circuit switch to see whether there are faulty components; "touching" is used to sense vibration and the temperature of the motor and components; "listening" is used to judge whether the equipment has abnormal sounds; "smelling" is used to detect whether there is a burnt smell or other peculiar smell.

Inspection using the five senses precedes evaluating the inspection results. Evaluating the inspection results belongs to after the second step of the equipment inspection process, namely inspection using the five senses; its evaluation content includes whether the fault judgment is correct, whether fault clues have been found, and whether the various inspection results are consistent. One of the core tasks is to evaluate whether the fault judgment is correct, and it is necessary to confirm whether effective fault clues have been found, requiring logical consistency among the various inspection results; this link is located before determining the fault location, namely the third step.

Evaluating the inspection results precedes determining the system structure and test method.

Determining the system structure and test method precedes system testing. During system testing, the measurement method most suitable for the system structure must be adopted; the operating requirement is to measure at suitable test points, and to compare the results obtained from input and feedback with normal values or performance; this step aims to finally check out the fault location and belongs to the link of further careful inspection using the five senses or instruments.

Criteria and personnel requirements of conventional fault diagnosis. The criteria of conventional fault diagnosis include being familiar with the equipment, understanding the fault symptom, determining the inspection method and keeping records; these criteria require attention to the conventional fault diagnosis method. The criteria require maintenance personnel to be familiar with the structure, working principles, component (assembly) functions and locations of the electrical equipment, and stipulate the use of the five sensory methods of asking, looking, touching, listening and smelling to understand the fault symptom, aiming to preliminarily diagnose the location or cause of the fault through sensory inspection.

Maintenance personnel are responsible for fault diagnosis and repair of marine electrical equipment and need to be familiar with equipment principles, structure and maintenance materials; they are required to be familiar with the structure, working principles, component (assembly) functions and locations of the electrical equipment, by the methods of asking, looking, touching, listening and smelling. In conventional fault diagnosis, it is necessary to understand the phenomena and make a preliminary diagnosis through asking, looking, touching, listening and smelling, and one must be very familiar with the whole ship's electrical equipment circuits, working principles and the locations of each component; the diagnostic accuracy mainly depends on personnel quality and the thoroughness of mastery of the equipment's technical performance. During maintenance, one must be familiar with the performance of electrical materials such as conductive and insulating materials and select them reasonably; in DC motor maintenance, it must be ensured that the brush and commutator are in good contact and that the surface is clean and smooth.

Radar equipment includes the display; the display belongs to radar equipment; the display includes cleaning the display air filter and cleaning the display surface; precautions for radar display installation require attention to the display; radar installation applies to the display.

Fault tree analysis is an analysis method used for electronic equipment faults; its English abbreviation is FTA, and its full name is Fault Tree Analysis. This method carries out reliability evaluation of system faults through a logical tree structure, and its concept comes from graph theory. Fault tree analysis was first used by Bell Labs in the United States in the design of the Minuteman missile control system, with the purpose of predicting random failure probability; thereafter it was successfully applied in the WASH-1400 report, quantitatively giving the risk of nuclear power plants for the first time and proving their safety. In the diagnosis of marine electrical equipment, fault tree analysis can be used to analyze the causes of the generator failing to build up voltage; in troubleshooting main engine starting faults, it is also called the fault signal flow chart tracing method.

The analysis tool used by fault tree analysis is the fault tree. Structurally, the fault tree belongs to a logical tree; it is a connected graph composed of vertices and edges and containing no closed loops, using graphical symbols to represent the logical combination among various events that cause an undesired event of the system. The fault tree develops downward from the tree root of the top event; the branches represent accident events and the nodes represent logical relationships, among which the most commonly used logical relationships are "AND" and "OR". When building a fault tree, generally one fault of the electrical equipment is selected as the top event, for example, motor fails to start. As many fault trees as there are faults of a device should be established correspondingly. The fault tree is also a basis for developing an equipment fault diagnosis expert system. During diagnosis, the branch-cutting method may be adopted, starting inspection from an intermediate event, so as to effectively reduce the inspection scope.

The fault tree contains three types of events: the top event, intermediate events and basic events. The top event is located at the top of the fault tree, namely the tree root position, and represents the undesired event of the system; the events at the next level are the intermediate events or basic events that can cause it to occur. When building a fault tree, usually a specific fault of the electrical equipment is selected as the top event, such as motor fails to start. The top event and the next-level events are connected through logical relationships such as "AND" and "OR", until component faults are traced. For complex large-scale systems, subsystem faults may be taken as the top event to build subtrees, and finally synthesized with transfer symbols. During diagnosis, if a certain intermediate event occurs, it may be regarded as a new top event and checked downward to locate the fault point.

Intermediate events are between the top event and basic events and represent events caused by other events. In the fault tree symbol table, an intermediate event is defined as a result event, formed by the combination of other events, and intermediate events are connected through logic gates (such as AND gates and OR gates). When building a fault tree, selecting appropriate intermediate events can make the hierarchy and logical thinking clearer; in complex systems, subsystem faults may be taken as intermediate events to further build subtrees for analysis. When diagnosing faults, the branch-cutting method may be adopted, starting inspection from a certain level of intermediate event to narrow the scope; if a certain intermediate event has not occurred, the inspection of the basic events associated with it may be excluded.

Basic events are located at the bottom of the fault tree and represent basic fault events, having the attribute of being no longer decomposable. In the fault tree, basic events are connected with the fault event represented by the top event, and belong to inherent fault events inside the system or events in the path leading to the top event. Basic events are one of the basic elements used in fault tree analysis to diagnose marine electrical equipment faults.

In marine electrical fault diagnosis, voltage and current are two basic electrical quantities that need to be measured. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after disconnecting the circuit. During fault diagnosis, it is necessary to check whether the current reading in the monitoring and indicating device is normal. The symbol corresponding to the current transformer is TA; it has the nature of a current source, with extremely large internal resistance, and the standard secondary current is 5A or 1A. The primary side of the current transformer carries the load current I, which is transformed into a secondary current connected to an AC ammeter or other series current elements; its secondary side must strictly not be open-circuited, the terminals of the external ammeter need a short-circuit connecting piece, and it may be disconnected only after wiring verification.

Motor fails to start is a common fault symptom of marine asynchronous motors and DC motors, referring to the state in which the motor cannot produce rotating torque or the speed is zero after being energized. The main causes of a three-phase cage asynchronous motor failing to start include no power supply, motor internal fault and mechanical fault. When checking this fault, the principle from simple to complex is followed: first check the power supply, then check whether the shaft is seized or the load is excessive, and finally check the interior of the motor. In a single-speed non-reversible AC drive system, the direct causes of failure to start include motor fault, no power and mechanical seizure. If the contactor KM is not closed, the motor will have no power, and its root cause may be coil fault, armature seizure or control circuit open circuit. During inspection, if KM is closed but the motor does not turn, other intermediate events need to be checked; if KM is not closed, check downward along this branch. The eight major causes of asynchronous motor failure to start cover no power supply, winding short circuit or open circuit, shaft seizure and excessive load, etc.; the main causes of DC motor failure to start include missing power supply, undervoltage, brush jamming and excitation circuit open circuit.

When building a fault tree, failure to start is often selected as the top event of electrical equipment, such as motor fails to start. The boundary conditions for analyzing this fault are usually set as normal power supply and normal control circuit. Motor fails to start corresponds to checking the power supply voltage, and also corresponds to checking the motor internal fault. If the power supply is not connected, failure to start will result; at this time the switch, fuse and each pair of contacts should be checked to find the fault point. Incorrect wiring of the control equipment will cause failure to start; at this time the wiring diagram should be checked and corrected. Undervoltage will cause failure to start; at this time the power supply voltage should be checked, and if it is indeed too low, appropriately raised. Stator winding phase-to-phase short circuit to earth, incorrect wiring and stator winding short circuit will cause failure to start; at this time the short circuit and open circuit parts should be found and repaired, and if the wiring is incorrect, the wiring should be corrected. Excessive load or the brake not being released, or a fault in the reducer, will cause failure to start; at this time the load should be reduced and the motor and reducer separated; if the motor can run normally, the reducer part should be checked.

Power supply problems will cause motor fails to start, mechanical problems will cause motor fails to start, excessive load will also cause motor fails to start, and motor internal fault will likewise cause motor fails to start. Excessive load is one of the basic causes (leaves) in the motor overheating fault tree, and is also one of the eight aspects of causes of three-phase asynchronous motor failure to start; when the motor fails to start, it is necessary to check whether the load is excessive to eliminate mechanical faults. A power supply fault will cause the RUN lamp to go out; at this time the power supply should be checked correspondingly. In an AC electric drive system, a power supply fault is one of the direct causes of motor overcurrent and thus overheating; a power supply fault is also an electrical supply abnormality cause of motor overheating, PLC control system fault and main engine remote control failure. In the PLC control system, because the switching inverter power supply is prone to faults and difficult to repair, the ship usually adopts the strategy of overall replacement; the PLC power supply fault inspection process starts with the POWER lamp status, and if it is out, the power supply, fuse and light-emitting diode are checked in sequence.

In an AC electric drive system, motor overcurrent is the direct cause of overheating, and local winding short circuit or phase failure is one of the main fault causes of AC motor overcurrent and overheating. Deterioration of heat dissipation conditions is one of the indirect causes of motor overheating, belonging to the basic fault leaf node under the intermediate event "poor motor heat dissipation", parallel with fan blade fault, jointly constituting the direct factors causing poor motor heat dissipation, and is one of the nine basic causes (leaves) causing motor overheating. Deterioration of heat dissipation conditions will cause the motor temperature rise to be high. Bearing fault is one of the direct causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, belonging to the excessive mechanical resistance branch; when an upper bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by very loud uneven noise and the characteristic of the bearing end cover overheating. Checking bearing fault requires the use of bearings, and checking the lubrication condition also requires the use of bearings. Marine motors include bearings and windings. The bearing is a mechanical component of the motor, used to support the rotation of the rotor, and its fault will cause motor overheating, vibration and abnormal noise. Ship motors work under long-term conditions of 15° list, 7.5° trim and 22.5° roll, which places higher requirements on the bearing structure. Before removing the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover must first be taken off; if the wear is not serious, it is generally not necessary to remove the bearing, and it is only necessary to clean and replace the grease.

A winding is a coil component wound from enameled wire in a motor or transformer, used to generate a magnetic field or induce an electromotive force. The winding insulation of a marine motor must undergo "three-proof" treatment against moisture, mold, and salt-oil mist, and be oil-resistant; the cold-state insulation resistance of a marine motor winding shall be no less than 5MΩ, and the hot-state insulation resistance shall be no less than 2MΩ.

The main switchboard contains the main switch, and the main switch is used to control the connection between the generator and the power grid. The main switch is an air circuit breaker used in the ship's power station to connect and disconnect the generator and the main busbar, having both switching and protection functions, and is mainly composed of an undervoltage release, a shunt release, an overcurrent trip unit, an arc extinguishing device, and so on. The main switch belongs to the undervoltage release, belongs to the shunt release, belongs to the overcurrent protection device, belongs to the arc extinguishing device, belongs to the auxiliary contact, and also belongs to the control and signal indication circuit. The DW14 circuit breaker adopts Japanese Terasaki technology and is provided with an additional AOJ-1s overcurrent trip unit. The generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree, and no residual magnetism voltage will cause the generator to fail to build up voltage; overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in an AC electric drive system; when U_n0 > U_fe, it indicates that the voltage regulator has no main regulating action.

The application of fault tree analysis (FTA) in the maintenance of marine electrical equipment is carried out around the fault tree, a graphical logic model; that is, fault tree analysis uses the fault tree as its analysis tool. The contactor contains a coil, and the coil is a component of marine electrical equipment; a KM coil fault is one of the direct causes of the contactor armature failing to close and the motor failing to start; a jammed armature will cause the contactor KM to fail to close, resulting in the motor having no power and failing to start. In a single-speed non-reversible AC electric drive system, a motor internal fault is one of the direct causes of failure to start, referring to faults occurring in internal components such as the motor stator winding and bearings, which will cause the motor to fail to start, automatic start failure, or excessive temperature rise; faults in the motor stator winding, bearings, etc. will also produce the phenomenon of excessive temperature rise, and in severe cases the motor will overheat or even burn out. In the single-speed non-reversible direct-start control system on board, a motor internal fault is one of the two major categories of common faults; apart from the main power supply, it is also a possible cause of the pump auxiliary unit failing to start automatically. In the marine auxiliary machinery electrical system, a motor internal fault and a control system fault are listed together as the two major categories of common faults. In a single-speed non-reversible AC electric drive system, the direct causes of failure to start include the motor internal fault, no power, and mechanical jamming. If KM has not closed, check downward along that branch.

Among the analysis methods for electronic equipment faults, the expert system diagnostic method is one category, which uses a computer model to simulate the expert's process of analysis and judgment, so as to handle complex problems that usually can only be solved by experts. The use of this method in the marine field is concentrated in the marine electrical equipment fault diagnosis expert system, which carries out fault diagnosis for complex, highly automated electrical equipment, and its reasoning results are consistent with the analysis conclusions of human experts.

The marine electrical equipment fault diagnosis expert system is composed of a knowledge base, an inference mechanism, an explanation mechanism, an inquiry mechanism, a knowledge acquisition mechanism, and a fault feature vector storage mechanism. Among them, the knowledge base undertakes the task of storing professional theoretical knowledge in the marine electrical field and electrical fault diagnosis experience, and is one of the core components of the whole system; the inference mechanism makes fault point judgments based on fault features and relevant theoretical knowledge and experience, and is likewise a core component of the system. The function of the explanation mechanism is to explain the expert's reasoning conclusions to the inquirer, so that people are convinced of the diagnosis result; the inquiry mechanism is responsible for contacting developers and users; the knowledge acquisition mechanism is used to modify the knowledge in the knowledge base;

the fault feature vector storage mechanism, in parallel with the knowledge base, inference mechanism, explanation mechanism, etc., is specially used to store fault feature vectors.

When the system runs, it first collects fault symptom features through the inquiry mechanism, stores them into the fault feature vector, and then queries the knowledge base for reasoning. The inference mechanism carries out logical reasoning based on the fault feature vector and the professional theory and experience in the knowledge base, may inquire of the user multiple times during operation to supplement fault feature information, and passes the final reasoning conclusion result to the explanation mechanism. After receiving the output result of the inference mechanism, the explanation mechanism explains the whole fault diagnosis process to the user in easy-to-understand or natural language. The knowledge in the knowledge base is not fixed and unchanging, and can be modified after experimental operation through the inquiry mechanism and the knowledge acquisition mechanism, so as to meet the needs of experimental operation. In the development stage, tools such as PC and CM.1 can be used to establish the inquiry, knowledge acquisition, inference, and explanation mechanisms; these mechanisms are pre-established in expert system development tools such as PC and CM.1 and need not be rebuilt. Knowledge acquisition is the most critical step in system development and determines the quality; when establishing the knowledge base, the collected written theory and expert experience need to be input into the computer according to the tool format, and production rules are often used to represent knowledge, or a frame structure may be used to represent knowledge. Fault tree analysis is the basis for developing an equipment fault diagnosis expert system.

The controllable phase compound excitation constant-voltage device is applied to marine electrical equipment, and its fault diagnosis can adopt fault tree analysis, with the corresponding principle diagram being. This device will exhibit such fault symptoms as the generator failing to build up voltage, generator no-load voltage low, and generator no-load voltage high; these three phenomena all belong to the fault manifestations of the controllable phase compound excitation constant-voltage device. If the residual magnetism voltage polarity is correct and the brushes and rotor are not open-circuited, it is determined to be a phase compound excitation device fault; a phase compound excitation device fault may be caused by a rectifier fault, with its credibility denoted as X1, may be caused by a phase-shifting reactor open circuit, with its credibility denoted as X2, and may also be caused by a compound excitation transformer fault, with its credibility denoted as X3.

As far as the electric motor is concerned, the fault symptom of failure to start may be caused by various reasons. The power supply not being connected will cause failure to start, and when troubleshooting it is necessary to check the switch, fuse, and each pair of contacts to find the fault point; incorrect wiring of the control equipment will cause failure to start, and the corresponding troubleshooting method is to check against the wiring diagram and correct it; undervoltage will cause failure to start; stator winding phase-to-phase short circuit to earth, incorrect wiring, and stator winding short circuit will cause failure to start, and when troubleshooting the short circuit and open circuit parts should be found and repaired; excessive load or the brake not being released, or a fault in the reducer, will also cause failure to start, and troubleshooting methods include reducing the load or separating the motor from the reducer for testing.

Under load operation, undervoltage will cause the speed to be low during load operation; excessive load or the brake not being released, or a fault in the reducer, will cause the speed to be low during load operation; bearing damage will likewise cause the speed to be low during load operation. The phenomenon of abnormal noise or excessive vibration during operation may be caused by mechanical friction, manifested as mechanical rubbing caused by an abnormal air gap between rotor and stator or an abnormal clearance of brake components, and when troubleshooting it is necessary to check the air gap between rotor and stator and the clearance between the brake wheel and brake band; it may also be caused by two-phase operation; if it cannot start after power-off and re-closing, there may be an open circuit in one phase causing two-phase operation, and it is necessary to check the power supply and the motor and repair them; bearing damage will cause abnormal noise or excessive vibration during operation, and the treatment method is to replace the damaged bearing; a bent shaft extension will cause abnormal noise or excessive vibration during operation, and the treatment method is to replace the shaft; loose coupling connection will cause abnormal noise or excessive vibration during operation, and the corresponding troubleshooting method is to check the loose part and tighten the coupling.

The phenomenon of motor temperature too high or smoking may be caused by excessive load or the brake not being released, or a fault in the reducer; may be caused by two-phase operation; may be caused by undervoltage; may be caused by stator winding phase-to-phase short circuit to earth, incorrect wiring, or stator winding short circuit; may be caused by mechanical friction; and may also be caused by poor ventilation and heat dissipation, the latter referring to a state that hinders heat dissipation and air circulation, and when troubleshooting it is necessary to remove objects obstructing ventilation to restore heat dissipation conditions. Bearing overheating may be caused by bearing damage, and may also be caused by insufficient lubricating oil or impurities in it; for insufficient lubricating oil or impurities in it, the troubleshooting method is to replace the bearing. The motor casing being live may be caused by poor earthing, and the cause needs to be found and corresponding measures taken to correct it; may also be caused by damp windings, damaged insulation, or dirt on the terminal board, and for damp windings the stator winding needs to be dried; and may also be caused by worn insulation of the lead-out wires. In addition, undervoltage will also cause difficulty in starting, reduced speed, excessive temperature rise, or poor contactor pull-in of marine electrical equipment; when an electric fan starts slowly and its speed decreases, the possible cause is that the power supply voltage is too low; when the electric fan fails to start, bearing damage is a possible mechanical cause, and the treatment method is to replace the bearing; when the electric drill speed is too slow, the possible cause is that the power supply voltage is too low, and it needs to be checked and adjusted.

In the fault diagnosis of marine electrical equipment, fault tree analysis belongs to the analysis methods for electronic equipment faults, and it uses the tool of the fault tree to carry out analysis. A fault tree is a connected logic tree that contains no closed loops, using graphical symbols to represent the logical combination among various events that cause an undesired event of the system; its structure contains a top event, intermediate events, and basic events, developing downward from the tree root of the top event, with branches representing accident events and nodes representing logical relationships, among which the most commonly used logical relationships are the AND relationship and the OR relationship. Fault tree analysis originates from graph theory, was first used by Bell Laboratories in the United States for the design of the Minuteman missile control system to predict random failure probability, and was successfully applied in the WASH-1400 report, quantitatively giving the risk of nuclear power plants for the first time and proving their safety; it is a reliability evaluation method that analyzes system faults through a logic tree structure.

The marine electrical equipment fault diagnosis expert system contains a knowledge base, and the knowledge base is one of the core components of the marine electrical equipment fault diagnosis expert system; its function is to store professional theoretical knowledge in the marine electrical field and electrical fault diagnosis experience, and its stored content includes professional theoretical knowledge in the marine electrical field and electrical fault diagnosis experience. The inference mechanism carries out logical reasoning and judgment on the fault feature vector based on the knowledge in the knowledge base, and can modify the knowledge therein after experimental operation through the inquiry mechanism and the knowledge acquisition mechanism. An expert system is a computer model using expert reasoning methods, used to handle complex problems that require expert analysis and judgment; in the marine field it is used for fault diagnosis of highly automated electrical equipment, and its output results are consistent with the analysis results of human experts; it is composed of a knowledge base, an inference mechanism, an explanation mechanism, an inquiry mechanism, etc., among which knowledge acquisition is the most critical step in system development and determines the quality, and production rules or a frame structure are often used to represent knowledge. The generator failing to build up voltage refers to the fault symptom in which the generator cannot build up output voltage under the condition of having residual magnetism voltage, and its causes include the generator having no residual magnetism voltage, an excitation circuit fault, and a phase compound excitation device fault. If the generator has no residual magnetism voltage, the generator needs to be magnetized; if the generator has residual magnetism voltage but cannot build up voltage, it is determined to be an excitation circuit fault; in an uncontrolled phase compound excitation voltage regulation system, a phase-shifting reactor open circuit will cause the generator to fail to build up voltage; the phase-shifting reactor is used to regulate voltage and is a key element in the phase compound excitation voltage regulation system, used to regulate voltage and realize the reactive load sharing of parallel-operating generators; if the air gap of the phase-shifting reactor is too large, it will cause the terminal voltage of the generator to be higher than the rated value, and if the air gap of the phase-shifting reactor is too small, it will cause the terminal voltage of the generator to be lower than the rated value. The rectifier converts alternating current into direct current; in the controllable phase compound excitation constant-voltage device, a rectifier fault is one of the sub-causes of a phase compound excitation device fault; if the UR rectifier has an open-circuit diode, it will cause a voltage deviation of |U0-Ufe| greater than ΔU1. The brush and the collector ring contact to transfer current, and an open circuit between the brush and the collector ring is one of the causes of a phase compound excitation device fault; a marine motor contains brushes, and checking the contact condition between the brush and the commutator, checking the brush holder condition, and checking the brush position all require the use of brushes.

The generator no-load voltage low fault has multiple causes, and the possibility of each cause is different; its causes include the UR rectifier having an open-circuit diode, VT being fully conducting, and the L inductance increasing; this fault analysis needs to give credibilities X1, X2, X3 according to component failure rate or expert experience, and this fault corresponds to the corresponding fault tree structure. In the fault tree for generator output voltage lower than rated value, the UR rectifier open-circuit diode is one of the possible causes; in the generator U0<Ufe fault, if |U0-Ufe|>ΔU1, it may be caused by the UR rectifier open-circuit diode.

A diode has unidirectional conductivity, is commonly denoted VD in circuits, and is used for rectification, isolation, voltage regulation, etc.; its main characteristic is unidirectional conductivity, with small conduction resistance under forward voltage and extremely large or infinite resistance under reverse voltage; according to function it is divided into rectifier diodes such as 1N4004, isolation diodes such as 1N4148, Schottky diodes such as BAT85, etc., and also includes light-emitting diodes and Zener diodes. The measurable performance of a diode includes polarity, unidirectional conductivity, forward voltage drop, and reverse resistance; the diode detection steps are applicable to diodes, marine electrical equipment uses diodes, and a multimeter is also used to detect diodes. The electrical graphical symbol of the full-wave bridge rectifier is UR; the RS_0 fuse is used for short circuit protection of semiconductor rectifiers and their complete sets, and the RS_3 fuse is used for internal short circuit protection of thyristor rectifiers and their complete sets.

Generator no-load voltage high is manifested as the no-load voltage being higher than the rated value and the voltage regulator having no main regulating action; when the no-load voltage Un0 is greater than the rated voltage Ufe, it is determined that the voltage regulator has no main regulating action, that is, when Un0>Ufe it indicates that the voltage regulator has no main regulating action. The voltage regulator having no main regulating action may be caused by VT open circuit, may be caused by the shunt resistor open circuit, and may also be caused by VT having no trigger pulse. In the generator no-load voltage high fault, the shunt resistor open circuit will cause the voltage regulator to have no main regulating action. A multimeter is used to measure resistance, voltage, and diodes; the measurable performance of voltage is the voltage value, and the measuring tools are the multimeter and the voltmeter; voltage is one of the instrument readings that need to be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis; the generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree; overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in an AC electric drive system.

The basic composition of the fault tree: fault tree analysis in the diagnosis of marine electrical equipment is carried out with the tool of the fault tree. A fault tree is a connected logic tree that contains no closed loops, and it uses graphical symbols to represent the logical combination relationships among various events that cause an undesired event of the system. In overall form, the fault tree develops downward from the tree root of the top event, with branches representing accident events and nodes representing logical relationships. Structurally, the fault tree is composed of a top event, intermediate events, and basic events; that is, the fault tree contains a top event, the fault tree contains intermediate events, and the fault tree contains basic events. The most commonly used logical relationships in a fault tree are the AND relationship and the OR relationship: the AND relationship means that the output event occurs only when all input events occur simultaneously, and the OR relationship means that the output event occurs when any one of the input events occurs. Taking the generator failing to build up voltage as an example, it can be used as the top event selected when constructing a fault tree, and is decomposed downward layer by layer from there until the basic events are found.

The role of electrical instruments in diagnosis: electrical instruments are the basic means of obtaining operating parameters in the maintenance and diagnosis of marine electrical equipment. According to use, electrical instruments can measure electrical quantities such as current, voltage, power, phase, and frequency; after conversion by a converter, electrical instruments can also indirectly measure non-electrical quantities such as temperature, pressure, and speed. According to working principle, electrical instruments are divided into magnetoelectric, electromagnetic, electrodynamic, induction, rectifier, etc.; according to the measured object, electrical instruments are divided into ammeters, voltmeters, wattmeters, frequency meters, and multi-purpose meters.

Measurement of voltage and current: voltage is one of the instrument readings that need to be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis. A multimeter can be used to measure the voltage value, and a voltmeter can also be used; the multimeter is used for voltage measurement, and the voltmeter is likewise used for voltage measurement. The generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree; overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in an AC electric drive system.

Current is one of the electrical quantities measured by electrical instruments, used to understand equipment status. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connecting it in series after breaking the circuit; a multimeter can also be used to measure current, and the multimeter is used for current measurement; the clamp-on ammeter is used for current measurement and can obtain current values without breaking the circuit. The measurement results of voltage and current, together with electrical quantity parameters such as power, phase, and frequency, jointly provide the basis for determining the top event, intermediate events, and basic events of the fault tree, enabling fault tree analysis to be practically applied in the diagnosis of marine electrical equipment.

Classified by working principle, common types include moving-coil, electromagnetic, electrodynamic, induction, and rectifier types; classified by measured object, there are ammeters, voltmeters, wattmeters, frequency meters, and multi-purpose meters; classified by type of working current, they can be divided into DC instruments, AC instruments, and AC/DC dual-purpose instruments; classified by mode of use, there are installed (switchboard-type) and portable instruments; classified by reading method, they can be divided into analog, digital, and recording types. Structure of typical instruments The wattmeter, also called the power meter, is used to measure electrical power, consists of a current coil and a voltage coil, and calculates power by detecting the load current and voltage. The current coil is connected in series between the power supply and the load to detect the circuit current, and the voltage coil is connected in parallel across the two ends of the measured circuit to detect voltage. The current coil and voltage coil are marked with corresponding terminals (such as "*"), and during measurement the currents of the two coils must flow in from or out of this terminal at the same time.

The multimeter internally contains a measuring circuit, which is used to convert different electrical quantities and ranges into signals measurable by the meter head. The multimeter can be used to measure voltage and current. The clamp-on ammeter is likewise used to measure current. The voltmeter is used to measure the voltage between two points in a circuit; voltage is one of the instrument readings that need to be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis, the generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree, and overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connecting it in series after breaking the circuit. The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part status, wire status, and equipment operating parameters, specifically involving whether parts are jammed or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, abraded, or burnt.

Before measurement, observe the symbol markings on the dial to understand the performance characteristics of the instrument, and carefully read the instrument's instruction manual to understand the precautions for use of the instrument and the working conditions required by the instrument (placement position, temperature, external magnetic field, AC current waveform and frequency). Before use, the symbol markings on the dial must be observed to understand the performance characteristics of the instrument, and the instruction manual must be carefully read to master the precautions and required working conditions. The working conditions required by the instrument specifically include placement position, temperature, and external magnetic field; AC current waveform and frequency are also key working conditions that need to be confirmed before using the instrument.

Wiring and reading during measurement During measurement, connect the instrument correctly into the measured circuit. When using a voltmeter to measure the voltage between two points in a circuit, the two test probes should be connected directly in parallel across these two points; when using an ammeter to measure the current of the branch in which a certain point of the circuit is located, the wire at that point should first be disconnected, and then the two broken ends should be connected respectively to the two test probes of the ammeter. When measuring current, the wire at the measured point should first be disconnected, and then the broken ends should be connected respectively to the ammeter test probes. Before use, it is necessary to understand the instrument's working condition requirements for AC current waveform and frequency. When measuring DC current and AC current, the wiring method should respectively conform to the measurement requirements of the respective current types.

For instruments requiring mechanical zeroing or electrical zeroing, the indication must also first be adjusted to zero before measurement. For analog instruments, when reading, the eye must face the pointer directly; when reading the value of an analog instrument, the eye must face the pointer directly.

Precautions for use The dials of voltmeters, ammeters, and wattmeters used on ships should have clear markings indicating their rated values; the dials of marine instruments should have clear markings indicating rated values. The instrument casing must not be opened arbitrarily or the internal mechanism removed; arbitrarily opening the instrument casing or removing the internal mechanism is prohibited.

It is strictly prohibited to place instruments beside generators, motors, or strong-current conductors; it is strictly prohibited to place instruments in places with high temperature or sharp hot-cold changes; it is strictly prohibited to place instruments in places with corrosive gases; it is strictly prohibited to place instruments in dark and damp places. It is prohibited to place instruments in high temperature, sharp hot-cold changes, or dark and damp places, and instruments must not be placed in environments with corrosive gases. Instruments should avoid high temperature, sharp hot-cold changes, and corrosive gas environments, and should avoid being stored in dark and damp places.

The multimeter is a multi-purpose instrument, and its basic structure can be divided into three parts: the meter head, the changeover switch, and the measuring circuit; that is, the multimeter contains the meter head, the multimeter contains the changeover switch, and the multimeter contains the measuring circuit. The meter head generally uses a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument as the measuring mechanism, and when the pointer is at full deflection the current flowing through the meter head is roughly between a few microamperes and several hundred microamperes. Since the current passing through the measuring mechanism of the instrument is fixed, and the moving-coil measuring mechanism can only pass microampere-level current, different conversion circuits are needed to measure various electrical quantities and different ranges. The role of the measuring circuit is to convert the different electrical quantities and different ranges being measured into signal forms acceptable to the meter head. The changeover switch is responsible for two things: first, selecting the measurement object, and second, selecting the range; its positions are divided into five areas: the ohms area, the AC voltage area, the DC voltage area, and the DC current mA and μA areas. If classified by display method, multimeters have two types, analog and digital; the analog multimeter belongs to multimeters, the digital multimeter also belongs to multimeters, the MF-47 multimeter likewise belongs to multimeters, and the MF-30 multimeter belongs to FU.

The meter head of the analog multimeter uses a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument, with full-deflection current at the microampere level. The meter head, together with the changeover switch and the measuring circuit, are the three major components of the basic structure of the multimeter. The number of scales on the dial varies with the model; common products such as the MF-30 have 4 scales, while the MF-47 has 6 scales, that is, 4 to 6 scales. Measuring DC current requires connecting the meter head in series into the measured circuit. Before measuring resistance, the two test probes must be shorted together so that the meter head pointer stops at zero, thereby completing zeroing.

The MF-30 multimeter is classified as an analog multimeter; the maximum range for voltage measurement is 500V, the maximum range for DC current measurement is 500mA, and the panel has only two test probe jacks, marked "+", "-", and "V" beside the jacks. The red test probe is always inserted into "+", and the black test probe is always inserted into "-", without change due to changeover switch position changes. The multiplier markings of the ohms range of this model are ×1, ×10, ×100, ×1k, ×10k, and the actual resistance value is obtained by multiplying the indication by the multiplier. The MF-47 multimeter can measure voltages up to 2500V and DC currents up to 5A, and the panel has four jacks: "+", "-", "2500V", and "5A". When the current exceeds 500mA, the red test probe is changed to the "5A" jack; when the voltage exceeds 1000V, the red test probe is changed to the "2500V" jack. Before using this model, check whether the meter pointer stops at zero and adjust it; before measuring resistance, cut off the circuit power supply, and if there is a capacitor in the circuit it must be discharged first; each time the resistance range is changed, electrical zeroing must be performed again; before measuring voltage or current, if the pointer deviates from zero, mechanical zeroing is required.

The multimeter can be used to measure resistance, voltage, current, and capacitance, and can also test diodes, transistors, thyristors, photosensitive devices, and thermocouples. The clamp-on ammeter is also used for current measurement; its difference from the analog multimeter is that the latter must break the circuit and then connect in series or parallel, relying on the internal changeover switch and shunt and voltage-divider resistors to work; the former uses the principle of the through-type current transformer, does not need to break the wire, and can directly clamp the wire to read AC current. The moving-coil instrument has high sensitivity and only allows microampere-level current to pass, and is often used as the meter head of the analog multimeter and also often as the core element of a DC ammeter. The DC ammeter is based on the moving-coil instrument, has very small internal resistance, must be connected in series in the measured circuit, and its terminals are marked with "+" and "-" polarity; reversed polarity will cause the pointer to deflect in the reverse direction.

Before using a multimeter to measure a certain electrical quantity, the position of the changeover switch and the jack in which the test probe is located must match the electrical quantity being measured, and observe whether the meter pointer is at zero; otherwise zero adjustment is required. This is a use requirement of the analog multimeter. Before measuring voltage or current, if the pointer is not at zero, mechanical zeroing must first be performed. When measuring voltage or current, if the upper limit of the value range of the voltage or current being measured cannot be determined, the changeover switch should be set to the maximum range, and then according to the actual measurement conditions, the changeover switch should be adjusted to a suitable range while disconnected from the measured point. During measurement with the multimeter, the position of the changeover switch must not be changed arbitrarily; if a range change is really needed, the test probes must first leave the measured point, and then the switch is turned to a suitable range. When measuring 2500V AC voltage or DC voltage, the red test probe must be inserted into the "2500V" jack, and safety must be noted. When measuring DC voltage or current, pay attention to the positive and negative polarity of the instrument. When measuring voltage, the red test probe should be connected to the point with higher potential in the measured circuit; when measuring current, the current should flow into the meter head from the red test probe. In the specific operation of DC current measurement, this means the red test probe is connected to the positive terminal of the circuit and the black test probe to the negative terminal. When measuring DC voltage, the two test probes should be connected in parallel across the power supply or component; when measuring DC current, the changeover switch is set to the milliampere range, the meter head is connected in series into the already broken branch, and after the test probes are properly connected, switch on the power supply and take the reading; after reading, restore the circuit and cut off the power supply. The multimeter is only suitable for measuring the effective value of sinusoidal voltage or current and cannot measure non-sinusoidal quantities. After using the multimeter, the changeover switch should be placed on the maximum AC voltage range to ensure the safety of the instrument. The structure of the multimeter is relatively complex, there are many types, and the layout of the changeover switch and jacks also differs; the instruction manual must be carefully read before use.

When measuring resistance in a circuit, at least one end of the measured resistor must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply in the circuit must be cut off. If there is a capacitor in the circuit, the capacitor should first be discharged before measurement; never measure resistance while the circuit is energized. During measurement, electrical zeroing must first be performed, and every time the range is changed, zeroing must be performed again. If zeroing cannot be achieved, it indicates that the battery voltage is low or the instrument has a fault. When measuring high-resistance components, the hands must not touch the component or the conductive rods of the meter head, otherwise accuracy will be affected. The range of the ohms position is marked in multiplier form, such as ×1k; the actual resistance value equals the pointer indication multiplied by the multiplier corresponding to the changeover switch. The polarity of the internal battery in the ohms area is opposite to the jack markings: the red test probe is connected to the negative pole of the battery, and the black test probe is connected to the positive pole of the battery.

A capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together with insulating material between them; its characteristic is that it blocks DC and passes AC, and in circuit diagrams it is usually numbered with "C" plus a number, such as C25, meaning capacitor number 25. The main performance indicators of a capacitor are capacitance, withstand voltage value, and withstand temperature value; types include electrolytic capacitors, ceramic capacitors, chip capacitors, monolithic capacitors, tantalum capacitors, and polyester capacitors, and units include farad (F), microfarad (uF), nanofarad (nF), and picofarad (pF). The obstructive effect on AC signals is called capacitive reactance, with the formula Xc=1/(2πfC). Marine electrical equipment uses capacitors, AC single-phase motors contain capacitors, and electric fans also contain capacitors. The capacitor testing steps apply to capacitors; capacitors will have capacitor faults, and capacitor faults belong to capacitors. When using an analog multimeter to detect earth leakage, the leakage resistance value is between tens and several hundred megohms (except electrolytic capacitors), the pointer cannot return to the infinity position, and the reading multiplied by the range is the leakage resistance. The larger the capacitance, the greater the amplitude of the pointer swinging to the right, and the slower the speed of swinging back. When an electrolytic capacitor is connected in the forward direction, the leakage current is relatively small; the end connected to the black test probe is the positive pole, by which the polarity can be determined. Before measuring circuit resistance, if there is a capacitor in the circuit, it must first be discharged to avoid damaging the instrument or affecting the measurement result.

The negative temperature coefficient thermistor sensor commonly used on ships can be checked for performance using the R×10 or R×100 range of a multimeter; insert it into hot water and observe how the resistance value changes with temperature. If the measured resistance is infinity, it indicates that the sensor is already open-circuited. When identifying the type of transistor, observe the magnitude and direction of the multimeter pointer deflection. The content of observation covers abnormal phenomena, part status, wire status, and equipment operating parameters, specifically referring to whether parts are jammed or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, abraded, or burnt. Load short circuit or overload corresponds to measurement with a multimeter; no-load power supply corresponds to switch on the power supply.

The multimeter is a multi-purpose instrument, and its basic structure consists of three parts: the meter head, the changeover switch, and the measuring circuit. The meter head usually uses a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument as the measuring mechanism, and at full scale the current flowing through the meter head is about a few microamperes to several hundred microamperes. The meter head is the core measuring component of the multimeter, and the number of scales varies with the model; common models such as the MF-30 have 4 scales, while the MF-47 has 6 scales. The changeover switch is used to select the measurement object and range, and its positions are divided into five parts: the ohms area, the AC voltage area, the DC voltage area, and the DC current mA and μA areas. The measuring circuit cooperates with the meter head and changeover switch to complete the measurement of various electrical quantities. Multimeters are divided into analog and digital types; the MF-47 multimeter is a specific model belonging to multimeters, the analog multimeter is one major category belonging to multimeters, and the digital multimeter belongs to another category.

When using a multimeter to measure resistance, at least one end of the measured resistor must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off. If there is a capacitor in the circuit, the capacitor should first be discharged before measuring resistance; never measure while energized. When measuring high-resistance components, the two hands must not touch the component or the conductive rods of the meter head, so as not to affect accuracy. When using the ohms range to measure resistance, electrical zeroing must be performed again every time the range is changed; if zeroing cannot be achieved, it indicates that the battery voltage is low or there is a fault. The ohms range is marked with multipliers, such as ×1k; the actual resistance value equals the pointer indication multiplied by the multiplier corresponding to the changeover switch, for example ×1, ×10, etc. Before measuring resistance, the test probes need to be shorted so that the meter head points at the zero position to complete zeroing.

A multimeter can be used to measure voltage. The maximum range of the MF-30 multimeter for measuring voltage is 500V, and the highest voltage the MF-47 multimeter can measure is 2500V. When measuring a voltage higher than 1000V, the red test lead should be inserted into the 2500V jack. When measuring DC voltage, the two test leads of the multimeter must be connected in parallel across the power supply or the two ends of the component. DC voltage measurement steps: select the range -> connect the circuit under test -> read the value; the reading must be obtained according to the position of the pointer on the corresponding scale line and the selected range. If the internal resistance r0 of the multimeter is not large enough compared with the resistance R under test, the equivalent resistance will decrease and the measured voltage value will be lower.

A multimeter can be used to measure current. The maximum range of the DC current range of a multimeter can reach 5A, such as the MF-47. When measuring DC current, the meter head must be connected in series in the circuit under test, with the red test lead connected to the positive end and the black test lead connected to the negative end. A clamp-on ammeter is also used to measure current; unlike a multimeter, which requires breaking the circuit to connect, the clamp-on ammeter uses the principle of a through-type current transformer and can directly clamp the wire to measure AC current without disconnecting it.

A multimeter can be used to measure capacitance. The larger the capacitance, the greater the swing of the multimeter pointer to the right and the slower its return speed. Before measurement, if there is a capacitor in the circuit, the capacitor must be discharged before measurement. Capacitor measurement steps: leakage check -> capacitance test -> electrolytic capacitor polarity discrimination. The leakage check is carried out using the resistance range R×1k or R×10k of the multimeter; during the leakage check of a normal capacitor, the pointer first deflects to zero and then slowly returns to infinity. If the pointer does not return to infinity, the reading multiplied by the range is the leakage resistance value. Generally, the leakage resistance of a capacitor is from tens to hundreds of megohms, except for electrolytic capacitors. When measuring capacitance, the two hands must not touch the conductive rods of the test leads, so as not to affect accuracy. For an electrolytic capacitor, the leakage current is small when connected in the forward direction; when the end connected to the black test lead is the positive electrode, the polarity can be discriminated on this basis. A capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together and separated by an insulating material in the middle; its characteristic is to block DC and pass AC, and in circuits it is generally represented by "C" plus a number, such as C25 indicating a capacitor numbered 25. The hindering effect of a capacitor on AC signals is called capacitive reactance, with the formula Xc=1/(2πfC), which is related to the signal frequency and capacitance.

A multimeter can be used to measure diodes. A diode has unidirectional conductivity; under forward voltage its conduction resistance is small, and under reverse voltage it is cut off. It is commonly used in rectification, isolation, voltage stabilization and polarity protection circuits. According to their function, they can be divided into rectifier diodes such as 1N4004, isolation diodes such as 1N4148, and Schottky diodes such as BAT85, and they are commonly represented by VD in circuits. Diodes include light-emitting diodes and Zener diodes. Diode measurement steps: discriminate polarity -> discriminate performance; usually the R×100 or R×1k range is selected, the R×10k range can be used for high-power diodes, and other ranges are prohibited to prevent small-power diodes from being burned out or damaged by reverse breakdown. Polarity is discriminated based on the characteristic that the forward bias resistance is small and the reverse bias resistance is large; in an analog multimeter, the black test lead corresponds to the positive electrode of the battery and the red test lead to the negative electrode. The measurement in which the resistance is smaller is the forward bias, and at this time the black test lead is connected to the anode; the measurement in which the resistance is larger is the reverse bias, and at this time the red test lead is connected to the anode. When an analog multimeter measures polarity, if the black test lead is connected to the anode and the resistance is small, it is forward bias, and the red test lead is connected to the cathode. When a digital multimeter measures polarity, if the red test lead is connected to the positive electrode and a voltage value below 1V is displayed, it is in the forward conduction state. The forward resistance of a silicon diode is several thousand to several tens of thousands of ohms, and the reverse resistance is several hundred kilohms or more; the forward resistance of a germanium diode is several hundred to several thousand ohms. If both the forward and reverse resistances are extremely large, it indicates an internal open circuit; if both are extremely small or display 0, it indicates an internal short circuit breakdown. The R×10k range can be used to measure high-power diodes, but note that the high voltage may cause reverse breakdown damage. The diode detection steps are applicable to diodes, and marine electrical equipment uses diodes.

A multimeter can be used to measure transistors.

A transistor contains two PN junctions inside and has current amplification capability; it is divided into NPN type and PNP type, and in circuits it is commonly represented by the letter "VT" plus a number, such as VT17 indicating a transistor numbered 17. Main models include PNP types such as A92 and 9015, and NPN types such as A42, 9014 and 9018. The transistor type is discriminated using the unidirectional conductivity of the PN junction: if a low resistance is measured with the red test lead connected to the base, it is PNP type; if a low resistance is measured with the black test lead connected to the base, it is NPN type. When discriminating the base of an NPN type, if the red test lead is connected to one pin and low resistance values are obtained when the black test lead measures the other two pins, then that pin is the base. When using the hFE range to discriminate the e/c poles, the pin corresponding to the measurement with the larger hFE value is consistent with the polarity. For medium- and small-power silicon transistors of good performance, the forward resistance of the emitter junction and collector junction is several hundred to one thousand ohms, and the reverse resistance is several hundred kilohms or more. The faster the penetration current increases with temperature, the worse the transistor performance; the greater the pointer deflection, the greater the penetration current and the more unstable the performance. A transistor may suffer a transistor fault; a transistor fault belongs to the transistor, and marine electrical equipment uses transistors.

A transistor may suffer a transistor fault, and a transistor fault belongs to the device category of the transistor. Marine electrical equipment uses transistors; the operating characteristics of NPN type and PNP type can complement each other, such as the complementary pair in an OTL circuit. A thyristor is also called SCR, also known as a silicon controlled rectifier, and a multimeter can be used to measure its polarity, inter-pole resistance and control electrode.

Resistors include photoresistors and also thermistors. A thermistor is a special semiconductor device whose resistance value changes with the surface temperature; the NTC negative temperature coefficient type is commonly used, that is, the resistance value decreases as the temperature rises, and it can be used for temperature compensation. On ships, thermistor sensors with a negative temperature coefficient are commonly used for temperature measurement; the thermistor sensor has a negative temperature coefficient characteristic, and its resistance value changes with temperature. During inspection, the R×10 or R×100 range of a multimeter can be used to measure the resistance between the two leads; insert the sensor into hot water, and under normal conditions a change in resistance value can be observed; if the measured resistance is infinite, it indicates that the sensor is open; use the R×10k range of the multimeter to measure the resistance between the terminal post and the metal shell; if it is not infinite, the insulation is poor. The thermal resistance sensor is a resistance-type temperature sensor commonly used on ships; its resistance value increases as the temperature rises, and during normal operation the resistance value increases as the temperature rises; when checking performance, insert the sensor into hot water and measure the resistance between the two terminal posts, observing the change in resistance value; if the measured resistance value is infinite, it indicates that the thermal resistance sensor is in an open state; a sensor is an information acquisition device of the ship monitoring and control system, divided into two major categories: analog and switching sensors; in the ship station antenna control platform, sensors are placed in the X-axis and Y-axis directions respectively, used to send error signals to control compensation motion when the ship pitches and rolls; analog sensors in the engine room monitoring and alarm system convert parameters into continuously changing electrical signals, suitable for scenarios where both equipment status is monitored and parameter values are displayed. The control platform includes sensors. In the generator no-load voltage high fault, an open shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

Photosensitive devices include types such as photosensitive cells, photoresistors, photodiodes and phototransistors, and resistance changes, electromotive force and current can be measured. A photosensitive cell generates electromotive force or current when exposed to light, and can be detected with the DC mV/mA range of a multimeter; if it is zero, it indicates failure. When testing non-cell devices such as photoresistors, use the R×1k range of a multimeter to compare the resistance values in light and dark; if the resistance value of the photosensitive device does not change between light and dark, it has failed; if it is zero, it is a short circuit; if it is infinite, it is an open circuit. A photoresistor is a semiconductor element whose resistance value changes with the intensity of external light; the resistance is small when the light is strong and large when the light is weak; it is made by depositing a cadmium sulfide (CdS) film on a ceramic substrate and belongs to semiconductor elements; in complete darkness the resistance can reach several megohms or more, and under stronger light it can drop to several thousand ohms or even below 1kΩ. During detection, the R×1k range of a multimeter can be used to measure in light and dark conditions respectively; under normal conditions the resistance value changes significantly; if the measured resistance value does not change, it indicates failure; if both are zero, it indicates a short circuit; if both are infinite, it indicates an open circuit. The automatic fuel oil boiler includes a photoresistor, which is used to detect the flame; when ignition succeeds, the resistance value of the photoresistor decreases, energizing 1JY, energizing 3JZ, energizing 4JZ; 4JZ (31, 28) opens, and the ignition transformer is de-energized.

When using a digital multimeter, the power switch must first be turned on; models without an automatic power-off function must have the power turned off after use. Digital multimeter use steps: turn on the power -> select the measurement function -> connect the object under test -> read the value -> turn off the power, that is, operate item by item in this order. When switching ranges, the test leads should be disconnected from the circuit under test; when replacing the battery or fuse, the POWER switch should be turned off and the test leads separated. The resistance range must not be used to measure current or voltage; do not connect a signal higher than the specified maximum test range; do not use the meter when the battery is not properly installed. 0.7V. When measuring the hFE of a transistor, insert the base into the B jack and the other two pins into the C and E jacks respectively, and take the larger value to determine the pin polarity.

A thermocouple is a temperature sensor with a simple structure and small thermal inertia; it detects the temperature of the object under test by outputting a thermoelectric electromotive force, and resistance and electromotive force can be measured; its electromotive force increases as the temperature rises. Under normal conditions the resistance between the two terminal posts is zero; if infinite is measured, it indicates that the hot end is open and has been damaged. When the hot end temperature rises, the generated electromotive force or current value increases as the temperature rises. If the resistance between the terminal post and the metal shell is not infinite, it indicates that the internal insulating ceramic tube is broken, resulting in poor insulation. The platinum-rhodium 10-platinum type (LB-3) has a measurement range of 0~+1300℃, and the allowable error at ≤600℃ is ±3℃; the tungsten-rhenium 5-tungsten-rhenium 20 type (WR) has a measurement range of 10~+2800℃, and the allowable error at >1000℃ is 1t.

A fuse is a circuit protection component made of protective conductive material, with characteristics such as a low melting point and certain mechanical strength; it is made of aluminum-tin alloy or aluminum-tin-antimony-bismuth alloy, etc., and is one of the commonly used components in electronic circuits, alongside resistors, capacitors, etc. When replacing the fuse of a digital multimeter, the power should be disconnected and a fuse matching the original model and specifications should be selected. The electric main engine remote control system includes fuses; in the main engine remote control system, fuse blowing is one of the common faults of electrical components.

In ship electrical maintenance, the insulation resistance tester is also customarily called a megohmmeter; the two refer to the same portable instrument, mainly used to measure and detect the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, electrical lines and cables, and the measured insulation resistance value is in megohms (MΩ). The main body of this instrument is composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter; the function of the hand-cranked generator is to provide power, while the moving-coil ratio meter undertakes the task of measuring insulation resistance, and the two cooperate to complete the entire measurement process. The structural feature of the moving-coil ratio meter is that it uses electromagnetic force to generate the counter torque; the ratio meter structure is often adopted as the measuring mechanism of the insulation resistance tester and belongs to the core measuring component of the instrument.

The hand-cranked generator is one of the main components of the portable insulation resistance tester and, together with the moving-coil ratio meter, constitutes the main body of the instrument; it generates DC high voltage by hand cranking to measure the insulation resistance of electrical equipment. According to the highest voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator, insulation resistance testers are divided into specifications such as 100V, 200V, 500V, 1000V and 2500V; the higher the voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator, the higher the upper limit of the insulation resistance value that the insulation resistance tester can measure.
