Local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of AC motors, and motor overcurrent is in turn a direct cause of overheating of AC electric drive systems.

Measuring tools and the ship power network In the process of maintenance and repair, electrical quantities such as resistance and current need to be measured with instruments. The measurable property of resistance is the resistance value, which can be measured with a multimeter; the measurable property of current is the current value, which can be measured with a multimeter, an ammeter or a clamp-on ammeter. When measuring resistance in a measuring circuit, at least one end of the measured resistance must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off; if there is capacitance in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring resistance, and never measure with power on. To measure current, an ammeter must be used, connected in series after breaking the circuit. When measuring the winding of low-voltage equipment with a rated voltage of 500V and above, a 1000～2500V insulation resistance tester should be selected. In the fault of generator no-load voltage high, an open shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

The ship power network to which marine motors are connected is part of the ship's power station and usually adopts a three-phase three-wire insulated system. Various marine generators are mostly of salient-pole construction, and their parameters need to take into account the requirements of the network short-circuit current.

Before dismantling a marine motor for maintenance, two marking tasks must be completed first; otherwise it will be difficult to restore the original assembly relationship after disassembly and reassembly. One of them is to mark the circuit terminals before disassembly; this operation must be completed before the motor is separated from the circuit, that is, it must be done before cutting off the wiring. The specific method is to mark and record each circuit terminal one by one; after marking, each circuit terminal must also be wrapped and insulated for protection, so as to prevent bare wire ends from touching each other or being polluted by moisture. The other is to mark the mating surfaces before disassembly; its main purpose is to ensure that the end cover positions remain unchanged before and after disassembly and reassembly, so as to maintain the concentricity between the stator bore and the rotor outer circle. During operation, use a flat chisel to make position marks at the joint between the end cover and the frame; the marks for the front and rear end covers should be different to prevent the two end covers from being installed interchangeably. For unfamiliar motor structures, marks must be made and recorded in the order of disassembly to prevent omission or wrong installation during assembly. For DC motors, marks must also be made at the joint between the brush rocker seat and the end cover seat ring, usually by painting a line with paint and disassembling after it dries. These practices together constitute making marks before dismantling: use a flat chisel to make position marks at the fit between the end cover and the frame spigot to ensure the end cover positions remain unchanged before and after disassembly and reassembly; for DC motors, paint marks should be made at the joint between the brush rocker seat and the end cover seat ring and disassembly done after drying, to ensure the brush position is correct. The main purpose of making marks before dismantling is to avoid affecting the concentricity between the stator bore and the rotor outer circle after disassembly and reassembly.

In the step of check the power supply voltage, what needs attention is exactly marking the circuit terminals before disassembly; when checking the motor internal fault, what needs attention is marking the mating surfaces before disassembly. Both markings are indispensable preparatory work before dismantling.

The conventional fault diagnosis method first uses observation in motor maintenance. The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part condition, wire condition and equipment operating parameters; specifically, it is necessary to see whether parts are jammed or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, scratched or burnt. Observation is also the preceding step of check the monitoring and indicating device; only after observation are the data of various monitoring and indicating devices checked. Observation belongs to the sub-link of the first step of conventional fault diagnosis, "carry out fault analysis while keeping the site unchanged".

Marine motors structurally include components such as bearings, windings, commutators, brushes and shafts. The brush is an important conductive element used to lead current in or out between the stationary part and the sliding part of a motor; DC motors, AC wound-rotor motors and synchronous generators all need to be equipped with brushes; the brush contacts the collector ring to transfer current, and common brushes are divided into three types: graphite, electrographite and metal-graphite, among which the graphite brush is soft in texture and suitable for motors with general commutation conditions and uniform load. The commutator is a rotating sliding contact component used to lead current in and out in DC motors and wound-rotor motors, and is composed of commutator segments. The winding is a coil component wound from enameled wire in a motor or transformer, used to generate a magnetic field or induce an electromotive force; the winding insulation of marine motors must undergo the "three-proof" treatment of moisture-proofing, mildew-proofing and salt-oil-mist-proofing, and must be oil-resistant. The shaft is a mechanical transmission component used to transmit torque and rotary motion, commonly found in motors, contactors and instruments. The core is a magnetic-conducting component in electromagnetic equipment, used to form the magnetic circuit, support the coil and serve as an insulation measurement reference point; a contactor contains a core, and when measuring the insulation resistance of an electrical equipment coil to ground, the terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester may be connected to the core; in a through-type current transformer, the large-current conductor under test is directly interlinked with the core to replace the primary winding.

Brush maintenance has clear quantitative requirements. When the contact area during brush grinding is less than 70%, it must be dealt with; when the contact area between the brush and the commutator is less than 70%, grinding treatment must be carried out; the axial clearance of the brush is 0.2～0.5mm; the pressure of an electrographite brush at major overhaul acceptance is usually about
2.45MPa. When the electric drill brush is not on the neutral line, causing large sparks, the brush position needs to be corrected; when poor contact between brush and commutator causes large sparks, the brush pressure needs to be adjusted. Adjusting the brush is a maintenance procedure in DC motor maintenance for correcting the brush position and pressure, correcting the brush position and contact state by marking for positioning or adjusting the pressure. Before removing the brush rocker of a DC motor, mark it with paint so that the brush position can be adjusted quickly and accurately; before removal, mark the joint between the brush rocker and the end cover with paint, and remove after drying to ensure the correct position during installation; according to the pre-made paint marks, the brush position of the DC motor can be adjusted quickly and accurately.

Commutator maintenance likewise has specific indicators. When dismantling a DC motor, care should be taken to prevent damage to the winding ends, commutator or collector ring; carbon powder must not accumulate in the commutator grooves, so as to avoid short circuit between segments; the commutator surface roughness Ra should be below 3.2μm, and it needs to be ground and polished with abrasive cloth; after the commutator is turned, it needs to be undercut so that the mica is 1～2mm below the commutator segments. If the commutator surface is too dirty or the brush is blocked, poor contact between brush and commutator will result, producing sparks. When checking the contact between brush and commutator, information on both the commutator and the brush is needed; when checking the brush holder, the brush is used; when checking the commutator segments, the commutator is used; when checking the brush position, the brush is likewise used.

The insulation condition of the winding directly determines whether drying treatment is required. When the winding insulation resistance is below 0.5MΩ, drying must be carried out to improve the insulation performance; when the winding contains salt causing low insulation, desalination treatment is required by washing with high-temperature high-pressure water or boiling in fresh water; the current drying method uses the copper loss of the stator winding to generate heat and drive out moisture, initially passing 30% of rated current and gradually increasing it. When dismantling the rotor, care must be taken to prevent damage to the winding ends, and during assembly the winding insulation must also be protected from damage. Local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of AC motors.

The bearing is the mechanical component of the motor, used to support the rotation of the rotor; its fault will cause motor overheating, vibration and abnormal noise; bearing fault is one of the direct causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, belonging to the branch of excessive mechanical resistance; when an upper bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by the characteristics of very loud uneven noise and overheating of the bearing end cover.

Bearing wear will cause increased clearance, vibration and overheating of the motor or mechanical components, manifested as damage to the bearing surface or out-of-tolerance fit clearance; bearing wear or damage will cause uneven clearance between the armature and each magnetic pole, causing excessive brush sparks; bearing wear or damage is one of the main causes of large armature vibration in DC motors. When rolling bearing wear causes excessive clearance, it is manifested as loud rotational noise, wobbling of the outer ring, or impact noise between the balls and the outer ring; the allowable wear value of bearings with an inner diameter of 20～59mm is about 10 times the original clearance, up to a maximum of
0.15～
0.25mm. The clearance of a new bearing is generally 0.01～0.02mm, and the maximum allowable wear value of bearings with an inner diameter of 20～59mm can reach
0.15～
0.25mm. If there is loud noise when the outer ring is turned, or impact noise from the balls when twisted or shaken, it indicates excessive clearance.

Bearing maintenance requires attention to three aspects: precautions for bearing disassembly, precautions for bearing cleaning and precautions for bearing installation. When checking bearing fault, attention must be paid to the precautions for bearing disassembly; when checking the lubrication condition, attention must be paid to the precautions for bearing installation. Motor bearings are generally shrink-fitted on the shaft, with the inner ring fitting tightly on the shaft; during disassembly, a puller may be used to cold-draw the bearing off; if the wear is not serious, it is usually only necessary to clean and replace the grease, and it is generally not necessary to remove the bearing; the purpose of disassembly is to prevent damage to the bearing. In bearing maintenance, bearings with not serious wear generally need not be removed, only cleaned and re-greased; bearings that are severely heated or whose oil is too dirty but can continue to be used need to be cleaned and maintained; the conventional cleaning process is to scrape off the dirty grease, soak in kerosene for 5～10min, scrub with a brush, and perform a second cleaning with gasoline; bearings with hardened grease that is difficult to clean may be immersed in hot oil at 100～120℃ to remove the oil contamination. When cleaning rolling bearings, they may be placed in kerosene to soak for 5～10min and then scrubbed; when the grease is hardened, they may be immersed in hot oil at 100～120℃ for cleaning. During cleaning, the hot oil temperature must not exceed 120℃; open flames are strictly prohibited for heating the oil, and fire prevention must be observed; sharp scrapers are prohibited for picking off oil contamination, so as to prevent damage to the bearing surface; after cleaning, if not used immediately, the bearing must be wrapped in oil paper and stored in a clean place.

Before bearing installation, the shaft journal must be checked to ensure it is smooth and free of rust, cracks, burrs or pitting; slight rust may be polished with fine sandpaper or an oilstone before installation. Installation commonly uses the driving-in method or the shrink-fitting method: the driving-in method requires applying machine oil to the shaft journal and lightly tapping with a soft metal tube against the inner ring until it reaches the specified position; the shrink-fitting method heats the bearing in oil at 100℃, placing it on a wire mesh rack to avoid direct heating, and after heating, takes out the bearing and immediately fits it onto the shaft journal, tapping it gently into place with a tube. The filling amount of bearing grease should be 1/3～1/2 of the bearing space volume; too much or too little will cause poor lubrication. When assembling and tightening the end cover and bearing cover screws, they should be tightened in sequence in the diagonal direction, so as to prevent damage to the spigot fitting surface and prevent eccentricity.

Before dismantling the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover must first be removed; if the wear is not serious, it is generally not necessary to remove the bearing, only to clean and replace the grease. When taking out the rotor, if there is a fan at one end of the rotor, it should be pulled out from the fan end to prevent jamming; for marine pole-changing variable-speed asynchronous motors such as cargo winches, it should be extracted from the end with the larger outer diameter, because there are two cores with different outer diameters on the shaft, and it must be extracted from the large-diameter end. During extraction, damage to the winding and core is strictly prohibited; the objects to be protected from damage include the winding ends, commutator or collector ring. The requirements for correctly placing the rotor are: the removed rotor should be placed on a support or wooden board to prevent rolling; when the ship is swaying, the placed rotor should be tied down securely; if the rotor is too heavy, a steel pipe may be fitted over the shaft and it may be pulled out manually or with an electric hoist. The requirements for correctly placing the rotor and for preventing damage during rotor extraction work together to ensure that the winding ends, commutator or collector ring are not damaged.

Precautions for magnetic pole disassembly include: before disassembly, the distance between the main poles should be recorded; during disassembly, the number of shims under each pole must be counted; if the shim thicknesses differ, they must also be marked, and attention should be paid to whether there are non-magnetic shims and to which pole they belong, in order to avoid incorrect assembly.

Marine motors operate for long periods in harsh environments such as high marine humidity, salt mist, vibration and confined spaces, which places special requirements on insulation, mechanical structure and electrical performance. Chinese standards specify an ambient temperature of 45℃ and require normal operation at a relative air humidity of 95%.

Insulation resistance is tested with the insulation resistance tester, also called the megohmmeter, a portable instrument composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, used to measure the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, lines and cables, and often adopting a ratio meter structure. The insulation resistance tester includes a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, has three terminal posts L, E and G, and is classified by the highest voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator into specifications such as 100V, 200V, 500V, 1000V and 2500V. When the winding insulation resistance of a marine motor is below 0.5MΩ, it needs to be tested with a 500V insulation resistance tester and dried. If the resistance is reduced due to insulation aging, the insulation performance cannot be improved by drying. After seawater enters the motor, desalination is required by boiling in fresh water with three changes of water and boiling in distilled water. When drying cannot improve the insulation resistance, or when the winding has oil dirt and dust, the motor winding should be cleaned. Cleaning methods are divided into cleaning with chemical agents and washing with high-temperature high-pressure water: when the insulation resistance is high but the surface has dirt, a motor cleaner may be used with a brush or spray gun for cleaning; because the cleaner contains volatile gases, cleaning with motor cleaner should be carried out in a well-ventilated place; low insulation resistance indicates salt content, and only high-temperature high-pressure water washing may be used, and only during maintenance periods; salt removal from windings on board may adopt the method of hot water soaking and boiling. These requirements together constitute the precautions for motor winding cleaning and are also important content of motor winding maintenance.

The drying process must comply with the corresponding temperature and recording specifications. Marine motors are mostly class E and class B insulation, with drying temperatures not exceeding 110℃ and 120℃ respectively, that is, the hot-air drying temperature for class E insulated marine motors does not exceed 110℃, and the hot-air drying temperature for class B insulated marine motors does not exceed 120℃. Within the first 2h of drying, record the temperature once every 30min; in the first 4h, raise the temperature by 15℃ per hour, and thereafter raise it by 30℃ per hour up to the maximum allowable value; during drying, measure the insulation resistance once every half hour or hour, and when the insulation resistance reaches above 5MΩ and no longer changes, drying may be stopped. Temperature rise monitoring requires attention to these drying precautions.

The maintenance of DC motors focuses on the commutator and brush system, among which commutator maintenance and brush grinding are the core work. When there is poor contact between brush and commutator, and the contact area is less than 70%, it must be repaired by grinding the brush. Brush and commutator maintenance requires ensuring good contact between the brush and the commutator, and that the commutator surface is smooth and clean with reliable insulation; regularly blow the brush powder and dust off the commutator with a hand blower or hair dryer, and wipe off dirt that cannot be blown off with a small amount of electrical cleaner; when the surface is found to be rough, the brush wears quickly, or there are black wear marks or burn marks, the commutator should be ground, first using 0# abrasive cloth to grind off the rough thin layer, then using old 00# abrasive cloth for rapid polishing. A rough commutator surface is manifested as rapid brush wear, black wear marks or burn marks, and requires first using 0# abrasive cloth to grind off the rough thin layer, then polishing with old abrasive cloth; after grinding, the surface roughness Ra should be controlled below 3.2μm, and normal maintenance requires the commutator surface to be smooth, clean and reliably insulated. Brush wear is a fault symptom of brush material loss during operation of DC motors and brushed generators, requiring regular cleaning of the commutator and replacement of worn brushes; during routine maintenance of DC motors, a hand blower or blower must be used to remove brush powder and dust near the winding ends and the commutator;

In the daily maintenance of marine motors, general cleaning is a basic item, and its object includes both the motor itself and the installation environment in which the motor is located. Removing external dirt is aimed at ensuring normal operation and heat dissipation of the motor. For enclosed motors, the ventilation ducts should be kept clean and the fan holes should be well ventilated; for protected motors, in addition to keeping the exterior clean, attention must also be paid to keeping the ventilation passages unobstructed. Without removing the end covers, the winding ends of protected motors can be wiped or blown. Marine motors include general cleaning as a maintenance item and also include working environment inspection. Working environment inspection must likewise not be neglected; the environment must meet the requirements specified for use, for example, no water, no corrosive gases, etc. The purpose of the inspection is to prevent damage to the insulation and other structural components of the motor, and this work falls within the scope of cleaning work in the daily maintenance and operation monitoring of marine motors. General cleaning requires attention to the precautions for cleaning motor windings; when wiping or blowing the winding ends, damage to the winding insulation should be avoided. Marine motors include bearings and also include bearing maintenance. The core work content of bearing maintenance includes adding oil and changing oil, and at the same time it is necessary to monitor whether the bearing temperature is normal and to judge the condition by listening to the operating sound. Checking the bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition are both carried out directly with the bearing as the object. Carbon powder produced by brush wear accumulating in the grooves may likewise cause short circuit between segments and must be cleaned regularly. Checking the contact condition between the brush and the commutator and checking the condition of the commutator segments both take the commutator as the main inspection object. Checking the contact condition between the brush and the commutator requires attention to power supply voltage monitoring; sparking caused by poor contact is often associated with fluctuations in terminal voltage. Graphite brush is made from natural graphite with binders such as pitch and coal tar added; it is relatively soft in texture and contains more impurities when not heated at high temperature, readily damaging the commutator, and is suitable for motors with ordinary commutation conditions and uniform load. Electrographite brush is made from graphite, coke, carbon black, etc. as raw materials, roasted at a high temperature above 2500°C; it has good wear resistance and is easy to machine, and is suitable for various types of motors and motors with difficult commutation conditions; during the major overhaul acceptance of DC motors, its pressure is generally controlled at about 2.45MPa. Checking the condition of the brush holder and checking the brush position are both centered on the brush. Checking the brush position requires attention to armature current monitoring; deviation of the brush position will cause abnormal changes in the armature current.

Almost all faults of a DC motor can be reflected in the commutation spark, and the color and size of the commutation spark best indicate the operating condition of the DC motor. Marine motors include commutation spark monitoring as a maintenance item. The commutation spark of a normally operating motor should meet the specified grade; if the spark is excessive, it indicates that the motor or load has some kind of fault, and the machine should be stopped for inspection. Maintenance management personnel must frequently observe the spark to become familiar with its grade, thereby judging faults. In terms of operating sound monitoring, marine motors include operating sound monitoring; a normally operating motor produces a uniform and continuous sound due to bearing friction, core magnetization, etc.; when there is a fault or abnormal mechanical components, the motor sound is abnormal and vibration occurs. A screwdriver can be used to contact the bearing cover, with the handle held to the ear to monitor the bearing operating sound; if a continuous "rumbling sound" or other noise is heard, it indicates that the bearing is abnormal and needs inspection and handling. A properly installed motor will not vibrate under normal conditions. The contactor includes a core; in contactor maintenance, it is necessary to measure the insulation resistance between contacts, between the coil and the core, and between live parts and earth, and when measuring, the voltage grade of the insulation resistance tester should be selected according to the rated voltage of the contactor.

In terms of operation monitoring, marine motors include power supply voltage monitoring, armature current monitoring and temperature rise monitoring. Power supply voltage monitoring is the primary item of operation monitoring for marine motors; the motor terminal voltage must be maintained at the rated value, and too high or too low a voltage will cause changes in armature current, torque and temperature rise; the difference between the power supply voltage value and the rated value must not exceed ±5%, and the degree of three-phase voltage unbalance must not exceed ±5%. Power supply voltage monitoring requires attention to the various limits specified for power supply voltage monitoring itself, that is, both the difference between the terminal voltage and the rated value and the three-phase unbalance must be controlled within the above ranges.

Armature current monitoring requires that the armature current be kept within the rated value during motor operation, and the degree of current unbalance of a three-phase asynchronous motor must not exceed ±10%; the rated current on the nameplate corresponds to the rated working state at an ambient temperature of 45°C, and if the ambient temperature exceeds 45°C, the allowable current for long-term operation must be less than the nameplate data. Armature current monitoring requires attention to the rated value and unbalance requirements specified for armature current monitoring, and these must not be exceeded during operation. Temperature rise monitoring requires that the temperature rise of a motor under the rated working state must not exceed the allowable value; if the temperature rise exceeds the allowable value, it indicates that there is a problem with the motor or the control equipment and load, etc., and when the temperature rise is abnormal the cause must be ascertained, and operation can continue only after the fault is eliminated; temperature rise can be monitored with a thermometer or judged by experience, such as by hand feel. Overvoltage is likewise one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems.

Measuring insulation resistance is one of the mandatory inspection and test items for acceptance of a motor after new installation or major overhaul; it is used to check the insulation performance of electrical equipment and is often carried out after major overhaul of the equipment or after shutdown following operation. The objects of insulation testing before and after assembly include insulation between windings and insulation to earth; the test results before and after assembly need to be compared, and only when the results show no difference and meet the requirements may the power-on test be carried out; after power-on, the temperature rise, no-load current, noise and smoothness of rotation need to be observed. In terms of appearance inspection, before power-on after major overhaul of a motor, the installation of components, rotor flexibility, shaft extension deflection and brush contact surface should be checked; for DC motors, the contact surface between the brush and the commutator, observed at a bright place, should not be less than 70%.

During long-term operation of marine motors, their internal components gradually deteriorate due to vibration, dampness, salt spray corrosion and normal wear, and maintenance work must be carried out item by item around observation, testing and trials. The marine motor itself is composed of several key components, including bearings, windings, commutator and brushes, and the working condition of these components directly determines whether the motor can operate reliably. The insulation of marine motor windings must undergo the "three-proof" treatment of moisture-proofing, mildew-proofing and salt-oil-mist-proofing, and must be oil-resistant. If the insulation resistance of the winding is low due to salt content, it needs to be desalinated by washing with high-temperature high-pressure water or by boiling in fresh water. Motor overcurrent is the direct cause of overheating in AC electric drive systems.

If a DC motor shows commutation spark during no-load operation, the step of checking the brush position should be carried out. When checking the brush position, it is necessary to confirm whether the brush jumps and its contact condition with the commutator, and at the same time attention should be paid to monitoring the armature current, using changes in the armature current to judge whether the brush position adjustment is appropriate. The greater the deviation of the brush position, the greater the spark produced by the DC motor; the phenomenon of excessive sparking under brush corresponds to the corrective measure of checking the brush position. The brush contacts the collector ring and serves to transmit current. When checking the contact condition between the brush and the commutator, the commutator is needed to see whether its surface is clean and whether there is burning and uneven wear, and at the same time the brush is needed to see its contact area, degree of wear and whether it moves freely in the brush holder; neither can be dispensed with. Checking the condition of the commutator segments is likewise inseparable from inspecting the commutator itself. Checking the condition of the brush holder must be centered on the brush, to see whether the brush holder is loose and whether the brushes are arranged in a straight line. After turning, undercutting is required so that the mica is 1–2mm below the commutator segments. Checking the bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition must both be centered on the bearing. Before removing the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover must first be taken off;

After all stator windings of a motor are replaced, a withstand voltage test must be carried out, the purpose of which is to determine the insulation strength of the windings to earth and between windings. For motors of 380V and power ≥1kW, the effective value of the test voltage is 1760V at a frequency of 50Hz; the windings should be able to withstand the test voltage for 1 minute continuously.

The no-load test is carried out after major overhaul or new installation of a motor, that is, no-load operation at rated voltage, to check electrical balance, rotation direction and mechanical condition. Before the test, a bridge must be used to measure the resistance of the three-phase windings, and the difference between the resistance values of the phases should be less than ±5%. At the start, an inching test should first be carried out to check whether the rotation direction meets the requirements of the mechanical load; if the rotation direction of an AC motor is reversed, it is corrected by swapping two phase connections, while for DC the excitation winding leads are swapped. Then the three-phase balanced rated voltage is applied to the stator windings to start, and the motor runs at no load for 30min. A clamp meter is used to measure the three-phase currents; the difference between the phase currents should not exceed ±10%, and the ratio of the no-load current to the rated current should conform to the value of normal operation of the motor before major overhaul.

When judging the nature of the noise, the power supply can be cut off under no load; if the noise disappears, it is electromagnetic noise, and if it disappears as the speed decreases, it is mechanical noise. In auxiliary machine commissioning, the no-load test needs to observe the rotation direction, speed and the starting and no-load currents of each gear under step-by-step forward and reverse operation.

The load test and temperature rise measurement should be carried out after the no-load test is all normal. For each 15% increase in load, the armature current and speed need to be measured once, until rated load. When measuring the stable temperature rise, the load operation time must not be less than 4 hours. The average temperature rise of the winding can be measured by inserting a thermometer through the lifting hole, and must not exceed the allowable value for the insulation class. During load operation, the bearing temperature must not exceed 95°C; if too high, the bearing quality and the type of lubricating grease need to be checked; if the bearing temperature is abnormal, the motor and the driven load machinery should also be checked for abnormalities.

Marine motors include many types, among which the marine asynchronous motor is the most widely used type, and the three-phase asynchronous motor used on most ships is the cage asynchronous motor. When analyzing the motor internal fault, the fault tree (FTA) method is usually adopted, that is, fault tree analysis uses the fault tree as a tool to carry out diagnosis. A fault tree is a connected logic tree containing no closed loops, using graphical symbols to represent the logical combination among various events that cause an undesired event of the system; it develops downward from the tree root of the top event, with branches representing accident events and nodes representing logical relationships. A fault tree includes a top event, intermediate events and basic events, among which the most commonly used logical relationships are the AND relationship and the OR relationship. When building a fault tree, electrical equipment faults such as motor fails to start are often selected as the top event, and its boundary conditions are usually set as normal power supply and normal control circuit.

For a three-phase cage asynchronous motor failing to start, the main causes include no power supply, motor internal fault and mechanical fault. When analyzing its fault, the fault tree (FTA) method is usually adopted, covering eight categories of causes such as failure to start and low speed. When checking this fault, the principle of from simple to complex and from the outside to the inside is followed: first check the power supply, then check whether the shaft is seized or the load is excessive, and finally check the interior of the motor. Specifically, a power supply problem will cause the motor to fail to start, a mechanical problem will cause the motor to fail to start, excessive load will likewise cause the motor to fail to start, and a motor internal fault will also cause the motor to fail to start. The eight major causes of an asynchronous motor failing to start cover no power supply, winding short circuit or open circuit, shaft seizure and excessive load, etc. In a single-speed non-reversible AC drive system, the direct causes of failure to start include motor fault, no power and mechanical seizure; failure of contactor KM to close will cause the motor to have no power, and its root cause may be coil fault, armature seizure or open control circuit. If a humming sound is heard when the motor fails to start, it indicates the presence of phase failure of the power supply or mechanical seizure; when phase failure causes locked-rotor, it should be stopped immediately to prevent the motor from burning out after long operation.

Motor fails to start corresponds to the step of checking the power supply; according to the principle of from simple to complex, first check whether there is a power supply; it also corresponds to checking the motor internal fault, which is applicable to the fault analysis of three-phase cage asynchronous motors, using the fault tree (FTA) method for analysis, following the inspection principle of from simple to complex and from the outside to the inside, and needs to be carried out after confirming that the power supply is normal, the shaft is not seized and the load is moderate, and is used to deal with the fault of motor fails to start or motor speed low after starting. When checking the power supply, attention must be paid to marking the circuit terminals before disassembly; when checking the motor internal fault, attention must be paid to marking the mating surfaces before disassembly. In addition, failure of the power supply to be connected will cause failure to start, incorrect wiring of the control equipment will cause failure to start, undervoltage will cause failure to start, short circuit to earth between stator winding phases, incorrect wiring and stator winding short circuit will cause failure to start, and excessive load or the brake not being released, or a fault in the reducer, will also cause failure to start. For failure to start, the switch, fuse and each pair of contacts should be checked to find the fault point; the wiring diagram should be checked and corrected; the power supply voltage should be checked, and if it is indeed too low, appropriately raised; the short circuit and open circuit locations should be found and repaired, and if the wiring is incorrect, the wiring should be corrected;

the load should be reduced, and the motor and reducer separated; if the motor can operate normally, the reducer part should be checked.

The fault of motor speed low after starting is applicable to the analysis of the cage three-phase asynchronous motor commonly used on ships, and there are eight possible causes of this fault. The inspection steps first require confirming whether the voltage is too low and whether the power supply has phase failure, and checking whether the line is incorrectly connected with the delta connection changed to the star connection; after excluding external factors, it is necessary to further check whether the load is excessive, and if all the above conditions are normal, it is necessary to further check the motor internal fault. Undervoltage will cause motor speed low after starting, phase failure of the power supply will cause motor speed low after starting, and incorrect line connection will cause motor speed low after starting, among which the line connecting the delta connection as the star connection is one of the possible causes of low speed after starting of an asynchronous motor. Motor speed low after starting corresponds to checking the power supply voltage, also corresponds to checking phase failure of the power supply, and also corresponds to checking the load. Checking phase failure of the power supply is one of the inspection steps for the fault of motor speed low after starting of a marine three-phase asynchronous motor, carried out after checking whether the voltage is too low and before checking the load, and performed in parallel with checking whether the line connects the delta connection as the star connection; if the power supply phase failure and wiring are normal, the motor itself needs to be further checked. When checking the load, if the motor fails to start, it is necessary to check whether the load is excessive to exclude mechanical causes; when the motor speed is low after starting, it is necessary to check whether the load is excessive as a preliminary troubleshooting step; this check follows the principle of from simple to complex and from the outside to the inside, and is located after the power supply and shaft seizure checks; if the load check is normal and the electrical parameters are correct, the motor internal fault is further checked.

For the fault symptom of motor temperature rise high, fault tree analysis shows that there are 12 causes of this fault, and the fault causes are divided into four categories: power supply fault, internal fault, mechanical fault and impaired heat dissipation. The specific causes in the power supply category include voltage not matching the rated value (U≠UN) and phase failure; the causes of motor internal fault include winding short circuit, open circuit, earthing and rotor open circuit; the causes of mechanical fault include bearing damage, stator-rotor rubbing and overload; the causes of heat dissipation fault include damaged fan blade, impaired ventilation and high ambient temperature. Phase failure of the power supply will cause motor temperature rise high, line voltage mismatch will cause motor temperature rise high, long-term overload will cause motor temperature rise high, and deterioration of heat dissipation conditions will cause motor temperature rise high. Motor temperature rise high corresponds to checking the power supply voltage and also corresponds to checking the long-term overload condition. In the fault tree where the motor speed is below the synchronous speed (n<n₀), low winding voltage is one of the main branches, and the direct causes of low winding voltage include low supply voltage and △→Y connection error; low supply voltage is a branch cause leading to low winding voltage. Long-term overload operation of an asynchronous motor will cause reduced insulation performance, ageing or mechanical damage, and may also lead to stator winding earthing fault. Marine motors include windings; a winding is the coil component wound from enameled wire in a motor or transformer, used to generate a magnetic field or induce an electromotive force; local short circuit or phase failure of a winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of an AC motor; the insulation of marine motor windings must undergo the "three-proof" treatment of moisture-proofing, mildew-proofing and salt-oil-mist-proofing and be oil-resistant.

In fault diagnosis, voltage is one of the instrument readings that need to be checked, and its voltage value can be measured with a multimeter or voltmeter. Generator failure to build up voltage is an optional top event when building a fault tree, and overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems. Low supply voltage will cause loud noise of the electromagnet (AC); when the AC electromagnet is noisy, the power supply voltage needs to be adjusted to 0.85–1.10 times the rated voltage; when the contactor contact is welded and the holding force is insufficient, it should be checked whether the power supply voltage is lower than 85% of the rated voltage. The current transformer corresponds to the symbol TA, has the nature of a current source, has an extremely large internal resistance, and its secondary standard current is 5A or 1A. The primary side of TA carries the load current I, which is transformed into a secondary current and connected to an AC ammeter or other series current element; its secondary side must never be open-circuited, the terminals of the external ammeter must have a shorting link, and it may be disconnected only after the wiring has been checked.

Marine motors operate in the harsh environment of ocean high humidity, salt spray, vibration and confined spaces, so their insulation, mechanical structure and electrical performance all have special requirements. Chinese standards specify an ambient temperature of 45℃ for marine motors and require them to still work normally under 95% relative air humidity; the winding insulation must undergo "three-proof" treatment against moisture, mold and salt-oil mist, and must also be oil-resistant. This broad category of marine motors includes marine asynchronous motors, marine DC motors and AC single-phase motors, etc.; their component parts involve bearings, windings, commutators, brushes and shafts, and routine maintenance work includes general cleaning, working environment inspection and bearing maintenance. When repairing marine asynchronous motors, fault tree analysis is often used to sort out the ins and outs of the fault, and the basic tool used in fault tree analysis is the fault tree. Its structure consists of the top event, intermediate events and basic events, and the most commonly used logical relationships are "AND" and "OR". Among these, the specific power-supply causes include voltage not matching the rated value (U≠UN) and phase failure, that is, a power supply phase failure will cause the motor temperature rise to be high, and line voltage not matching will likewise cause the motor temperature rise to be high; mechanical fault causes include bearing damage, stator-rotor rubbing and overload, and long-term overload will cause the motor temperature rise to be high; heat-dissipation fault causes include damaged fan blades, obstructed ventilation and high ambient temperature, that is, deterioration of heat-dissipation conditions will cause the motor temperature rise to be high. During inspection, voltage and current are both electrical quantities that need to be read with instruments; a multimeter can be used to measure voltage and can also be used to measure current, a clamp-on ammeter is likewise used to measure current, and in addition a voltmeter and an ammeter are also commonly used measuring tools. Bearing damage is one of the specific causes under the mechanical fault branch; once bearing damage is confirmed, a bearing of the same model and same specification must be replaced; if lubricating oil deterioration is also present, the lubricating oil must also be cleaned and replaced.

Large noise during motor operation is another common fault symptom; this fault is caused by 16 specific causes and can likewise be analyzed by means of a fault tree. The noise produced during motor operation is divided into two types, electromagnetic noise and mechanical noise; electromagnetic noise is caused by electromagnetic asymmetry in the motor, mechanical noise is caused by the mechanical parts of the motor, and both will cause large noise during motor operation. The nature of the noise is judged by the no-load test: during the no-load test, cut off the power supply; if the noise disappears immediately, it can be judged as electromagnetic noise caused by electromagnetic asymmetry; if the noise decreases markedly as the speed decreases and disappears only at low speed, it is judged as mechanical noise caused by the mechanical parts; if after cutting off the power supply the noise only weakens but does not completely disappear, this indicates that electromagnetic noise and mechanical noise exist simultaneously. This judgment process corresponds respectively to the two maintenance procedures of checking electromagnetic noise and checking mechanical noise, and the two are used to determine the subsequent inspection direction in the fault of large noise during motor operation, that is, large noise during motor operation corresponds to checking electromagnetic noise and also corresponds to checking mechanical noise. The no-load test itself is a test in which, after major repair of the motor or at new installation, the motor is run at no load under rated voltage to check electrical balance, rotation direction and mechanical state; before the test, the three-phase winding resistances need to be measured with a bridge, and the resistance values of the phases should differ by less than ±5%; at the start, an inching test should first be carried out to check whether the rotation direction meets the mechanical load requirements.

Excessive vibration during motor operation is generally caused by electromagnetic asymmetry or by mechanical aspects; there are seven aspects of causes for this fault, and it can be analyzed from the two aspects of electromagnetic and mechanical by constructing a fault tree. Electromagnetic noise will cause excessive vibration during motor operation, and mechanical noise will likewise cause excessive vibration during motor operation, so this fault also corresponds to the two inspection tasks of checking electromagnetic noise and checking mechanical noise. Bearing overheating is another fault symptom requiring key attention; its fault causes are mainly summarized in three aspects: bearing fault, lubrication fault and installation fault, that is, bearing fault will cause bearing overheating, lubrication fault will cause bearing overheating, and installation fault will also cause bearing overheating. During diagnosis, if the noise disappears during no-load operation, this indicates poor coupling installation; if the noise still exists and is accompanied by vibration, this points to a fault of the shaft or the bearing itself.

If after cutting off the power supply the vibration lightens only as the speed drops, this indicates that the overheating is caused by a mechanical fault rather than electromagnetic asymmetry. For bearing overheating, the corresponding inspection work includes checking bearing fault, checking the lubrication condition and checking the installation condition, among which checking bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition both revolve around the bearing. When checking bearing fault, this procedure is started when the motor reaches rated speed and noise is heard on auscultation; first disengage the coupling so that the motor runs at no load to eliminate the factor of poor installation; if noise and vibration still exist during no-load operation, it is judged as a fault of the shaft or the bearing itself, and after confirming bearing fault the motor must be dismantled for inspection. When checking the lubrication condition, if there is no noise when the motor reaches rated speed, this indicates a lubrication fault. When checking the installation condition, at the instant of cutting off the power supply during no-load operation of the motor, if the vibration disappears it is judged as caused by electromagnetic asymmetry, and if the vibration lightens or disappears only after the speed drops it is judged as caused by a mechanical fault; for bearing overheating, if the noise disappears after disengaging the coupling it is judged as poor coupling installation, and if the noise still exists and there is vibration it is judged as a fault of the shaft or the bearing itself. In addition, too much, too little or deteriorated lubricating oil can all cause bearing overheating, and when adding oil it must not exceed 2/3 of the bearing chamber space; improper assembly of the motor end cover or bearing cover and poor assembly of the generator set are also common causes of bearing overheating.

In the maintenance involving thermal relays and circuit breakers, there are also two types of fault causes related to the re-tripping operation that need to be explained together. When the thermal relay cannot reset, one cause lies in the interval between re-tripping and tripping being too short, that is, the time between the two operations of re-tripping and tripping is too short, and the corresponding maintenance method is to perform manual reset re-tripping at about 5mm. When the shunt trip unit of the circuit breaker cannot make the circuit breaker open, one cause is that the re-tripping contact surface is too large, and the treatment method for this fault is readjustment of the re-tripping contact surface.

In the maintenance of marine asynchronous motors, fault tree analysis is a commonly used diagnostic means; it uses the fault tree, a graphical tool, to sort out the ins and outs of the fault. Taking the generator failing to build up voltage as an example, it can serve as an optional top event when building a fault tree, and incorrect wiring is precisely one of the causes leading to the generator voltage failing to build up normally.

Various instruments are indispensable in the diagnostic process. A multimeter is a multi-purpose instrument composed of a meter head, a changeover switch and a measuring circuit, and is divided into two types, analog and digital, among which the analog multimeter and the digital multimeter both belong to the category of multimeters, and the MF-47 multimeter likewise belongs to multimeters; it can measure a maximum voltage of 2500V and a maximum DC current of 5A, and the panel is provided with four jacks "+", "-", "2500V" and "5A". The current flowing through the meter head of a multimeter at full scale is about several microamperes to several hundred microamperes. With a multimeter, various electrical quantities and devices such as resistance, voltage, current, capacitance, diodes, transistors, thyristors, photosensitive devices and thermocouples can be measured. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after breaking the circuit, and a clamp-on ammeter is likewise used to measure current. When measuring resistance in a circuit, at least one end of the resistance under test must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off; if there is a capacitor in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring resistance, and never measure with power on.

Measurement of insulation resistance relies on the insulation resistance tester, also called a megohmmeter, which is composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, and has three terminal posts L, E and G; it is mainly used to measure and detect the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, electrical lines and cables. The insulation resistance tester is divided by the highest voltage emitted by the hand-cranked generator into specifications such as 100V, 200V, 500V, 1000V and 2500V. When measuring the insulation resistance of an electrical equipment coil to earth, terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester can be connected to the iron core. The insulation resistance tester internally contains two measuring coils, a voltage circuit and a current circuit, and the accuracy of their relative positions needs to be checked. Selection principle for the insulation resistance tester: select according to the rated working voltage of the object under test -> also take into account not damaging the object under test.

Precautions for use of the insulation resistance tester: carry out open-circuit and short-circuit tests before measurement -> it is strictly forbidden to measure while electrical equipment is energized -> discharge the equipment under test after measurement -> the surface of the equipment under test must be wiped clean -> place it horizontally on flat, hard ground -> keep the speed within the specified range -> use a guard ring when necessary -> pay attention to safety and avoid electric shock -> select the instrument according to the rated voltage of the equipment -> use single-strand wire for connection -> it is strictly forbidden to measure low-voltage electronic equipment. Error adjustment procedure for the insulation resistance tester: check the electrical circuit and mechanical mechanism -> adjust the "∞" position -> adjust the "0" position -> fine-tune the pointer or guide wire. Calibration methods for the insulation resistance tester: calibration with a standard resistor -> calibration with a self-made resistance box -> rough calibration.

Overheating and vibration faults of motors are often closely related to mechanical parts. Bearing damage is one of the mechanical fault causes leading to excessively high motor temperature rise, and bearing fault is also one of the direct causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, belonging to the branch of excessive mechanical resistance. When upper bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by very loud uneven noise and the feature of bearing end cover overheating. The winding conductors of a motor have an insulation layer on their surface, and in the normal state the turns are insulated from one another; the function of the insulation layer is to electrically insulate the conductive core wires and prevent short circuit or earthing between core wires, and in the structure of a marine cable it is located between the conductive copper core wire and the protective layer; a marine cable contains an insulation layer. A contactor contains an iron core and a coil; the coil is an electrical component made by winding a certain number of turns of insulated wire on an insulating bobbin, and has the characteristic of passing DC and blocking AC; a KM coil fault is one of the direct causes of the contactor armature failing to close and the motor fails to start. Bearing fault, lubrication fault and installation fault will all cause bearing overheating, bearing damage will also cause bearing overheating, and insufficient or contaminated lubricating oil will likewise cause bearing overheating. Improper assembly of the motor end cover, poor assembly of the generator set or a bent shaft can all cause bearing overheating. For bearing overheating, the corresponding troubleshooting directions are checking bearing fault, checking the lubrication condition and checking the installation condition, among which checking bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition both need to be carried out with the aid of the bearing as a component. When the generator bearing overheats, troubleshooting can be carried out by observing the output current and power and controlling them below the rated values.

Excessively high motor temperature rise is also related to long-term overload and incorrect wiring. Long-term overload is one of the specific causes under the mechanical fault branch in the fault tree of excessively high motor temperature rise; in the inspection procedure for high motor temperature rise, it is necessary to check whether there is long-term overload on the mechanical side, that is, check the long-term overload condition. Long-term overload will also cause generator overheating. In DC motors, long-term overload is one of the root causes of armature winding overheating; long-term overload operation of the cargo winch fan will cause the thermal relay to operate, so that high and medium speeds cannot run. Incorrect wiring will cause the generator voltage to fail to build up normally; winding incorrect wiring causes the current direction to reverse, resulting in severe motor vibration, abnormal noise and serious three-phase current imbalance; if the power supply is not cut off in time, winding incorrect wiring may cause the motor winding to burn out.

Repair of broken bars in a squirrel-cage rotor can adopt the welding method: enlarge the crack, heat the rotor to about 450℃, and then gas-weld and repair with a brazing filler metal composed of tin (63%), zinc (33%) and aluminum (4%). The mechanism of welding is to heat the weldment so that the filler metal melts, atomic diffusion occurs between the weldment and the filler metal, and after solidification an alloy bonding layer is formed at their interface; this bonding layer has good electrical conductivity and mechanical strength, and welding quality directly affects the performance of electronic products. When checking inter-turn and inter-phase short circuit faults of the stator winding, a megohmmeter can be used to judge by measuring the inter-phase insulation resistance.

In the maintenance of marine asynchronous motors, broken bars in a squirrel-cage rotor are a relatively common fault form, among which a broken ring refers to one or several cracks in the end ring. For cast-aluminum rotors, end ring cracking can generally be found by visual inspection; maintenance personnel can make a preliminary judgment with this intuitive feature and can observe the position and direction of the crack at the rotor end without dismantling. For the broken-bar fault, the welding method can be used for repair: first enlarge the end ring crack so that the part to be repaired exposes a clean metal surface, then heat the rotor to about 450℃, and subsequently gas-weld and repair with a brazing filler metal composed of tin (63%), zinc (33%) and aluminum (4%). If the bar replacement method is used for repair, the original end ring must first be turned off with a lathe so as to take out the aluminum bars, and then the guide bars are reassembled according to the original slot positions. For copper-bar rotors, when replacing bars the new end ring should be drilled according to the slot positions, then fitted onto the copper bars and firmly brazed with phosphor copper, so that a reliable conductive connection is formed between each guide bar and the end ring; for small motors, the copper bars protruding from the slots can also be bent and fused into a whole to serve as the end ring, thereby omitting the separate machining of the end ring. The end ring, as the annular conductive part at the end of the squirrel-cage rotor, together with the cage bars forms the short-circuit winding, and its integrity directly affects the conductive performance of the rotor; once the end ring cracks or separates from the guide bars, the rotor circuit resistance increases, and both the starting and running performance of the motor are affected. In the rotating magnetic field method, placing the shading coil in the center of the stator cavity can indicate the rotation of the magnetic field; although this use differs in occasion from the role of the end ring in the rotor, both reflect the function of annular conductive parts in the detection and constitution of the motor magnetic field. The shading coil itself is a copper annular part installed on the pole face of the iron core of an AC electromagnet, used to eliminate armature vibration noise; once the shading coil breaks or falls off, the AC electromagnet will produce relatively large noise; when the shading coil is damaged it can be repaired by copper welding, or the shading coil can be directly replaced, and after repair it should be confirmed that it fits well against the iron core pole face. Desoldering of the end ring of the shaded-pole winding of an electric fan will cause failure to start, and open welding between the guide bars and the end ring of a traction motor will cause faults during load operation; these cases all show that the integrity of the end ring and its related connection parts is a necessary condition for the normal operation of motors and electrical appliances, and during maintenance the end ring welds and the guide bar connections should be listed as key inspection points.

Excessively high motor temperature rise is a problem often encountered in operation, and the mechanical fault branch in its fault tree includes the specific cause of bearing damage. After bearing damage, a bearing of the same model and same specification must be replaced; bearing damage will cause low speed during load operation, will also cause abnormal noise or excessive vibration during operation, and will also cause bearing overheating; these three phenomena often appear simultaneously and can serve as circumstantial evidence for judging bearing failure. When diagnosing bearing overheating, if the noise disappears during no-load operation, this indicates poor coupling installation; checking bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition both need to revolve around the bearing as a component, the former focusing on wear and pitting of the raceway, rolling elements and cage, and the latter focusing on whether the grease is dried out, deteriorated or mixed with impurities. The marine motor itself contains parts such as bearings, windings and the shaft, among which the bearing is used to support the rotation of the rotor, and its fault will cause motor overheating, vibration and abnormal noise. The fault of the bearing running on the inner circle manifests as the mating surface between the bearing inner ring and the shaft turning black, and in severe cases the mating surface becomes roughened; this shows that the fit state between the shaft and the bearing is an important basis for judging the fault, and when the fit is too loose, repair of the shaft journal or replacement of the bearing should be considered. The shaft, as a mechanical transmission part, is used to transmit torque and rotational motion and is commonly found in motors, contactors and instruments; the movable parts of the two units of an electrodynamic three-phase wattmeter are fixed on the same shaft, and the total torque is the algebraic sum of the torques of the two units; the changeover switch is composed of a contact system, an operating handle, a shaft and a panel, assembled by bolts. Motor overcurrent is a direct cause of overheating in AC electric drive systems, and overvoltage is also one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, so monitoring of current and voltage cannot be ignored in fault diagnosis, and during operation instrument readings should be combined to judge whether the motor is in an abnormal working condition. The MF-47 multimeter is a type of multimeter, capable of measuring a maximum voltage of 2500V and a maximum DC current of 5A, and the panel is provided with four jacks "+", "-", "2500V" and "5A"; when measuring high voltage or large current, the test leads should be inserted into the corresponding jacks and the range checked; the analog multimeter and the digital multimeter are likewise common types of multimeters, the former reading by deflection of the meter head pointer and the latter displaying measurement results digitally.

Voltage is one of the instrument readings that must be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis. The generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree. When measuring voltage, the corresponding range should be selected according to whether the circuit under test is DC or AC. A contactor contains a core and a coil. A KM coil fault is one of the direct causes of the contactor armature failing to close and the motor failing to start. During maintenance, check whether the coil leads are loose and whether the coil is burnt. The core is the magnetic-conducting component in electromagnetic equipment, used to form the magnetic circuit, support the coil, and serve as a reference point for insulation measurement;

Once a partial short circuit or phase failure occurs in the winding of a marine asynchronous motor during operation, it often causes an abnormal rise in current, and current is one of the important electrical quantities for judging the operating state of the motor. The current value can be measured with a multimeter, an ammeter, or a clamp-on ammeter, among which the clamp-on ammeter is suitable for on-site use because it can measure without disconnecting the circuit; if an ammeter is used for measurement, the circuit must be disconnected and the ammeter connected in series. Corresponding to current, resistance is also a basic electrical quantity measured by electrical instruments, and its resistance value can be measured with a multimeter. These measurement principles also apply to the inspection of components such as motor windings and contactor coils. Whether a coil has an open circuit must be determined by measuring its resistance with a multimeter after power is cut off; if the resistance is in an open-circuit state, it can be judged. The reason resistance measurement emphasizes disconnecting one end and cutting off the power supply is that if the branch under test is still connected in parallel with the circuit, the measured value will be the equivalent resistance after paralleling and cannot reflect the true state of the coil itself; capacitor discharge is to avoid the superposition of the meter's internal power supply and the charge stored in the capacitor, which would affect the reading or even damage the meter.

A contactor is a key component in the motor control circuit, and it contains a core and a coil. In a through-type current transformer, the large-current conductor under test is directly linked with the core to replace the primary winding. When the contactor fails to pick up and the coil has an open circuit, the resistance should be measured with the power off to determine the open circuit, and then the step of replacing the coil should be carried out; when the contactor coil overheats due to an internal partial short circuit, the resistance comparison method can be used to determine it, and the coil also needs to be replaced. The so-called resistance comparison method is to compare the measured resistance of the faulty coil with the resistance of an intact coil of the same model; if it is obviously too small, it indicates that there is a short-circuit path between turns. This correspondence between coil short circuit and replacing the coil shows that a partial short circuit cannot be restored by simple adjustment and must be replaced. The engine room has high humidity, heavy salt mist, and much oil mist, so ordinary insulation treatment is difficult to withstand for a long time; therefore, after rewinding or replacement, the winding still needs to have its insulation performance restored according to the "three-proof" requirements.

After the motor winding coil is replaced, varnish impregnation treatment must be carried out to improve insulation and mechanical strength; after replacing the coil or rewinding, it must be pre-dried to remove moisture before varnish impregnation. If varnish impregnation is carried out directly while moisture remains in the winding, the varnish liquid is difficult to penetrate into the insulation, and air gaps are likely to remain after drying, so that both insulation strength and mechanical strength fail to meet requirements; therefore, drying is an indispensable step before varnish impregnation. After varnish impregnation and drying, excess attached varnish must be scraped off and an appearance inspection carried out. Appearance inspection is an inspection step before acceptance of marine electrical equipment, covering installation workmanship, mechanical assembly, and appearance quality; for motors, before energizing after major repair, check component installation, rotor flexibility, shaft extension runout, and brush contact surface. Checking component installation is to confirm that all parts have been reassembled in their original positions and that no fasteners are missing; checking rotor flexibility is to turn the rotor to confirm that it rotates freely without jamming or friction; checking shaft extension runout is to confirm that the radial runout of the shaft extension is within the allowable range; checking the brush contact surface is to confirm that the brush is in good contact with the commutator or slip ring and that the pressure is appropriate. These checks connect with the appearance inspection after varnish impregnation and constitute steps that cannot be skipped after replacing the coil.

In the maintenance of small motors, the selection of slot insulation material is related to the winding insulation class. For small motors with Class E insulation, a composite of polyester film and blue shell paper can be used as slot insulation; specifically,

0.05mm thick polyester film composited with blue shell paper. The thickness range of blue shell paper is 0.1~0.4mm, the commonly used thickness is 0.15mm, and the insulation strength is 7kV/mm; as slot insulation, one layer of
0.15mm thick blue shell paper is commonly used. The thickness of polyester film is 0.006~0.10mm, the insulation strength is greater than 130kV/mm, the measured breakdown voltage value is 130~230 kV/mm, and the heat resistance class is Class E; it is a commonly used solid insulating material on ships. The combined use of blue shell paper and polyester film can satisfy the requirements of both heat resistance class and insulation strength: blue shell paper is thicker and provides good mechanical support, while polyester film has high insulation strength and a heat resistance class of Class E; when laminated, they can both withstand mechanical friction during coil insertion and meet the heat resistance requirements of Class E insulation. When selecting, note that the commonly used thickness of blue shell paper is 0.15mm, while that of polyester film is 0.05mm; improper thickness matching will affect the slot fill factor and coil insertion quality.

Broken bars in a squirrel-cage rotor can be repaired by welding. Enlarging the crack is to allow the brazing filler metal to penetrate deep into the fracture and avoid merely overlapping on the surface; heating the rotor to about 450°C is to make the brazing filler metal fully wet during repair welding and form an alloy bonding layer with the cage bar metal. Broken input wiring also corresponds to the maintenance procedure of welding, that is, restoring the continuity of the conductor by welding. Although the objects are different in the two cases, both rely on the mechanism of heating and melting the solder, producing atomic diffusion, and solidifying into an alloy bonding layer to achieve connection; therefore, the quality of welding directly affects the reliability of the conductive path after repair.

In summary, the links involved in motor maintenance, such as measurement, selection of insulating materials, coil replacement, and welding, are interrelated: measuring resistance and current with a multimeter and measuring current with a clamp-on ammeter are the basis for judging coil short circuit, open circuit, and winding overcurrent; the insulation state of the core and coil in the contactor and the winding in the marine motor is directly related to varnish impregnation, drying, and appearance inspection after replacement; the combined use of blue shell paper and polyester film provides a slot insulation scheme for small motors with Class E insulation; and broken bars in squirrel-cage rotors and broken input wiring are repaired by welding respectively.

During the maintenance of marine asynchronous motors, resistance measurement is a basic and frequent operation. The measurable property of resistance is the resistance value, and the determination of the resistance value is completed with a multimeter, that is, the multimeter is used to measure resistance; by using the resistance range of the multimeter to measure the object under test, the resistance value can be read directly. This correspondence constitutes a basic means for judging whether windings, leads, and various connection circuits are normal. During measurement, an appropriate resistance range of the multimeter should be selected so that the pointer or digital display falls in an easily readable interval, so as to judge the measured resistance value. For the stator winding, rotor winding, lead joints of the motor, and various resistance elements in the control circuit, this method can be used to measure point by point, using the measured resistance value and the normal value or the comparison among the three phases as the basis for judgment, thereby determining whether there is an open circuit, short circuit, poor contact, or resistance deviation. Therefore, the operating sequence should be: first cut off the power supply, then discharge the capacitor in the circuit, then disconnect at least one end of the resistor under test from the circuit, and finally measure with a multimeter; after measurement, restore the wiring in the reverse order. For circuits such as motor windings where inductance and capacitance coexist, this sequence must especially be followed; the two links of discharge and disconnection must not be omitted in a hurry to obtain a reading.

In the maintenance practice of marine asynchronous motors, resistance measurement often extends to the related control and excitation circuits. This phenomenon shows that although the resistance element is simple in structure, its on-off state is directly related to whether the entire regulation link can work normally. Once the shunt resistor is open, the voltage regulator loses its main regulation channel, and the no-load voltage of the generator cannot be pulled back to the normal range. At this time, measure the resistance of the shunt resistor with a multimeter; if it displays infinity or obviously deviates from the normal value, it can be judged to be open. Therefore, when troubleshooting such faults, it is also necessary to use a multimeter to measure the resistance of the relevant resistors, and follow the principles of first cutting off power, then disconnecting at least one end of the resistor under test, and discharging the capacitor first if present, to confirm point by point whether the resistor is open, short-circuited, or deviated in resistance, thereby providing a reliable basis for the maintenance of the motor and its supporting electrical equipment.

Marine DC motors have basically been eliminated in marine power systems, but they still account for a certain proportion in deck G-M systems; because of their good speed regulation performance and improvements in manufacturing technology, they have been retained in some ship applications. Within the broad category of marine motors, the maintenance of marine DC motors has its particularities, among which excessive sparking under the brush is the most common fault, and most faults can be reflected by it. Around this fault symptom, it is necessary to sort out its causes, the components involved, and the corresponding maintenance and inspection steps.

One direct source of excessive sparking under the brush is motor overload. When a DC motor is overloaded, the current flowing per unit area of the brush increases, commutation becomes difficult, and sparks are thus generated under the brush. Motor overload is a fault state in which the motor operating current or power exceeds the rated value; in DC motors it causes difficult commutation and excessive sparking, while in generators it triggers overload protection; generator output power or current exceeding its rated value is defined as overload. For generators without automatic step unloading devices, when overload reaches 125%~135% of rated current, tripping occurs after a delay of 15~30s.

Poor contact between brush and commutator can also cause excessive sparking under the brush, and this is one of the common faults of DC motors. Its causes include a dirty commutator surface, insufficient brush spring force, or brush sticking. The effective contact area between the brush and the commutator must be greater than 70%; when the contact area is less than 70%, it must be repaired by grinding the brush. Maintenance methods include adjusting brush pressure, dressing or replacing the brush. In DC generators, this poor contact leads to low output voltage or failure to build up voltage; in motors, it may lead to failure to start due to excessive contact resistance. Protruding mica between commutator segments can also cause poor contact and trigger sparking.
