Since the current passing through the measuring mechanism of the instrument is fixed, and the moving-coil measuring mechanism can only pass microampere-level current, different conversion circuits are required to measure various electrical quantities and different ranges. The function of the measuring circuit is to convert the different measured electrical quantities and different ranges into signal forms that the meter head can accept. The changeover switch is responsible for two things: first, selecting the measurement object, and second, selecting the range; its positions are divided into five areas: the ohms area, the AC voltage area, the DC voltage area, and the DC current mA and μA areas.

If classified by display mode, multimeters fall into two types: analog and digital. The analog multimeter belongs to multimeters, the digital multimeter also belongs to multimeters, the MF-47 multimeter likewise belongs to multimeters, and the MF-30 multimeter belongs to FU.

The meter head of the analog multimeter uses a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument, with a full-scale current at the microampere level. The meter head, together with the changeover switch and the measuring circuit, are the three major components of the basic structure of the multimeter. The number of scales on the dial varies with the model; common products such as the MF-30 have 4 scales, while the MF-47 has 6 scales, that is, 4 to 6 scales. Measuring DC current requires connecting the meter head in series into the circuit under test. Before measuring resistance, the two test probes must be shorted together so that the meter head pointer rests at zero, thereby completing zero adjustment.

The MF-30 multimeter is classified as an analog multimeter; the maximum range for voltage measurement is 500V, and the maximum range for DC current measurement is 500mA. Only two test probe jacks are provided on the panel, marked "+", "-" and "V" beside the holes. The red test probe is always inserted into "+", and the black test probe is always inserted into "-", without being changed according to the changeover switch position.

The multiplier markings of the ohms ranges of this model are ×1, ×10, ×100, ×1k, ×10k, and the actual resistance value is obtained by multiplying the indicated value by the multiplier. The MF-47 multimeter can measure voltages up to 2500V and DC currents up to 5A, and the panel is provided with four jacks: "+", "-", "2500V" and "5A". When the current exceeds 500mA, the red test probe is moved to the "5A" jack; when the voltage exceeds 1000V, the red test probe is moved to the "2500V" jack. Before using this model, check whether the pointer rests at zero and adjust it; before measuring resistance, cut off the circuit power supply, and if there is a capacitor in the circuit, discharge it first; each time the resistance range is changed, electrical zero adjustment must be performed again; before measuring voltage or current, if the pointer deviates from zero, mechanical zero adjustment is required.

A multimeter can be used to measure resistance, voltage, current and capacitance, and can also test diode, transistor, thyristor, photosensitive device and thermocouple. The clamp-on ammeter is also used for current measurement; its difference from the analog multimeter is that the latter must disconnect the circuit and then be connected in series or in parallel, relying on the internal changeover switch and shunt and multiplier resistors to work, while the former uses the principle of the through-type current transformer, does not need to disconnect the conductor, and can directly clamp the conductor to read the AC current. The moving-coil instrument has high sensitivity and only allows microampere-level current to pass; it is often used as the meter head of the analog multimeter and also often as the core element of the DC ammeter. The DC ammeter is based on the moving-coil instrument and has a very small internal resistance; it must be connected in series in the circuit under test, and its terminals are marked with "+" and "-" polarity; reversed polarity will cause the pointer to deflect in the reverse direction.

Before using a multimeter to measure a certain quantity, the position of the changeover switch and the jack in which the test leads are inserted must match the quantity to be measured, and observation must be made as to whether the pointer is at the zero position; otherwise, zero adjustment is required. This item belongs to the usage requirements of the analog multimeter. Before measuring voltage or current, if the pointer is not at the zero position, mechanical zeroing must first be performed. When measuring voltage or current, if the upper limit of the numerical range of the voltage or current to be measured cannot be determined, the changeover switch should be set to the maximum range, and then, according to the actual measurement conditions, the changeover switch should be adjusted to a suitable range while disconnected from the measurement point. During the measurement process, the position of the changeover switch of the multimeter must not be changed at will; if a range change is really necessary, the test leads must first be moved away from the measured point, and then the switch turned to the suitable range.

When measuring an AC voltage or DC voltage of 2500V, the red test lead must be inserted into the "2500V" jack, and safety must be observed. When measuring DC voltage or current, attention must be paid to the positive and negative polarity of the instrument. When measuring voltage, the red test lead should be connected to the point of higher potential in the measuring circuit; when measuring current, the current should flow from the red test lead into the meter head. In the specific operation of DC current measurement, this means the red test lead is connected to the positive terminal of the circuit and the black test lead to the negative terminal. When measuring DC voltage, the two test leads should be connected in parallel across the power supply or the component; when measuring DC current, the changeover switch is set to the milliampere range, the meter head is connected in series into the disconnected branch, and after the test leads are properly connected, switch on the power supply and take the reading; after reading, restore the circuit and cut off the power supply. The multimeter is only suitable for measuring the effective value of sinusoidal voltage or current and cannot measure non-sinusoidal quantities. After the multimeter is used, the changeover switch should be set to the maximum AC voltage range to ensure the safety of the instrument. The structure of the multimeter is relatively complex, there are many types, and the layout of the changeover switch and jacks also differs; the instruction manual must be read carefully before use.

When measuring a resistor in a measuring circuit, at least one end of the resistor to be measured must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply in the circuit must be disconnected. If a capacitor exists in the circuit, the capacitor should first be discharged before measurement; never measure a resistor while the circuit is energized. Before measurement, electrical zeroing must first be performed, and zeroing must be repeated every time the range is changed. If zeroing cannot be achieved, it indicates that the battery voltage is low or the instrument has a fault. When measuring a high-resistance component, the hands must not touch the component or the conductive tips of the meter head, otherwise accuracy will be affected. The ranges of the ohmmeter are marked in the form of multipliers, for example ×1k; the actual resistance value equals the pointer indication multiplied by the multiplier corresponding to the changeover switch. The polarity of the internal battery in the ohmmeter section is opposite to the jack markings: the red test lead is connected to the negative terminal of the battery, and the black test lead is connected to the positive terminal of the battery.

A capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together with an insulating material between them; its characteristic is that it blocks direct current and passes alternating current. In circuit diagrams it is usually numbered with "C" plus a number, for example C25 is the capacitor numbered 25. The main performance indicators of a capacitor are capacitance, withstand voltage value and temperature withstand value; types include electrolytic capacitor, ceramic capacitor, chip capacitor, monolithic capacitor, tantalum capacitor and polyester capacitor; units include farad (F), microfarad (uF), nanofarad (nF) and picofarad (pF). The opposition encountered by an AC signal is called capacitive reactance, and the formula is Xc=1/(2πfC). Marine electrical equipment uses capacitors; an AC single-phase motor contains a capacitor, and an electric fan also contains a capacitor. The capacitor detection steps apply to the capacitor; the capacitor may develop a capacitor fault, and a capacitor fault belongs to the capacitor.

When using an analog multimeter to detect earth leakage, the leakage resistance value is between tens and several hundred megohms (except for electrolytic capacitors), the pointer cannot return to the infinity position, and the reading multiplied by the range is the leakage resistance. The larger the capacitance, the greater the amplitude of the pointer swinging to the right, and the slower the speed of swinging back. When an electrolytic capacitor is connected in the forward direction, the leakage current is relatively small; the end connected to the black test lead is the positive pole, and the polarity can be judged on this basis. Before measuring the resistance of the measuring circuit, if there is a capacitor in the circuit, it must be discharged first, so as to avoid damaging the instrument or affecting the measurement result.

For the negative temperature coefficient thermistor sensor commonly used on ships, the R×10 or R×100 range of a multimeter can be used to check its performance; insert it into hot water and observe how the resistance value changes with temperature. If the measured resistance is infinity, it indicates that the sensor is already open-circuited.

When identifying the type of transistor, observe the magnitude and direction of the deflection of the multimeter pointer. The content of observation covers abnormal phenomena, part status, conductor status and equipment operating parameters, specifically referring to whether parts are stuck or damaged, and whether conductors are loose, broken, abraded or burnt. Load short circuit or overload corresponds to measurement with a multimeter, and no-load power supply corresponds to switch on the power supply.

A multimeter is a multi-purpose instrument, and its basic structure consists of three parts: the meter head, the changeover switch and the measuring circuit. The meter head usually adopts a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument as the measuring mechanism, and the current flowing through the meter head at full scale is about several microamperes to several hundred microamperes. The meter head is the core measuring component of the multimeter, and the number of scales varies with the model; common models such as MF-30 have 4 scales, while MF-47 has 6 scales. The changeover switch is used to select the measurement object and range, and its positions are divided into five parts: the ohms region, the AC voltage region, the DC voltage region, and the DC current mA and μA regions. The measuring circuit, together with the meter head and the changeover switch, completes the measurement of various electrical quantities.

Multimeters are divided into two types: analog and digital. The MF-47 multimeter is a specific model of multimeter, the analog multimeter is one major category of multimeter, and the digital multimeter is another category.

When using a multimeter to measure resistance, at least one end of the resistor under test must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off. If there is a capacitor in the circuit, the capacitor should be discharged first before measuring resistance; never measure with power on. When measuring high-resistance components, the two hands must not touch the component or the conductive tips of the meter head, so as to avoid affecting accuracy. When using the ohms range to measure resistance, electrical zero adjustment must be performed again every time the range is changed; if zero adjustment cannot be achieved, it indicates that the battery voltage is low or there is a fault. Ohms range ranges are marked by multipliers, such as ×1k; the actual resistance value equals the pointer indication multiplied by the multiplier corresponding to the changeover switch, for example ×1, ×10, etc. Before carrying out resistance measurement, the test leads need to be shorted so that the meter head points to the zero position to complete zero adjustment.

A multimeter can be used to measure voltage. The maximum range of the MF-30 multimeter for measuring voltage is 500V, and the highest voltage that the MF-47 multimeter can measure is 2500V. When measuring a voltage higher than 1000V, the red test lead should be inserted into the 2500V jack. When measuring DC voltage, the two test leads of the multimeter must be connected in parallel across the power supply or the two ends of the component. DC voltage measurement steps: select the range -> connect the circuit under test -> read the reading; the reading needs to be obtained according to the position of the pointer on the corresponding scale line and the selected range. If the internal resistance r0 of the multimeter is not large enough compared with the resistor R under test, it will cause the equivalent resistance to decrease and the voltage measurement value to drop.

A multimeter can be used to measure current. The maximum range of the DC current range of a multimeter can reach 5A, such as the MF-47. When measuring DC current, the meter head must be connected in series in the circuit under test, with the red test lead connected to the positive terminal and the black test lead connected to the negative terminal. The clamp-on ammeter is also used to measure current. Unlike the multimeter, which requires breaking the circuit to connect, the clamp-on ammeter uses the principle of the through-type current transformer and can directly clamp and measure AC current without disconnecting the conductor.

A multimeter can be used to measure capacitance. The larger the capacitance, the greater the swing of the multimeter pointer to the right and the slower the return speed. Before measurement, if capacitance exists in the circuit, the capacitor must be discharged first before measurement. Capacitor measurement steps: earth leakage check -> capacitance test -> electrolytic capacitor polarity discrimination. The earth leakage check is performed using the multimeter resistance range R×1k or R×10k; during the earth leakage check of a normal capacitor, the pointer first deflects to zero and then slowly returns to infinity. If the pointer does not return to infinity, the reading multiplied by the range is the leakage resistance value. Generally, the leakage resistance of a capacitor is from several tens to several hundreds of megohms, except for electrolytic capacitors. When measuring capacitance, the two hands must not touch the conductive rods of the test probes so as not to affect accuracy. For an electrolytic capacitor, the leakage current is small when connected in the forward direction; when the end connected to the black test probe is the positive electrode, polarity can be discriminated on this basis. A capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together and separated by an insulating material in the middle; its characteristic is blocking direct current and passing alternating current, and in circuits it is generally represented by "C" plus a number, for example C25 represents the capacitor numbered 25. The obstructive effect of a capacitor on alternating current signals is called capacitive reactance, with the formula Xc=1/(2πfC), which is related to the signal frequency and capacitance.

A multimeter can be used to measure diodes. A diode has unidirectional conductivity; under forward voltage the conduction resistance is small, and under reverse voltage it is cut off. It is commonly used in rectification, isolation, voltage regulation and polarity protection circuits. According to function, it can be divided into rectifier diodes such as 1N4004, isolation diodes such as 1N4148, and Schottky diodes such as BAT85, and is commonly represented by VD in circuits. Diodes include light-emitting diodes and Zener diodes. Diode measurement steps: discriminate polarity -> discriminate performance; usually the R×100 or R×1k range is selected, the R×10k range may be used for high-power diodes, and other ranges are prohibited to prevent small-power diodes from being burned out or damaged by reverse breakdown. Polarity is discriminated based on the characteristic that the forward bias resistance is small and the reverse bias resistance is large; in an analog multimeter, the black test probe corresponds to the positive electrode of the battery, and the red test probe corresponds to the negative electrode.

The measurement with the smaller resistance is forward bias; at this time the black test probe is connected to the anode. The measurement with the larger resistance is reverse bias; at this time the red test probe is connected to the anode. When an analog multimeter is used to measure polarity, the black test probe is connected to the anode and the one with small resistance is forward bias, and the red test probe is connected to the cathode. When a digital multimeter is used to measure polarity, the red test probe is connected to the positive electrode and a displayed voltage value below 1V indicates the forward conduction state. The forward resistance of a silicon diode is several thousand to several tens of thousands of ohms, and the reverse resistance is several hundred thousand ohms or more; the forward resistance of a germanium diode is several hundred to several thousand ohms. If both forward and reverse resistances are extremely large, it indicates an internal open circuit; if both are extremely small or display 0, it indicates an internal short circuit breakdown. The R×10k range may be used to measure high-power diodes, but note that high voltage may cause reverse breakdown damage. The diode detection steps are applicable to diodes, and marine electrical equipment uses diodes.

A multimeter can be used to measure transistors.

A transistor contains two PN junctions internally and has current amplification capability. It is divided into NPN type and PNP type, and in circuits it is commonly represented by the letter "VT" plus a number, for example VT17 represents the transistor numbered 17. Main models include PNP types such as A92 and 9015, and NPN types such as A42, 9014 and 9018. The unidirectional conductivity of the PN junction is used to discriminate the transistor type: if a low resistance is measured with the red test probe connected to the base, it is PNP type; if a low resistance is measured with the black test probe connected to the base, it is NPN type. When discriminating the base of an NPN type, if the red test probe is connected to one pin and low resistance values are measured with the black test probe on the other two pins, then that pin is the base. When the hFE range is used to discriminate the e/c electrodes, the measurement with the larger hFE value corresponds to pins consistent with the polarity. For medium- and small-power silicon transistors of good performance, the forward resistance of the emitter junction and collector junction is several hundred to one thousand ohms, and the reverse resistance is several hundred thousand ohms or more. The faster the penetration current increases with temperature, the worse the transistor performance; the greater the pointer deflection, the larger the penetration current and the more unstable the performance.

A transistor may suffer a transistor fault; a transistor fault belongs to the transistor, and marine electrical equipment uses transistors.

This whole set of practices belongs to a sub-step of the first step of traditional fault diagnosis, "carrying out fault analysis while keeping the site intact." Distinguished by display mode, multimeters are divided into two types, analog and digital; the MF-47 multimeter belongs to the multimeter, the analog multimeter belongs to the multimeter, and the digital multimeter also belongs to the multimeter. Before measuring resistance, electrical zeroing is required, and zeroing must be repeated every time the range is changed; if zeroing cannot be achieved, it indicates low battery voltage or a fault. Current, as one of the quantities measured by electrical instruments, is used to understand equipment status; measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after breaking the circuit, and a clamp-on ammeter can likewise be used to measure current. Motor overcurrent is the direct cause of overheating in AC electric drive systems.

Diodes include light-emitting diodes and also include Zener diodes. The forward resistance of a germanium tube is several hundred to several thousand ohms. The measurable performance of a transistor includes tube type, base, collector, emitter and current amplification factor. The larger the pointer deflection, the larger the penetration current and the more unstable the performance. A transistor may suffer a transistor fault, and a transistor fault belongs to the device category of the transistor. Marine electrical equipment uses transistors; the operating characteristics of NPN and PNP types can complement each other, such as the complementary pair in an OTL circuit. A thyristor is also called SCR, also called a silicon controlled rectifier; a multimeter can be used to measure its polarity, inter-electrode resistance and control electrode.

Resistors include photoresistors and also include thermistors. A thermistor is a special semiconductor device whose resistance value changes with the surface temperature; the NTC negative temperature coefficient type is commonly used, that is, the resistance value decreases as the temperature rises, and it can be used for temperature compensation. Ships commonly use thermistor sensors with a negative temperature coefficient for temperature measurement; a thermistor sensor has a negative temperature coefficient characteristic, and its resistance value changes with temperature.

During inspection, the R×10 or R×100 range of a multimeter can be used to measure the resistance between the two leads; insert the sensor into hot water, and under normal conditions a change in resistance value can be observed; if the measured resistance is infinite, it indicates that the sensor is open-circuited; use the R×10k range of the multimeter to measure the resistance between the terminal post and the metal shell; if it is not infinite, the insulation is poor. The resistance temperature sensor is a resistance-type temperature sensor commonly used on ships; its resistance value increases as the temperature rises, and during normal operation the resistance value increases as the temperature rises; when checking performance, insert the sensor into hot water and measure the resistance between the two terminal posts, observing the change in resistance value; if the measured resistance value is infinite, it indicates that the resistance temperature sensor is in an open-circuit state; a sensor is an information acquisition device of a ship's monitoring and control system, divided into two major categories, analog and switching sensors; in the ship station antenna control platform, sensors are placed in the X-axis and Y-axis directions respectively, used to send error signals to control compensation motion when the ship pitches and rolls; analog sensors in the engine room monitoring and alarm system convert parameters into continuously changing electrical signals, suitable for scenarios where both equipment status is monitored and parameter values are displayed. The control platform includes sensors. In the generator no-load voltage high fault, an open circuit in the shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

Photosensitive devices include types such as photosensitive cells, photoresistors, photodiodes and phototransistors, and resistance changes, electromotive force and current can be measured. A photosensitive cell generates electromotive force or current when exposed to light, and can be detected with the DC mV/mA range of a multimeter; if it is zero, it indicates failure. When testing non-cell devices such as photoresistors, use the R×1k range of a multimeter to compare the resistance values in light and dark; if the resistance value of the photosensitive device does not change between light and dark, it has failed; if it is zero, it is a short circuit; if it is infinite, it is an open circuit. A photoresistor is a semiconductor element whose resistance value changes with the intensity of external light; the resistance is small in strong light and large in weak light; it is made by depositing a layer of cadmium sulfide (CdS) film on a ceramic substrate and belongs to semiconductor elements; in complete darkness the resistance value can reach several megohms or more, and under relatively strong light it can drop to several thousand ohms or even below 1kΩ. During detection, the R×1k range of a multimeter can be used to measure in light and dark places respectively; under normal conditions the resistance value changes significantly; if the measured resistance value does not change, it indicates failure; if both are zero, it indicates a short circuit; if both are infinite, it indicates an open circuit. The automatic fuel oil boiler includes a photoresistor; this photoresistor is used to detect the flame; when ignition succeeds, the resistance value of the photoresistor decreases, energizing 1JY, energizing 3JZ, energizing 4JZ; 4JZ (31, 28) opens, and the ignition transformer is de-energized.

When the meter head is at full scale, the current flowing through it is about a few microamperes to several hundred microamperes; the meter head of an analog multimeter usually adopts a high-sensitivity moving-coil instrument. The clamp-on ammeter is likewise used to measure current and, in combination with the multimeter, can meet the current measurement needs of different occasions. If zeroing cannot be achieved, it indicates that the battery voltage is low or a fault exists. The dial of the MF-47 analog multimeter has six scales, while common models such as the MF-30 have four scales.

When using a digital multimeter, the power switch must first be turned on; for models without an automatic power-off function, the power must be turned off after use. Digital multimeter operating steps: turn on the power -> select the measurement function -> connect the object under test -> read the value -> turn off the power, that is, operate item by item in this order.

When switching ranges, the test leads should be disconnected from the circuit under test; when replacing the battery or fuse, the POWER switch should be turned off and the test leads separated. The resistance range must not be used to measure current or voltage; do not connect a signal higher than the specified maximum test range; do not use the meter when the battery is not properly installed. Precautions for use and maintenance of the digital multimeter: do not casually disassemble or replace the internal wiring -> avoid strong impacts -> keep dry -> do not connect a signal higher than the specified maximum test range -> the resistance range must not be used to measure current or voltage -> do not use when the battery is not properly installed -> disconnect the test leads when switching ranges -> disconnect the power when replacing the battery or fuse. Specifically, it is forbidden to casually disassemble or replace the internal wiring; strong impacts should be avoided to prevent damage to the housing and internal parts; it must be kept dry and must not be wetted by rain;

During measurement, no signal higher than the specified maximum range may be connected; it is strictly forbidden to use the resistance range to directly measure current or voltage; it is forbidden to use the meter when the battery is not installed in place.

When using a multimeter to test capacitance, the leakage resistance measured by an analog multimeter for earth leakage is several tens to several hundred megohms, except for electrolytic capacitors. When a digital multimeter measures capacitance, the changeover switch needs to be turned to a suitable range, and the reading is relatively accurate only after it has stabilized. When testing an electrolytic capacitor for leakage, the value indication is first a relatively small resistance value, then slowly increases until infinity. A capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together and separated by an insulating material in between; its characteristic is to block direct current and pass alternating current, and in circuit diagrams it is usually denoted by the letter C plus a number, such as C25; diodes include types such as the light-emitting diode and the Zener diode. When testing a diode, the red test lead connects to the positive pole of the internal power supply and the black test lead is the negative pole, which is opposite to the polarity of the analog multimeter. The forward resistance of a germanium transistor is several hundred to several thousand ohms. Transistors are used in marine electrical equipment. The larger the pointer deflection, the larger the penetration current and the more unstable the performance.

When a digital multimeter tests the performance of an NPN transistor, the red test lead connects to the base and the black test lead connects to the emitter or collector; the displayed value for a silicon transistor is generally
0.5~
0.7V. When measuring the transistor hFE, insert the base into the B jack and insert the other two pins into the C and E jacks respectively, and take the larger value to determine the pin polarity.

A thermocouple is a temperature sensor with a simple structure and small thermal inertia; it detects the temperature level of the object under test by outputting a thermal electromotive force, can measure resistance and electromotive force, and its electromotive force increases as the temperature rises. Under normal conditions, the resistance between the two terminal posts is zero; if infinity is measured, it indicates that the hot end is open-circuited and has been damaged. When the hot-end temperature rises, the generated electromotive force or current value increases as the temperature rises. When the resistance between the terminal post and the metal housing is not infinity, it indicates that the internal insulating ceramic tube is broken, resulting in poor insulation.

The platinum-rhodium 10-platinum type (LB-3) has a measuring range of 0~+1300℃, and the permissible error is ±3℃ when ≤600℃; the tungsten-rhenium 5-tungsten-rhenium 20 type (WR) has a measuring range of 10~+2800℃, and the permissible error is 1t when >1000℃.

The fuse is a circuit protection component made of protective conductive material, featuring a low melting point and a certain mechanical strength; it is made of aluminum-tin alloy or aluminum-tin-antimony-bismuth alloy, etc., and is one of the commonly used components in electronic circuits, alongside the resistor and capacitance. When replacing the fuse of a digital multimeter, the power supply should be disconnected and a fuse matching the original model and specifications should be selected. The electric-type main engine remote control system contains fuses; in the main engine remote control system, fuse blowing is one of the common faults of electrical components.

In ship electrical maintenance, the insulation resistance tester is also customarily called a megohmmeter; the two refer to the same portable instrument, mainly used to measure and detect the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, electrical lines and cables, and the measured insulation resistance value is in megohms (MΩ). The main body of this instrument is composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, wherein the function of the hand-cranked generator is to provide the power supply, and the moving-coil ratio meter undertakes the task of measuring the insulation resistance; the two cooperate to complete the entire measurement process. The structural feature of the moving-coil ratio meter is that it uses electromagnetic force to generate the counter torque; the ratio meter structure is often adopted as the measuring mechanism of the insulation resistance tester, and it is the core measuring component of the instrument.

The hand-cranked generator is one of the main components of the portable insulation resistance tester and, together with the moving-coil ratio meter, constitutes the main body of the instrument; it generates a high DC voltage by hand cranking to measure the insulation resistance of electrical equipment.

According to the highest voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator, the insulation resistance tester is divided into specifications such as 100V, 200V, 500V, 1000V and 2500V; the higher the voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator, the higher the upper limit of the insulation resistance value that the insulation resistance tester can measure. When selecting, it is necessary to ensure that the highest voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator is higher than the rated working voltage of the object under test, while not damaging the object under test. When measuring equipment with a rated voltage of 500V and above, an insulation resistance tester of 1000~2500V specification should be selected; when measuring the winding of low-voltage equipment with a rated voltage of 500V and above, an insulation resistance tester of 1000~2500V should likewise be selected. When the insulation resistance of the marine motor winding is lower than 0.5MΩ, a 500V insulation resistance tester is required for detection and drying treatment; the insulation resistance between phases and to earth of the marine transformer is measured with a 500V tester and should be not less than

0.5MΩ.

The insulation resistance tester is provided with three terminal posts, namely L (line, connected to the conductor), E (earthing, connected to the casing or earth) and the guard terminal G (connected to the guard ring). When measuring the insulation resistance of a cable, the guard ring should be connected to the innermost insulation layer to eliminate errors. The marine cable contains an insulation layer, whose purpose is to electrically insulate the conductive core wires and prevent short circuit or earthing between core wires; in the marine cable structure it is located between the conductive copper core wire and the protective layer.

Before using the insulation resistance tester, an open-circuit test and a short-circuit test are required; during the open-circuit test, turn the handle clockwise at a speed of 120r/min so that the instrument pointer points to infinity, and during the short-circuit test the pointer should point to 0, with the speed usually being 120r/min. Before use, it is also necessary to observe whether the pointer points to infinity during the open-circuit test.

The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part status, conductor status, and equipment operating parameters, whether parts are seized or damaged, and whether conductors are loose, broken, abraded or burnt; observation is also the preceding step of checking the monitoring and indicating device, and only after observation is completed does the check of the monitoring and indicating device begin. The insulation resistance tester internally contains two measuring coils, the voltage circuit and the current circuit, and the accuracy of their relative positions must be checked; in the voltage circuit a potentiometer is connected in series as a regulator, used to adjust the pointer to the "∞" position error. The potentiometer has three pins, among which the resistance between two pins is fixed, and the resistance between the third pin and either pin changes with shaft rotation; the volume potentiometer on electronic equipment is such a component, generally considered manually adjustable; in automatic boiler combustion regulation, the potentiometer R1 driven by the pressure regulator YBD and the feedback potentiometer R10 form a bridge balance, and automatic oil-fired boilers contain such potentiometers.

When using an insulation resistance tester, improper wiring and operation will affect the measurement results and even endanger personal safety; improper operation is one of the fault causes of the ship power system, referring to equipment abnormality or system trip caused by human operating errors, with common manifestations including improper closing operation, unbalanced generator load control and improper operation caused by observation errors; during parallel operation, improper grasp of the closing moment or reversed adjustment direction of load sharing can cause the generator reverse power protection to trip, and improper operation can cause a single-phase earthing fault of the power system. It is strictly forbidden to use an insulation resistance tester on live equipment; before and after measuring large-capacity equipment, sufficient discharge is required to prevent electric shock. It is strictly forbidden to use an insulation resistance tester to measure the insulation resistance of low-voltage electrical equipment such as electronic equipment, instruments and sensors, so as to avoid breakdown of the electronic devices therein; it is likewise strictly forbidden to use an insulation resistance tester to test diodes, transistors and integrated circuits, so as to avoid high voltage breakdown of the electronic devices.

A diode has unidirectional conductivity, with small conduction resistance under forward voltage and cutoff under reverse voltage; by function it can be divided into rectifier diodes (such as 1N4004), isolation diodes (such as 1N4148) and Schottky diodes, etc., and is commonly denoted by VD in circuits; diodes include light-emitting diodes and Zener diodes. A transistor internally contains two PN junctions and has current amplification capability, and is divided into NPN type and PNP type, commonly denoted in circuits by the letter "VT" plus a number, such as VT17; main models include A92, 9015 (PNP type) and A42, 9014, 9018, etc. (NPN type). An integrated circuit has the advantages of small size, light weight, high reliability and stable performance, commonly in 14-pin or 16-pin packages, and is divided into CMOS circuits and TTL circuits; the pin numbers start from the notch or dot and are numbered counterclockwise, and for ease of maintenance and replacement a chip socket is often welded on the circuit board for direct plugging; common package forms include pins with inner hooks on four sides (PLCC), gull-wing pins on two sides (SOIC), dual in-line pins (DIP) and power integrated circuit packages.

Capacitors, diodes, transistors and integrated circuits are used in marine electrical equipment; a capacitor is composed of two metal films placed close together and separated by insulating material in the middle, its characteristic being to block direct current and pass alternating current, and it is generally denoted in circuits by "C" plus a number, such as C25 denoting the capacitor numbered 25; its hindering effect on alternating current signals is called capacitive reactance, with the formula Xc=1/(2πfC); main performance indicators include capacitance, withstand voltage value (maximum working voltage) and temperature resistance value; types include electrolytic capacitor, ceramic capacitor, chip capacitor, monolithic capacitor, tantalum capacitor and polyester capacitor; units include farad (F), microfarad (uF), nanofarad (nF) and picofarad (pF). The capacitor detection steps apply to capacitors; a capacitor fault may occur in a capacitor, and a capacitor fault belongs to the capacitor; the diode detection steps apply to diodes; a transistor fault may occur in a transistor, and a transistor fault belongs to the transistor.

AC single-phase motors and electric fans both contain capacitors. A sensor is an information acquisition device of the ship monitoring and control system, divided into two major categories: analog sensors and switching sensors. In the ship station antenna control platform, sensors are placed in the X-axis and Y-axis directions respectively, used to send error signals to control compensation motion when the ship pitches and rolls. The analog sensors in the engine room monitoring and alarm system convert parameters into continuously changing electrical signals, suitable for scenarios where both equipment status is monitored and parameter values are displayed; the control platform contains sensors.

Electrical quantities such as resistance, voltage, current and capacitance can be measured with a multimeter. A multimeter can measure the resistance value of a resistor, the voltage value of a voltage, the current value of a current, the capacitance value of a capacitor, and the relevant parameters of diodes and transistors; a clamp-on ammeter is used to measure current. When measuring a resistor in a measuring circuit, at least one end of the resistor under test must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off. If a capacitor exists in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring the resistor; never measure with power on. To measure current, an ammeter must be used, connected in series after breaking the circuit.

Undervoltage will cause the motor speed low after starting, failure to start, low speed during load operation, and excessive temperature or smoking of the motor; it will also cause difficulty in starting, reduced speed, excessive temperature rise or poor contactor pull-in of marine electrical equipment. When an electric fan starts slowly and its speed decreases, the possible cause is undervoltage of the power supply; when an electric drill rotates too slowly, the possible cause is undervoltage of the power supply, which needs to be checked and adjusted. A contactor contains a coil, which is made by winding a certain number of turns of insulated wire on an insulated bobbin and has the characteristic of passing DC and blocking AC. A KM coil fault is one of the direct causes of the contactor armature failing to close and the motor fails to start. The current coil of a wattmeter is connected in series between the power supply and the load to detect current, and the voltage coil is connected in parallel across the two ends of the circuit under test. In the fault of generator no-load voltage high, an open-circuit shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

The insulation resistance tester is a portable instrument composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, used to measure the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, lines and cables, and often adopts a ratio meter structure. The meter has three terminal posts, where L connects to the conductor, E connects to the casing or earth, and G is the guard terminal post, connected to the guard ring. Before use, an open-circuit test must be performed, and the pointer should point to ∞; then a short circuit test is performed, and the pointer should point to 0. The cranking speed is usually 120 r/min. When the scale error of the insulation resistance tester is large, the guide wire can be re-welded; by slightly lengthening or shortening the guide wire, the residual torque is used to change the scale characteristics. Welding is a process in which solder is melted by heating, atomic diffusion occurs between the weldment and the solder, and after solidification an alloy bonding layer with good electrical conductivity and mechanical strength is formed; welding quality directly affects the performance of electronic products.

For the fault of broken input wiring, the corresponding treatment is welding.

Steps for measuring the insulation resistance of a coil to earth in electrical equipment: cut off the power supply -> connect the terminal posts -> measure and read. The first step must be to cut off the power supply of the electrical equipment under test, then connect the terminal posts and measure and read. When connecting, the E end of the insulation resistance tester connects to the casing or core, and the L end connects to the coil conductor; when the phases of multi-phase equipment are not connected, the L end needs to be connected to each phase coil conductor one by one; coils not involved in the measurement can be earthed to avoid interference from induced voltage. Then crank the generator to the rated speed, and read the insulation resistance value after the pointer stabilizes. The core is a component of marine electrical equipment; when measuring the insulation resistance of a coil to earth, terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester can be connected to the core; the coil is also a component of marine electrical equipment, made by winding a certain number of turns of insulated wire on an insulated bobbin, and has the characteristic of passing DC and blocking AC.

Steps for measuring the insulation resistance of a line to earth: cut off the power supply -> connect the terminal posts -> turn the handle -> read the reading. In the first step, the power supply of the line to be tested must be cut off; terminal post L of the insulation resistance tester should be connected to the line to be tested; when measuring on board, terminal post E should be connected to the hull as the earthing end; then turn the generator of the insulation resistance tester until the rated speed is reached; after the pointer stabilizes, the indicated scale value is the insulation resistance value of the line to earth. Steps for measuring the insulation resistance between lines: cut off the power supply -> connect the terminal posts -> turn the handle -> read the reading. In the first step, the power supply of the line under test must likewise be cut off; terminal posts L and E of the insulation resistance tester are connected respectively to the two lines under test; turn the generator of the insulation resistance tester to the rated speed; after the pointer stabilizes, the indicated scale value is the insulation resistance value between the lines.

A multimeter can be used to measure the resistance value of a resistor, and can also be used to measure the voltage value of a voltage; a voltmeter is likewise used to measure voltage values.

Structure and principle of the clamp-on ammeter The clamp-on ammeter is a measuring instrument composed of a current transformer and an ammeter, and its working principle is based on a single-turn through-type current transformer. During measurement, the conductor under test passes through the core window of the transformer, acting as the primary winding, while the secondary winding of the transformer itself is connected to the ammeter. The current induced in the secondary winding drives the pointer to deflect, thereby indicating the value of the current under test. Since the conductor under test directly serves as the primary winding and participates in electromagnetic induction, there is no need to cut off the circuit under test during measurement; this is an important feature that distinguishes the clamp-on ammeter from ordinary ammeters.

The through-type current transformer is a type of current transformer; its primary winding has very few turns, and the conductor can even pass directly through the core to link with the magnetic circuit. When the number of primary winding turns is reduced to a certain extent, a dedicated primary winding need not be wound, and the current-carrying conductor can instead be passed directly through the core hole. Taking the HL-25 through-type transformer as an example, when the primary current I1 is 600A, the conductor only needs to pass through once; when I1 is 100A, a flexible wire can be passed through the transformer hole six times; when I1 is 150A, the conductor passes through four times. This practice of adapting to different current ranges by changing the number of passes is precisely the flexibility of the through-type structure.

A current transformer is used in a circuit to transform the current ratio, and its symbol is TA, that is, the current transformer corresponds to the symbol TA, and the standard current on the secondary side is usually 5A. By structure, it can be divided into coil type, busbar type and through-type, etc.; one end of the secondary side is required to be earthed, and during operation it is equivalent to a short circuit transformer; during operation, the secondary winding must strictly not be open-circuited. The current transformer contained in the clamp-on ammeter belongs to this through-type category; it combines the transformer and the ammeter in one unit, facilitating on-site measurement.

Method of using the clamp-on ammeter Method of using the clamp-on ammeter: wipe off oil dirt on the clamp jaw -> check the pointer zero position -> select the maximum range setting -> adjust to a suitable range -> clamp the conductor under test -> read the reading -> after measurement, turn the range switch to the maximum. In specific operation, first wipe off oil dirt on the clamp jaw and check the pointer zero position, adjusting the mechanical zero position if necessary. Before measurement, first select the maximum range setting for a trial measurement, then change to a suitable range according to the actual situation. During measurement, squeeze the trigger firmly to open the core, pass the conductor under test through the core gap, then release the trigger; when the core closes, the reading can be taken. To reduce errors, the conductor under test should be placed in the center of the magnetic core window (clamp jaw). After measurement, the range switch should be turned to the maximum setting.

The clamp-on ammeter can be used to detect the starting current of the motor; in this case the range must be greater than 7 times the rated current, and it can also be used to check the balance of the three-phase currents. Current is one of the basic quantities measured by electrical instruments, and its measuring tools include the multimeter, the ammeter and the clamp-on ammeter. An ordinary ammeter requires the circuit to be disconnected before being connected in series, whereas the clamp-on ammeter uses the principle of the through-type current transformer to directly clamp the conductor and measure the AC current without cutting off the circuit. Motor overcurrent is the direct cause of overheating of the AC electric drive system, and local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is also one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating; therefore, accurate measurement of current helps to understand the operating state of the equipment.

Association with fault diagnosis and the multimeter In the conventional fault diagnosis method, observation is an important step of the first stage. Interviewing the operator is the step preceding observation, that is, first learn from the operator about the conditions before and after the fault occurred, and then proceed to observation. The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, the state of parts, the state of conductors and the operating parameters of the equipment, specifically such as whether the parts are jammed or damaged, and whether the conductors are loose, broken, abraded or burnt. Observation is also the step preceding checking the monitoring and indicating device; only after observation is completed is the monitoring and indicating device further checked. This process helps to carry out fault analysis while keeping the site as it is.

The multimeter internally contains a changeover switch and a measuring circuit. The changeover switch is used to select the measurement object and the range, and the measuring circuit is responsible for converting different quantities and different ranges into signals measurable by the meter head. Among the three basic components of the MF-30 and MF-47 analog multimeters is the measuring circuit, because the magnetoelectric meter head can only pass a microampere-level current, and different quantities and ranges need to be measured through the conversion circuit. Both the multimeter and the clamp-on ammeter can be used to measure current, but the two are connected into the circuit in different ways. The changeover switch used for current measurement has a transition state when switching circuits, so as to ensure that the secondary side of the transformer is not left open.

The core is one of the component parts of marine electrical equipment. In the through-type current transformer, the large-current conductor under measurement is directly linked with the core to replace the primary winding; in the clamp-on ammeter, the core can be opened by squeezing the trigger, so as to pass through the conductor under measurement without cutting off the circuit. The contactor also contains a core. When measuring the insulation resistance of the coil of electrical equipment to ground, terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester can be connected to the core. In the coil-type current transformer, the primary winding is already wound on the core, whereas the busbar type has no such structure.

Basic composition and measuring principle of the wattmeter The wattmeter, also called the watt meter, is an instrument used to measure electric power. It consists of two parts, the current coil and the voltage coil, and calculates power by detecting the load current and voltage. In the measuring connection, the current coil is connected in series between the power supply and the load to detect the circuit current; the voltage coil is connected in parallel across the two ends of the circuit under measurement to detect the voltage. The wattmeter internally contains a current coil and a voltage coil, which work together and neither can be dispensed with.

The role of the current coil in the wattmeter is to detect the load current, and its connection mode is series, that is, connected in series between the power supply and the load. The branch in which the voltage coil is located has an additional resistor connected in series, and is then connected in parallel across the two ends of the circuit under measurement to detect the circuit voltage. The voltage range of the wattmeter is realized precisely by connecting additional resistors of different resistance values in series with the voltage coil. With different resistance values of the additional resistor, the proportion of voltage divided by the voltage coil branch differs, and thus the same meter head can correspond to multiple voltage ranges.

Both the current coil and the voltage coil are marked with corresponding terminals, usually indicated by the "*" symbol. During measurement, the currents of the two coils must flow in from the corresponding terminals at the same time or flow out from the corresponding terminals at the same time, so that the pointer deflects in the clockwise direction. If the corresponding terminals are connected in reverse during wiring, the pointer will deflect in the reverse direction and normal reading will be impossible. Therefore, before wiring, the "*" mark on the terminals should be identified first, and then the connection method on the power supply side and the load side should be determined according to the corresponding-terminal rule.

Multi-range wattmeter and D34-W wattmeter The multi-range wattmeter is a portable wattmeter and usually has two current ranges and two or three voltage ranges. The two current ranges are realized by connecting two completely identical current coils in series or in parallel: when the two coils are connected in series, the current range is smaller, and when connected in parallel, the current range is larger. The voltage ranges are realized by connecting additional resistors of different resistance values in series with the voltage coil.

All range terminals, the common terminal and the like-named terminals are all brought out and fixed on the terminal posts of the dial, so that the user can select different range combinations according to measurement needs. The scale of a multi-range wattmeter is marked only with the number of divisions and not with watt values, so when reading it is necessary to multiply by the division constant to obtain the power value. The division constant C equals the rated value of the voltage range divided by the rated value of the current range and then divided by the number of full-scale divisions.

The D34-W wattmeter is a portable multi-range wattmeter having two current ranges and three voltage ranges. Its rated currents are 0.25A and 0.5A, and its rated voltages are 25V, 50V and 100V. When the 0.25A and 100V ranges are selected, its power range is 25W; when the 0.5A and 25V ranges are selected, its power range is
1
2.5W.

This meter switches ranges by changing the two current coils from series to parallel connection by means of a connecting strip. Because it is a portable wattmeter, the D34-W wattmeter usually has multiple ranges rather than a single range. When using it, first select the range according to the approximate range of the current and voltage of the circuit under test, and then convert the reading according to the division constant corresponding to the selected range.

Wiring rules of the wattmeter and loss handling When wiring, the current terminal post of the wattmeter marked with "*" must be connected to one end of the power supply, and the other end to the load end; the voltage terminal post marked with "*" must be connected to the "*" end of the current terminal post. This rule ensures that the currents of the current coil and the voltage coil flow in simultaneously from the like-named terminals, so that the pointer deflects correctly. If the "*" end of the voltage terminal post is mistakenly connected to the other end of the current terminal post, the pointer will deflect in the reverse direction.

The power value measured by the wattmeter includes the power loss of the current coil itself; when accurate measurement is required, this loss should be subtracted from the reading. In addition, the reading of a multi-range wattmeter must be multiplied by the division constant C, where C equals the rated value of the voltage range divided by the rated value of the current range and then divided by the number of full-scale divisions. That is, first calculate the number of watts represented by each division from the rated value of the selected voltage range and the rated value of the current range, and then multiply the number of divisions deflected by the pointer by this constant to obtain the actual power value.

Measurement methods of active power in three-phase circuits Measurement methods of active power in three-phase circuits: one-wattmeter method -> two-wattmeter method -> three-wattmeter method; these three methods are respectively applicable to different three-phase circuit conditions. For a symmetrical three-phase circuit (three-wire or four-wire system), the one-wattmeter method can be used; after measuring the single-phase power, multiply by 3 to obtain the total power.

The two-wattmeter method is applicable to three-phase three-wire loads and can be used regardless of whether the load is symmetrical. The wiring principle of the two-wattmeter method is: the current coils of the two meters should be connected to two different phase lines, with the "*" ends connected to the power supply side; the like-named terminals of the voltage coils of each meter should be connected to the like-named terminals of their respective current coils. In the two-wattmeter method, the other ends of the voltage coils are all connected to the phase line that has no current coil, so that the voltage is the line voltage. Under normal conditions, the total power of the two-wattmeter method is the sum of the readings of the two meters, that is, P=P1+P2. When the load cosφ<0.5 (φ>60°), one meter must have a negative reading; in this case the current coil must be reversed and the difference taken for calculation. The three-wattmeter method is used for three-phase four-wire circuits, with one wattmeter connected to each phase, and the sum of the three readings is the total three-phase power.

The movable parts of the two units of the electrodynamic three-phase wattmeter are fixed on the same shaft, and the total torque is the algebraic sum of the torques of the two units.

The shaft, as a mechanical transmission component, is used to transmit torque and rotational motion, and is commonly found in motors, contactors and instruments. The changeover switch is composed of a contact system, an operating handle, a shaft and a panel, assembled by bolts.

Other instruments and components related to power measurement: the multimeter contains a measuring circuit, whose function is to convert different electrical quantities and different ranges. The multimeter uses measured quantities such as resistance, voltage and current for detection, wherein the measurable property of resistance is the resistance value, the measurable property of voltage is the voltage value, and the measurable property of current is the current value. The clamp-on ammeter likewise uses current for measurement. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after breaking the circuit. When measuring a resistor in a circuit, at least one end of the resistor under test must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off; if capacitance exists in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring the resistor, and never measure with power on.

When selecting a voltage transformer, the rated voltage ratio of the transformer should be selected according to the rated voltage of the voltage coil of the instrument used. A KM coil fault is one of the direct causes of the contactor armature failing to close and the motor fails to start. Local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of AC motors; the winding insulation of a marine motor must undergo "three-proof" treatment of moisture-proofing, mildew-proofing and salt-oil-mist-proofing, and be oil-resistant.

In a reverse power relay, if the voltage coil or current coil is burnt out, the relay will not function, i.e., the reverse power relay fails. Reverse power relay failure may be caused by a burnt-out current coil, and the coil must be checked and replaced. Failure to wire as required can also cause reverse power relay failure. In addition, in the generator no-load voltage high fault, an open shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

Voltage is one of the instrument readings to be checked in marine electrical fault diagnosis, and current is one of the electrical quantities measured by electrical instruments, used to understand equipment status.

In marine low-voltage power systems, the measuring circuit refers to the specific wiring and conversion circuits for voltage, current and power, and its basic function is to convert different electrical quantities and different ranges. For a multimeter, the measuring circuit is the internal circuit part used to convert different electrical quantities and ranges into signals measurable by the meter head; together with the changeover switch and the meter head, it constitutes the three basic components of an analog multimeter, and the MF-30 multimeter and MF-47 multimeter both belong to this category. Since a magnetoelectric meter head can only pass microampere-level current, a conversion circuit is necessary to measure different electrical quantities and ranges. A multimeter contains a changeover switch and also contains a measuring circuit; a multimeter uses voltage and also uses current. A clamp-on ammeter, on the other hand, contains a current transformer and uses current. A wattmeter, also called a power meter, is composed of a current coil and a voltage coil and is used to measure electrical power, wherein the current coil is connected in series between the power supply and the load to detect the circuit current, and the voltage coil is connected in parallel across the two ends of the circuit under test to detect voltage; the two coils are marked with corresponding terminals, and during measurement the current must flow in or out from the corresponding terminals simultaneously.

AC voltage measuring circuit: AC single-phase voltage measuring circuit -> AC three-phase voltage direct measuring circuit. This classification indicates that AC voltage measuring circuits are divided into two types, the AC single-phase voltage measuring circuit and the AC three-phase voltage direct measuring circuit, belonging to direct voltage measuring circuits, as distinct from indirect measuring circuits. Its wiring method is that the voltmeter is connected directly across any two phases of the line through the fuse FU for measurement. In a marine low-voltage three-phase three-wire system, the "single-phase voltage" measured by this circuit is essentially a line voltage. For a 380V line rated voltage, the range upper limit calculated according to specifications is 456V; for a 390～400V generator rated voltage, the range upper limit calculated according to specifications is 480V. Based on the above parameter requirements, a voltmeter with a 0～500V range should be selected for this circuit. In the AC three-phase voltage direct measuring circuit, phase B requires two pairs of contacts to be connected to the changeover switch. AC voltage measurement steps: select the range -> connect the circuit under test -> read the value, that is, first select an appropriate range, then connect the instrument to the circuit under test, and finally read the indicated value.

The fuse is used for overload and short circuit protection in the ship's power system, its symbol is FU, and it is a protective electrical appliance; when overload or short circuit occurs in the power network or electrical equipment, it automatically cuts off the circuit by melting the fuse element. It belongs to the distribution electrical appliances and has the characteristics of maintaining thermal stability and electrodynamic stability when a short circuit fault occurs. The RL93 series is of the screw type, voltage 380V, current 6~600A, used for circuit overload or short circuit protection. In the AC voltage measuring circuit, the voltmeter is connected directly across two phases of the line through FU. In circuit diagrams, FU serves as a protective element, and its graphical symbol is identified as FU; fuse blowing of FU is one of the causes of the contactor KM coil being de-energized and unable to close. The fuse corresponds to the symbol FU, and the MF-30 multimeter also falls within the scope of protective elements identified by FU.

The changeover switch on the main switchboard is mainly used to select indication and measurement points, set operating states and issue operating commands, and has the functions of selecting the measurement object and selecting the range. It is composed of a contact system, an operating handle, a shaft and a panel, assembled with bolts. The changeover switch used for current measurement has a transition state when switching circuits, so as to ensure that the secondary side of the transformer is not open-circuited. The LW95-15-LH2/2 changeover switch indicates the open and closed states of the contacts at different positions through a closing table. In the multimeter, the changeover switch positions are divided into five parts: the ohms region, the AC voltage region, the DC voltage region, the DC current mA and μA; when measuring resistance, the actual value equals the pointer indication multiplied by the multiplier corresponding to the changeover switch, such as ×1, ×10, etc.

The voltage transformer symbol is TV, its function is to transform the voltage ratio, the secondary side voltage is 100V, and its characteristic is that one end of the secondary side is earthed. The voltage transformer corresponds to TV. Its working principle is consistent with that of the transformer, but the internal resistance is extremely small, and the output voltage hardly changes with the load. When working, it is equivalent to a no-load transformer, the secondary side must strictly not be short-circuited, and a fuse must be installed on the primary side for short circuit protection. One end of the secondary side must be earthed to prevent high voltage breakdown from endangering safety, and the earthed end must correspond to the middle phase of the primary side, such as phase B.

The voltage ratios commonly used on the main switchboard are 380/110V and 440/110V, and the accuracy class is usually not lower than
0.5 class. The primary winding terminals are marked A and X, and the secondary winding is marked a and x, where A and a are the dotted terminals. TV has the nature of a voltage source, with extremely small internal resistance; when the load changes, the output voltage is almost unchanged and the phase shift is extremely small; when working, it is equivalent to a no-load transformer, and the secondary side must strictly not be short-circuited; the primary side terminals are denoted by A and X, the secondary side by a and x, and A and a are the dotted terminals; the secondary side standard voltage is usually 100V, and in a 440V, 60Hz system it is 110V; the earthed end of the secondary side must correspond to the middle phase of the primary side, that is, phase B, phase V or phase L2. In the ship's switchboard, the measured line voltage UCA is synthesized by vector addition of two TVs connected in a "V" shape. When selecting, the rated capacity should be not less than the power consumed by all measuring instruments, and the primary rated voltage should be equal to or slightly greater than the voltage of the line being measured.

The current transformer symbol is TA, its function is to transform the current ratio, the secondary side current is 5A, the types include the coil type, busbar type and through-type, and its characteristic is that one end of the secondary side is earthed. The current transformer corresponds to TA, and the through-type current transformer belongs to the current transformer. Its primary side terminals are denoted by L1 and L2, and the secondary side by K1 and K2. When working, it is equivalent to a short-circuited transformer, and during operation the secondary winding must strictly not be open-circuited. It has the nature of a current source, with extremely large internal resistance; when the load changes, the output current is almost unchanged. One end of the secondary side must be earthed to prevent high voltage on the primary side from breaking down the insulation and endangering personal safety. When the AC current exceeds the 5A range, it needs to be transformed through a current transformer for measurement. With the through-type structure, when the number of primary turns is reduced to a certain extent, the primary winding may be omitted and the conductor directly threaded through; the HL-25 type is threaded through only once at 600A, and at 100A a flexible wire can be threaded through six times.

The primary side of TA carries load current I, which is converted into secondary current and connected to an AC ammeter or other series current elements; the secondary side must never be open-circuited, the external ammeter terminals must have a short-circuit connecting piece, and it may only be opened after wiring has been checked; during operation it is equivalent to a short-circuit transformer, and to prevent high voltage from breaking down the insulation and endangering safety, one end of the secondary side must be earthed; the primary winding is divided into the coil type and the busbar type, the latter being the through-core type with no independent primary winding. Inside the circuit breaker, TA is used to provide current detection sampling, and the nameplate indicates the reference current I0 and the current ratio ITA; the current ratio is selected according to the rated current, for example when the generator rated current is 720A, the TA specification may be 800/5A.

In the AC current measuring circuit, the secondary side of the current transformer must never be open-circuited and must be connected in series. The interior of the AC ammeter is a low-resistance current element, with two non-polarized terminals brought out, so the connections may be exchanged. A terminal is a metal contact component used in electrical systems to connect conductors to equipment or circuit nodes, commonly found in PLC interfaces, instruments and control circuits; in the main engine remote control system, poor contact or corrosion of terminals is one of the common faults of electrical components; if the terminals of the thermal relay have poor contact, the heat generated by the contact resistance will cause an error in the operating value. The electric main engine remote control system contains terminals.

In the DC current measuring circuit, the shunt must be installed on the positive side of the power supply. DC ammeters of larger capacity require an external shunt to extend the range, with standard output voltages of 50mV and 75mV, of which 75mV is most commonly used, and the specification requires that it must be installed at the "+" pole position of the DC circuit. The shunt is a precision resistor element used to extend the range of a DC ammeter, connected in series in the measured circuit, often made of shunt manganin, whose resistance maximum-point temperature is higher than that of general-purpose manganin, and the resistance temperature coefficient of shunt manganin ranges from 0 to 40×10⁻⁶/℃. DC current measurement steps: select the range -> connect the measured circuit -> read, that is, first select a suitable range, then connect the instrument to the measured circuit, and finally read the indicated value. The DC ammeter uses a moving-coil instrument, with "+" and "-" polarity marked on the connections, and reversed connection will cause the pointer to deflect in reverse; the internal resistance of a DC ammeter is very small, so it must be connected in series in the measured circuit; the current range of the ammeter is usually 75mV, and the scale on the face directly displays the rated current value of the shunt; the specification requires that the shunt must be installed at the "+" pole position of the circuit.

The moving-coil instrument is an electrical instrument with high sensitivity, which can only pass microampere-level current. The connections are marked with "+" and "-" polarity, and if connected in reverse the pointer will deflect in reverse; DC applications of larger capacity require an external shunt, and the commonly used shunt output voltage is 75mV;

In AC current measurement, a moving-coil instrument structure with a transmitter is now also used. When the moving-coil instrument is at full scale, the current flowing through its meter head is about several microamperes to several hundred microamperes, and it is usually used as a high-sensitivity meter head in analog multimeters such as MF-30 and MF-47. The electromagnetic instrument is an electrical instrument used to measure AC current; in the past it was often used for AC current measurement, and now it is mostly replaced by the moving-coil instrument with a transmitter; as an AC ammeter, its interior is a current element with very low internal resistance; two terminals are brought out, with no polarity, so the connections may be exchanged; it is usually made in standard 1A and 5A ranges, and domestically the 5A range is generally used. Current is one of the quantities measured by electrical instruments, used to understand equipment status; measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after breaking the circuit; motor overcurrent is the direct cause of overheating in AC electric drive systems.

The control transformer is used to supply power to the control circuit, and its characteristic is isolation from the main circuit. Its capacity is expressed in VA or kVA, i.e. apparent power; the secondary rated current is limited by the selected capacity and has nothing to do with the active or reactive nature of the current;

So that an insulation fault in the control circuit does not affect the main circuit; it is used in the main switchboard for the main circuit to provide operating power or voltage signals to the control circuit. The main switchboard is the control center for the concentration and distribution of electrical energy in the power station; the ship power station contains the main switchboard, the main switchboard contains the main switch, and also contains the switchboard-type insulation resistance meter. The main circuit provides operating power or voltage signals to the relevant control circuits through the control transformer, achieving electrical isolation. The voltage transformer ratios frequently used in the main switchboard have two specifications, 380/110V and 440/110V. The main switchboard has the functions of making and breaking circuits, protection and alarm, parameter detection and power adjustment; its main functions include making or breaking circuits, protection devices operating and giving alarms, detecting and displaying various electrical parameters, and being able to regulate the voltage and frequency of the power station and the active and reactive power of generator sets operating in parallel.

On the main switchboard, the changeover switch undertakes the tasks of selecting indication and measurement points, setting operating states and issuing operating commands.

When working, it is equivalent to a no-load transformer, and the secondary side must strictly not be short-circuited. The standard current of the secondary side of the current transformer is 5A or 1A. The clamp-on ammeter contains a current transformer and uses this principle to measure current, allowing AC current to be measured by directly clamping the conductor without disconnecting it.

In the coil-type current transformer, the primary winding is already wound on the core, whereas the busbar type has no such structure. The core is the magnetic conductive component in electromagnetic equipment, used to form the magnetic circuit, support the coil, and serve as the reference point for insulation measurement; when measuring the insulation resistance of the coil of electrical equipment to ground, terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester can be connected to the core; in the through-type current transformer, the large current conductor under test is directly linked with the core to replace the primary winding. The insulation resistance tester internally contains two measuring coils, the voltage circuit and the current circuit, and their relative positions must be checked for accuracy.
