Fuses are made of protective conductive material and have the characteristics of a low melting point and a certain mechanical strength; the material is aluminum-tin alloy or aluminum-tin-antimony-bismuth alloy, etc.; in the main engine remote control system, fuse blowing is one of the common faults of electrical components.

A diode has unidirectional conductivity and is commonly denoted VD in circuits, and is used for rectification, isolation, voltage stabilization, etc. Its main characteristic is unidirectional conductivity: under forward voltage the conduction resistance is small, and under reverse voltage the resistance is extremely large or infinite. According to function, it is divided into rectifier diodes (such as 1N4004), isolation diodes (such as 1N4148), Schottky diodes (such as BAT85), etc. Diodes include light-emitting diodes and Zener diodes. A light-emitting diode can emit red, green and yellow light, has unidirectional conductivity, and its circuit symbol has two more arrows than an ordinary diode; it is commonly used as a circuit working status indicator or to form a large-screen color electronic display screen; its external dimensions include diameters of 3mm, 5mm and 2mm×5mm rectangular; the working current is generally 1～30mA depending on the model, and in actual use a current-limiting resistor must be connected in series to prevent damage; the conduction voltage is
above 1.7V.

For light-emitting diodes, attention must be paid to the precautions for using light-emitting diodes. The diode testing steps apply to diodes. The multimeter is used to measure voltage and diodes; marine electrical equipment uses diodes. Voltage is one of the instrument readings to be checked in ship electrical fault diagnosis; the generator failing to build up voltage is an optional top event when constructing a fault tree; overvoltage is one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems.

The conventional fault diagnosis method uses observation. Interviewing the operator is the step preceding observation. Observation is a sub-step of the first step of conventional fault diagnosis, "carry out fault analysis while keeping the site unchanged"; the content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part condition, wire condition and equipment operating parameters, specifically including whether parts are jammed or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, abraded or burnt. Observation is the step preceding checking the monitoring and indicating device.

The input interface, together with the CPU and memory, forms the basic structure of the PLC. The input/output interface circuit is the channel through which the CPU exchanges information with the outside, and is easily damaged by external equipment faults. When the X400/X401 indicator lamps are off and the voltage across both ends is normal, it is determined to be an input interface processing circuit fault and replacement is required; if the voltage measured after removing the wiring is still abnormal, it indicates an input interface processing circuit fault and the input interface circuit must be replaced. If all PLC inputs are abnormal and wiring problems have been ruled out, it is usually determined to be an input interface circuit fault and replacement is required; this step belongs to the end of the troubleshooting flow of first checking the external wiring and load, then checking the PLC internal circuit.

One of the common fault symptoms of the PLC control system is that a certain input relay cannot be energized; its possible fault causes include input signal source (device) fault, input wiring break, loose input terminal or poor contact of the input terminal, input on-time too short, and input circuit fault. When the fault cause is an input signal source (device) fault, the corresponding treatment method is to replace the input device, that is, to perform the maintenance procedure of replacing the input device. The PLC control system may also exhibit random output actions; PLC supply voltage too low is one of the common fault causes of this phenomenon, and the corresponding treatment method is to adjust the power supply output.

In addition, the PLC control system may suffer faults such as POWER lamp off, fuse blowing repeatedly, RUN lamp off, all inputs failing to energize, and all PLC inputs abnormal. When the POWER lamp is off and the fuse is not blown, check whether the light-emitting diode is broken down; if so, replace the light-emitting diode.

Detection and replacement of semiconductor devices is common content in PLC maintenance. A transistor contains two PN junctions internally and has current amplification capability; it is divided into NPN type and PNP type, and is commonly denoted in circuits by "VT" plus a number, e.g., VT17 denotes transistor No. 17. Main models include PNP types such as A92 and 9015, and NPN types such as A42, 9014 and 9018. A transistor may suffer a transistor fault, and a transistor fault belongs to the device category of transistor. A thyristor is also called SCR, also known as a silicon controlled rectifier; its measurable performance includes polarity, inter-electrode resistance and control electrode. Marine electrical equipment widely uses diodes and transistors.

The fuse corresponds to the symbol FU and has overload protection and short circuit protection functions; it is a protective device that, when the power grid or electrical equipment suffers overload and short circuit, automatically cuts off the circuit by melting the fuse element. It belongs to distribution apparatus and has the characteristics of maintaining thermal stability and dynamic stability when a short circuit fault occurs. The RL93 series is of the screw type, voltage 380V, current 6~600A, used for circuit overload or short circuit protection.

Contactor-type faults are likewise closely related to the PLC control circuit. Power supply voltage too low or fluctuating greatly, insufficient capacity of the operating power supply, short circuit inside the coil, jamming of moving parts, excessive spring reaction force, rusted or skewed shaft, rated voltage of the coil higher than the rated voltage of the line, and too large contact gap, i.e., too large armature air gap, will all cause the contactor to fail to pick up or have insufficient holding force with a buzzing sound when the start button is pressed. Failure or deficiency of the armature reaction spring, contact fusion welding, jamming of moving parts, rusted or skewed shaft, and oil sludge adhering to the core pole face will all cause the contactor not to release or to release slowly when the stop button is pressed.

The interior of the PLC adopts a bus-type structure to complete the transmission of data and instructions; once the bus fails, the impact often spreads to the entire input/output channel. On the input side, a CPU bus fault is one of the causes of abnormal actions of relays numbered in units of 8 points; when such regular abnormalities occur, the treatment measure of replacing the CPU unit should be taken for the CPU bus fault. Another clue in parallel with this is a loose "COM" screw, which likewise causes abnormal actions of relays numbered in units of 8 points; the treatment is to tighten the loose "COM" screw. Loose screws in a broader scope will also cause the shunt trip unit to fail to trip the circuit breaker, and the corresponding treatment is likewise to tighten the screw.

Random input action is a relatively common type of abnormality in PLC control systems, and its causes fall into three parallel paths. Too low an input signal level is the primary fault cause of random input action; when troubleshooting, check the power supply and input devices. Poor input contact is one of the main causes of random input action, and terminal wiring needs to be checked. Excessive input noise is one of the three major causes of random input action, and the elimination measure is to add shielding or filtering measures. These three items are listed in sequence in the fault list, with poor input contact located after too low an input signal level and before excessive input noise. Poor input contact means that the input signal cannot be transmitted stably due to a contact problem; together with too low an input signal level and excessive input noise, it constitutes the complete set of causes of random input action. A similar situation exists on the output side: poor contact will cause random output action, and terminal wiring must likewise be checked during handling; if input noise is too large, shielding or filtering measures need to be added, and when output circuit noise is too large, shielding or filtering measures are also adopted.

A certain input relay being normally closed is another type of fault symptom occurring in PLC control systems; its direct cause is determined to be an input circuit fault, and the handling method is to check the circuit or replace the relevant components. In the troubleshooting table, this symptom is listed alongside items such as broken input wiring and loose terminals, with input circuit fault listed as item 5. Input circuit fault belongs to problems at the input circuit level and is distinguished from broken wiring or loose terminals; it may cause a certain input relay to be normally closed and may also cause random input action, and the corresponding maintenance procedure is to check the circuit or replace, that is, to check the faulty circuit or directly replace the damaged component.

On the input side there are also several fault causes that will cause a certain input relay to fail to pick up, each corresponding to a different handling method. Broken input wiring will cause a certain input relay to fail to pick up, and the handling measure is welding; welding is heating the solder to melt it, producing atomic diffusion between the workpiece and the solder, and after solidification forming an alloy bonding layer at their interface, which has good electrical conductivity and mechanical strength.

Loose input terminals or poor input terminal contact will likewise cause a certain input relay to fail to pick up, and the corresponding elimination method is to perform a reconnect operation; this is listed alongside broken input wiring and too short an input ON time as common input-side faults. Too short an input ON time will also cause a certain input relay to fail to pick up, and the corresponding handling measure is to adjust the relevant parameters, which belongs to the parameter correction step in input circuit troubleshooting. When an input circuit fault causes a certain input relay to fail to pick up, perform check the circuit or replace. In addition, poor input terminal contact will cause the POWER lamp to go out, and the handling method is reconnect; this is listed alongside loose input terminals, and both belong to input-side connection faults. Power supply fault corresponds to check the power supply. When the PLC power supply terminals have no output voltage, the operation of checking the terminal wiring should be performed.

When the indicator lamp state is inconsistent with the actual relay action, the problem mostly lies in the indicating element itself. When the phenomenon of correct input relay action but the indicator lamp being out occurs in a PLC control system, its direct cause is LED damage, and the handling method is to replace the LED. The same applies on the output side: LED damage will cause normal output relay action but the indicator lamp being out, and the LED likewise needs to be replaced; this step is the direct measure for solving relay status indication failure.

On the output circuit side, poor contact (terminal block) corresponds to reconnect, poor output terminal contact corresponds to reconnect, and poor contact of the terminal connection block also corresponds to reconnect. Poor contact of the output terminal block will cause all outputs to fail to connect, and the handling method is reconnect; poor output terminal contact will cause a certain output relay to fail to pick up, and the handling method is likewise reconnect. An I/O bus fault in the CPU will cause poor terminal connection contact, and the handling method is reconnect; when all inputs fail to connect and the cause is loose terminal contacts, reconnect is also adopted, and loose terminal contacts correspond to reconnect.

In the automatic control of the diesel generator set, output terminal 20 energizes and actuates the coil of the run-signal intermediate relay K₂, and during automatic starting, output terminal 18 outputs a start command to energize the coil of the start-output intermediate relay K₃.

Diagnosing output faults cannot be separated from checking voltage and current. The voltage value can be measured with a multimeter or voltmeter, and the current value can be measured with a multimeter, ammeter or clamp-on ammeter, among which the clamp-on ammeter is used for current measurement. Measuring current requires an ammeter, which is connected in series after the circuit is disconnected. A fuse blown will cause the POWER lamp of the PLC to go out, and the treatment method at this time is to replace the fuse. The causes of the fuse blowing repeatedly include load short circuit, overload, incorrect input voltage setting or too small capacity. From the manifestation at the time of fuse blowing, under overload current the fuse blowing noise is not loud, the fuse element is broken at only one or two places, and there is no scorching or large amount of vapor adhesion inside the tube; at the breaking limit current, that is, during a short circuit, the noise is loud, there is firelight, the fuse element is broken into multiple sections, and the tube wall has vapor or scorching. Replacing the fuse should generally be carried out with the fuse removed under the condition of no power; if live replacement is permitted, the load must first be cut off to prevent danger; before replacing with a new fuse element, the slag, soot and dust on the inner surface of the tube and on the contact surfaces must be carefully wiped clean.

When the PLC control system has outputs that all cannot be switched on, one of the causes is that no load power supply is applied, and the corresponding treatment is to switch on the power supply; a bad load power supply or too low voltage can also cause this phenomenon, and the power supply needs to be adjusted or repaired; poor contact (terminal block) can likewise cause outputs that all cannot be switched on, and the treatment method for this cause is to reconnect; a fuse blown in the power supply is one of the causes of this fault, and the fuse needs to be replaced; an output circuit (circuit) fault can also cause this phenomenon, and the treatment measure is to replace the output interface circuit. When the PLC control system has outputs that all cannot be switched off, the direct cause is an output interface circuit fault, and the treatment method is likewise to replace the output interface circuit; this phenomenon is distinguished from the local fault in which a certain output relay cannot be switched off.

For faults of a single output relay, it is necessary to distinguish according to the indicator lamp state. When a certain output relay of the PLC control system cannot be switched on and the indicator lamp is out, the possible cause is that the output on-time is too short, or it may be an output circuit fault; if it is due to too short on-time, the treatment measure is to modify the output program, and if it is due to an output circuit fault, then replace the output interface circuit. When a certain output relay of the PLC control system cannot be switched on and the indicator lamp is lit, it may be caused by damage to the output relay, and the relay needs to be replaced; it may be caused by a broken output wiring, and the wire needs to be soldered or the wiring replaced; it may be caused by poor contact of the output terminal, and the treatment measure is to reconnect; it may also be caused by an output drive circuit fault, and the output interface circuit needs to be replaced. A broken output wiring is distinguished from poor contact and drive circuit fault: the former requires soldering the wire or replacing the wiring, poor contact requires reconnecting, and a drive circuit fault requires replacing the interface circuit. It may also be caused by excessive leakage current of the output drive transistor, and the treatment is to replace the output transistor; this situation is distinguished from the drive circuit fault or program address duplication fault when the indicator lamp is lit. It may also be caused by duplication of the port address in the output instruction, and the program needs to be modified;

This situation is distinguished from the case in which it cannot be switched off but the indicator lamp is out, the latter being mostly relay damage or drive transistor leakage.

At the maintenance operation level, reconnecting is used to handle various terminal-type faults: when the input terminal is loose or the input terminal has poor contact, the treatment method is to reconnect; when the POWER lamp is out and the cause is poor contact of the input terminal, the treatment method is to reconnect; when inputs all cannot be switched on and the cause is a loose terminal contact, the treatment method is to reconnect. Modifying the program is used to solve faults caused by program logic errors, address conflicts or missing instructions: when the RUN lamp is out and the cause is that there is no END indication in the program, the treatment method is to modify the program; when a certain output relay cannot be switched off while the indicator lamp is lit and the cause is duplication of the port address in the output instruction, the treatment method is to modify the program;

When a certain output relay cannot be energized and the indicator lamp is off, and the cause is that the output ON time is too short, the handling method is to modify the output program.

The internal data and instruction transmission of the PLC is accomplished by means of a bus-type structure; once a fault occurs in the bus, both the input relays and the output relays may act abnormally. On the output side, an I/O bus fault in the CPU is one of the causes of abnormal actions of the output relays; its manifestation is listed alongside loose "COM" screws, fuse blown, and poor terminal connection contact, all of which cause the numbers of the abnormally acting relays to follow the pattern of 8 units; for an I/O bus fault in the CPU, the corresponding maintenance measure is to replace the CPU module. Poor contact of the terminal connection block likewise causes the numbers of the abnormally acting relays to be 8 units, and the handling method is to reconnect. When the number of the abnormally acting relay is 8 units, if it is ascertained that the cause is a loose "COM" screw, retightening should be performed; if it is ascertained that the cause is fuse blown, the fuse should be replaced.

Random output action is a relatively common fault symptom in PLC control systems; too low PLC supply voltage, poor contact, and excessive input noise can all cause random output action. The handling method corresponding to too low PLC supply voltage is to adjust the power supply output, and this step is also one of the first troubleshooting measures for dealing with the random output action problem. The handling method corresponding to poor contact is to check the terminal wiring. The measure corresponding to excessive input noise is to add shielding or filtering measures; this measure is used both to solve random input action caused by excessive input signal noise and to solve random output action caused by excessive noise in the output circuit. In addition, a loose "COM" screw causes abnormal action with the relay number being 8 units, and fuse blown may also cause random output action; the former requires retightening, and the latter requires replacing the fuse.

When none of the outputs can be energized, one of the causes is fuse blown in the power supply, in which case the fuse should be replaced to restore the circuit; if the cause is poor contact of the output terminal block, the handling method is to reconnect. When a certain output relay cannot be energized and this is caused by poor contact of the output terminal, reconnection is likewise adopted. Similar situations exist on the input side: when the input relay operates correctly but the indicator lamp is off, it is judged as LED damage, and the LED likewise needs to be replaced; this step is the direct measure for solving failure of the relay status indication.

One of the possible causes of the POWER lamp being off is fuse blown in the input circuit, in which case the handling method is to replace the fuse; when none of the inputs can be energized and this is caused by loose terminal contacts, the handling method is also to reconnect. Loose input terminals or poor contact of the input terminals corresponds to reconnection, while poor input contact corresponds to checking the terminal wiring. Excessive input noise corresponds to adding shielding or filtering measures. When abnormal action is caused by a loose "COM" screw of the input/output module, tightening should be performed. A loose screw can also cause the shunt trip unit to fail to trip the circuit breaker, and the corresponding handling method is to tighten the screw.

Faults on the input side of the PLC are often reflected first by the indicator lamp status. When the POWER lamp is off, the three causes of fuse blown, poor contact of the input terminals, and broken input power supply wiring can be considered in turn; all of them will cause the POWER lamp to be off. Among them, fuse blown corresponds to the handling method of replacing the fuse, poor contact of the input terminals corresponds to the handling method of reconnecting, and broken input power supply wiring corresponds to the handling method of replacing the wiring. Broken input power supply wiring will also cause the contactor to fail to pick up; at this time there is no voltage across the two ends of the coil, and the circuit must be checked to eliminate the broken wiring. The environmental conditions on board ship are harsh, and wire terminals and terminals are prone to rusting, thereby causing poor contact in the PLC input and output circuits; loose fastening screws and wire terminals will likewise cause poor contact, increasing the contact resistance and thereby possibly causing faults such as local overheating, phase failure, and short circuit between phases.

Troubleshooting a POWER light that is off also involves the link of power supply fault. In a microcomputer monitoring system, a power supply fault in an integrated circuit chip on the circuit board can cause the system to shut down completely with no fault information output.

A RUN light that is off is another typical manifestation. For the fault caused by no END indication in the program, the handling method is to modify the program and add the END indication; for the RUN light being off caused by a power supply fault, the handling method is to check the power supply; for the fault caused by duplicate I/O port addresses, the handling method is to modify the port addresses.

For the phenomenon that none of the inputs can be connected, the fault causes include no power supplied to the input signal source, input signal source power supply voltage too low, terminal contact loose, and terminal board poor contact.

When no power is supplied to the input signal source, the relevant power supply should be connected; when the input signal source power supply voltage is too low, the power supply voltage should be adjusted to meet the requirements; when the terminal contact is loose, the terminal should be reconnected; when the terminal board has poor contact, it should be handled and then reconnected. Input signal source power supply voltage too low, together with no power supplied to the input signal source and terminal contact loose, constitutes the causes of input failure; it means the power supply voltage of the input signal source is lower than the specified value. Power supply voltage too low also manifests in other situations: in a circuit breaker, power supply voltage too low makes the electromagnetic force generated by the shunt trip unit coil insufficient, and the circuit breaker cannot break; when a DC motor starts, power supply voltage too low makes the starting torque less than the load torque, causing the motor to stall and fail to start.

All PLC inputs abnormal is listed separately among common faults; its root cause is a fault in the PLC input interface circuit, and the handling method is to directly replace the input interface circuit. The input terminal cooperates with the COM terminal to form the interface of the input circuit; the diesel generator set controller receives fault signals through input terminals of specific numbers, and the overspeed fault signal is input from terminal 10 of the controller to execute immediate shutdown. In addition, COM screw loose, input circuit fault, poor contact (terminal strip), input wiring broken, load power supply bad or voltage too low, and terminal connection strip poor contact are also fault causes on the input side that need to be checked. Among them, input circuit fault and input wiring broken both belong to faults in the input circuit and wiring, and should be checked together with the terminal wiring and line continuity during inspection.

Fuse blowing repeatedly is another fault manifestation in the PLC control system. Load short circuit or overload, incorrect input voltage setting, and fuse capacity too small all cause fuse blowing repeatedly. For load short circuit or overload, use a multimeter to measure and troubleshoot during handling; for incorrect input voltage setting, reconnect correctly; for fuse capacity too small, replace with a larger-capacity fuse. Load short circuit not only causes fuse blowing repeatedly but also causes contactor contact welding; when handling contact welding, the load short circuit fault must be eliminated first before replacing the contact. Fuse blown itself is one of the possible causes of the POWER light being off in the PLC system and also one of the possible causes of all PLC outputs failing to be connected; when the PLC operates abnormally and the relay number is 8 units, the possible cause is likewise fuse blown.

Troubleshooting the above fault symptoms cannot be done without a multimeter. A multimeter is a multi-purpose instrument; it consists of three parts: the meter head, the changeover switch and the measuring circuit, and the current flowing through the meter head at full scale is about a few microamperes to several hundred microamperes. Distinguished by display mode, the analog multimeter is a multimeter, and the digital multimeter is also a multimeter. The MF-47 multimeter is one type of multimeter; it can measure a maximum voltage of 2500V and a maximum DC current of 5A, and its panel has four jacks: "+", "-", "2500V" and "5A". A multimeter can be used to measure resistor, voltage, current, capacitance, diode, transistor, thyristor, photosensitive device, thermocouple, etc. In PLC maintenance, troubleshooting of load short circuit or overload requires measurement with a multimeter, and handling of repeated fuse blowing likewise requires measurement with a multimeter to find the cause.

Fault handling on the output side also has corresponding steps. When the output is abnormal, the output interface circuit can be replaced, and the output program modified if necessary; where a relay is damaged, the relay should be replaced; where an output transistor is damaged, the output transistor should be replaced; where the output port circuit is damaged, the output port circuit should be replaced; where wiring is broken or loosely connected, the wire should be soldered or replaced. When the thermal relay malfunctions, it can be adjusted or repaired. These handling steps, together with the input-side steps of replacing wiring, reconnecting correctly, changing to a larger-capacity fuse, modifying the port address, connecting the relevant power supply, adjusting the power supply voltage to meet requirements, and reconnecting after handling, constitute the specific operations for different fault symptoms in PLC maintenance.

Composition and operating environment of marine motors Marine motors are the core power equipment in the ship's electric drive system, and their scope is relatively wide; classified by function and structure, they include main types such as marine asynchronous motors, marine DC motors and AC single-phase motors. Besides these complete machines, marine motors structurally also include key components such as bearings, windings, commutators, brushes and shafts, and the condition of these components directly determines whether the motor can operate reliably.

The marine environment is characterized by high humidity, salt spray, vibration and narrow installation space; marine motors operate under such harsh conditions, and therefore special requirements are placed on insulation performance, mechanical structure and electrical performance. Chinese standards stipulate that the ambient temperature for marine electrical equipment is 45℃, and require that it can work normally under conditions of 95% relative air humidity. To adapt to this environment, winding insulation must undergo "three-proof" treatment against moisture, mold and salt-oil mist, and must also have oil resistance.

Matching relationship of marine transformers Also belonging to the category of marine electrical equipment together with marine motors are marine transformers. Transformers commonly used on ships include three-phase, single-phase and special-purpose types, and their structural forms are mostly dry-type, air-cooled and waterproof. Among them, transformers used to supply loads such as lighting and electric heating are mostly three-phase transformers with relatively large capacity. Marine transformers and marine motors cooperate with each other in the ship's power grid to jointly ensure the power supply and drive requirements of various loads.

Routine maintenance items of marine motors The maintenance work of marine motors includes several aspects, which can be summarized as general cleaning, working environment inspection, bearing maintenance, power supply voltage monitoring, armature current monitoring, temperature rise monitoring, operating sound listening and commutation spark monitoring.

General cleaning aims to keep the inside and outside of the motor clean and prevent the accumulation of dust, oil dirt and salt mist from affecting heat dissipation and insulation. The working environment check focuses on whether there is abnormal dampness, corrosive gas or debris hindering ventilation around the motor. Bearing maintenance carries out regular treatment of the lubrication and wear condition of the bearing to ensure stable operation of the shaft. Power supply voltage monitoring requires attention to whether the supply voltage is within the allowable range, avoiding damage to the winding caused by abnormal voltage. Armature current monitoring is used to grasp the magnitude of the current in the armature circuit and prevent overload operation. Temperature rise monitoring determines whether the temperature of each part of the motor exceeds the allowable limit by detecting it. Running sound listening uses hearing to distinguish whether there is abnormal sound during motor operation, so as to discover mechanical or electromagnetic hidden dangers early. Commutation spark monitoring targets the working state of the commutator and brush of the DC motor and observes whether the spark grade is within the normal range.

The above maintenance items are interrelated and together constitute the basic content of daily inspection and repair of marine motors. Marine asynchronous motors, marine DC motors and AC single-phase motors all need to cover these items during maintenance, and the inspection and upkeep of components such as the bearing, winding, commutator, brush and shaft run through all the monitoring and maintenance work.

Basic requirements for marine motors Marine motors are a class of equipment that operates in the harsh environments of ships such as high marine humidity, salt mist, vibration and narrow spaces, and have special requirements for insulation, mechanical structure and electrical performance. According to the provisions of Chinese standards, the ambient temperature of marine motors is considered as 45°C, and they must maintain normal operation under the condition of air relative humidity reaching 95%. This humidity condition imposes requirements on the insulation system of the motor far higher than those for land-use products; therefore, the winding insulation of marine motors must undergo "three-proof" treatment of moisture proofing, mildew proofing and salt-oil-mist proofing, and must also have oil resistance. The winding is the coil component wound from enameled wire in a motor or transformer, which undertakes the function of generating a magnetic field or inducing an electromotive force, and its insulation state directly determines whether the motor can operate at sea for a long time. According to the assessment index of insulation resistance, the cold-state insulation resistance of the winding of a marine motor should be not less than 5MΩ, and the hot-state insulation resistance should be not less than 2MΩ. Marine motors mostly use Class E and Class B insulation, and the drying temperatures do not exceed 110°C and 120°C respectively; if the insulation resistance of the winding is low due to salt content, it is necessary to rinse with high-temperature and high-pressure water or adopt the method of boiling in fresh water for desalination treatment.

In terms of mechanical structure, marine motors must ensure normal operation under the conditions of long-term 15° list, 7.5° trim and 22.5° roll. This inclination and rolling condition imposes higher requirements on the bearing structure; the bearing, as the mechanical component supporting the rotation of the rotor, has a working state whose reliability is directly related to whether the motor can continue to operate during rolling. Likewise, the brush must not jam in the brush holder under long-term list and roll; the brush holder, as the device fixing the brush, must have its connecting parts ensured not to loosen. In addition to the above requirements, marine motors should also have the characteristics of impact resistance, vibration resistance and bump resistance, and be small in size, light in weight and easy to disassemble and assemble. For the windlass motor, there is also a special requirement, that is, it must meet 25 starts within 30min and allow locked-rotor for 1min.

Composition and operation monitoring of marine motors The major category of marine motors includes varieties such as marine asynchronous motors, marine DC motors and AC single-phase motors. As for a specific marine motor, its composition includes components such as the bearing, winding, commutator, brush and shaft. Around these components, the daily maintenance of marine motors involves contents such as general cleaning, working environment check, bearing maintenance, power supply voltage monitoring, armature current monitoring, temperature rise monitoring, running sound listening and commutation spark monitoring.

When the phenomenon of excessive sparking under brush occurs, it is necessary to check the contact condition between the brush and the commutator, check the condition of the brush holder, check the position of the brush, and at the same time also check the vibration condition of the armature and the condition of the commutator segments. If the clearance fit between the brush and the brush holder is too tight, it will cause jamming and cause excessive brush sparking; once the brush holder is loose, the brushes are not arranged in a straight line, which will also affect commutation and increase sparking. When grinding the contact surface between the brush and the commutator, the brush must be placed in the brush holder for the operation. Regarding the bearing, checking the bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition both belong to the scope of bearing maintenance; bearing fault is one of the direct causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems and belongs to the branch of excessive mechanical resistance; when a bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by great non-uniform noise and the characteristic of overheating of the bearing end cover. Local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of AC motors, and motor overcurrent is also a direct cause of overheating of AC electric drive systems.

Measuring tools and the ship power grid: during maintenance and repair, electrical quantities such as resistance and current need to be measured with instruments. The measurable property of resistance is the resistance value, which can be measured with a multimeter; the measurable property of current is the current value, which can be measured with a multimeter, an ammeter or a clamp-on ammeter. When measuring the resistance in a measuring circuit, at least one end of the resistor under test must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off; if capacitance exists in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring the resistance, and never measure with power on. To measure current, an ammeter must be used, and the circuit is disconnected and then connected in series. When measuring the winding of low-voltage equipment with a rated voltage of 500V and above, a 1000～2500V insulation resistance tester should be selected. In the fault of generator no-load voltage high, an open-circuit shunt resistor will cause the voltage regulator to lose its main regulating function.

The ship power grid to which the marine motor is connected is part of the ship power station and usually adopts a three-phase three-wire insulated system. Various marine generators are mostly of salient-pole construction, and their parameters need to take into account the requirements of the grid short circuit current.

Before dismantling a marine motor for maintenance, two marking tasks must be completed first; otherwise it is very difficult to restore the original assembly relationship after disassembly and reassembly. One of them is to mark the circuit ends before disassembly; this operation must be completed before the motor is separated from the circuit, that is, it must be done before disconnecting the wiring. The specific method is to mark each circuit end one by one and make a record; after marking, each circuit end must also be wrapped and insulated for protection, so as to prevent the wire ends from being exposed, touching each other, or being contaminated by moisture. The other is to mark the mating surfaces before disassembly, whose main purpose is to ensure that the end shield positions remain unchanged before and after disassembly and reassembly, so as to maintain the concentricity of the stator bore and the rotor outer circle. During the operation, use a flat chisel to punch position marks at the joint between the end shield and the frame; the marks for the front and rear end shields should be different, to prevent the two end shields from being installed in exchanged positions.

For unfamiliar motor structures, marks must be made and recorded in the order of disassembly, to prevent omission or wrong installation during assembly. For DC motors, marks also need to be made at the joint between the brush rocker and the end shield seat ring, usually by drawing a line with paint and disassembling after it dries. Together, these practices constitute making marks before disassembly: punch position marks with a flat chisel at the fit between the end shield and the frame spigot, to ensure that the end shield positions remain unchanged before and after disassembly and reassembly; for DC motors, mark the joint between the brush rocker and the end shield seat ring with paint and disassemble after it dries, to ensure the correct brush position. The main purpose of making marks before disassembly is to avoid affecting the concentricity of the stator bore and the rotor outer circle after disassembly and reassembly.

In the step of check the power supply voltage, what needs attention is marking the circuit ends before disassembly; when checking for motor internal fault, what needs attention is marking the mating surfaces before disassembly. Both of these markings are indispensable preparatory work before disassembly.

The conventional fault diagnosis method first uses observation in motor maintenance. The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part condition, wire condition and equipment operating parameters; specifically, it is necessary to see whether parts are jammed or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, abraded or burnt. Observation is also the preceding step of check the monitoring and indicating device; only after observation are the data of various monitoring and indicating devices checked. Observation belongs to a sub-step of the first step of conventional fault diagnosis, "carry out fault analysis while keeping the site unchanged".

A marine motor structurally includes components such as the bearing, winding, commutator, brush and shaft. The brush is an important conductive element used to lead current in or out between the stationary part and the sliding part of a motor; DC motors, AC wound-rotor motors and synchronous generators all need to be equipped with brushes; the brush contacts the collector ring to transfer current, and common brushes are divided into three types: graphite, electrographite and metal graphite, among which the graphite brush is soft in texture and suitable for motors with general commutation conditions and uniform load. The commutator is a rotating sliding contact component used to lead current in and out in DC motors and wound-rotor motors, and is composed of commutator segments. The winding is a coil component wound from enameled wire in a motor or transformer, used to generate a magnetic field or induce an electromotive force; the winding insulation of a marine motor must undergo the "three-proof" treatment of moisture-proofing, mildew-proofing and salt-oil-mist-proofing, and must be oil-resistant. The shaft is a mechanical transmission component used to transmit torque and rotary motion, and is commonly found in motors, contactors and instruments. The core is a magnetic conductive component in electromagnetic equipment, used to form the magnetic circuit, support the coil and serve as a reference point for insulation measurement; a contactor contains a core, and when measuring the insulation resistance of an electrical equipment coil to ground, terminal post E of the insulation resistance tester can be connected to the core; in a through-type current transformer, the large-current conductor under test is directly interlinked with the core to replace the primary winding.

The maintenance of brushes has explicit quantitative requirements. When the contact area during brush grinding is less than 70%, it must be dealt with; when the contact area between brush and commutator is less than 70%, grinding treatment must be carried out; the axial clearance of the brush is 0.2～0.5mm; the pressure of the electrographitic graphite brush during overhaul acceptance is usually about 2.45MPa. When the electric drill brush is not on the neutral line, causing large sparks, the brush position needs to be corrected; when poor contact between brush and commutator causes large sparks, the brush pressure needs to be adjusted. Adjusting the brush is a maintenance procedure in DC motor maintenance for correcting the brush position and pressure, correcting the brush position and contact state by marking the position or adjusting the pressure. Before removing the brush rocker of a DC motor, paint marks are made so as to adjust the brush position quickly and accurately; before removal, paint marks are made at the joint between the brush rocker and the end cover, and removal is carried out after drying to ensure the position is correct during installation;

According to the paint marks made in advance, the brush position of the DC motor can be adjusted quickly and accurately.

The maintenance of the commutator also has specific indicators. When disassembling a DC motor, care should be taken to prevent damage to the winding ends, commutator or collector rings; carbon powder must not accumulate in the commutator grooves, so as to avoid short circuit between segments; the surface roughness Ra of the commutator should be below 3.2μm, and it needs to be ground and polished with abrasive cloth; after the commutator is turned, it needs to be undercut so that the mica is 1～2mm lower than the commutator segments. If the commutator surface is too dirty or the brush is stuck, it will cause poor contact between brush and commutator and produce sparks. When checking the contact between brush and commutator, information on both the commutator and the brush is used at the same time; when checking the brush holder, the brush is used; when checking the commutator segments, the commutator is used; when checking the brush position, the brush is likewise used.

The insulation condition of the winding directly determines whether drying treatment is required. When the insulation resistance of the winding is lower than 0.5MΩ, drying must be carried out to improve the insulation performance; when the winding contains salt causing low insulation, desalination treatment is required by washing with high-temperature and high-pressure water or boiling in fresh water; the current drying method uses the copper loss of the stator winding to generate heat and drive out moisture, initially passing 30% of the rated current and gradually increasing it. When disassembling the rotor, care must be taken to prevent damage to the winding ends, and during assembly the winding insulation must also be protected from damage. Local short circuit or phase failure of the winding is one of the main fault causes of overcurrent and overheating of AC motors.

The bearing is the mechanical component of the motor, used to support the rotation of the rotor; its fault will cause motor overheating, vibration and abnormal noise; bearing fault is one of the direct causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems, belonging to the branch of excessive mechanical resistance; when an upper bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by very loud uneven noise and the characteristic of an overheated bearing end cover.

Bearing wear will cause increased clearance, vibration and overheating of the motor or mechanical components, manifested as damage to the bearing surface or excessive fit clearance; bearing wear or damage will cause uneven clearance between the armature and the magnetic poles, causing excessive brush sparks; bearing wear or damage is one of the main causes of large armature vibration in DC motors. When wear of a rolling bearing causes excessive clearance, it is manifested as loud rotational noise, wobbling of the outer ring, or impact noise between the balls and the outer ring; the allowable wear value for bearings with an inner diameter of 20～59mm is about 10 times the original clearance, up to a maximum of 0.15～0.25mm. The clearance of a new bearing is generally 0.01～0.02mm, and the maximum allowable wear value for bearings with an inner diameter of 20～59mm can reach 0.15～0.25mm.

If there is loud noise when turning the outer ring, or if the balls make a knocking sound when twisted or shaken, it indicates that the clearance is too large.

Bearing maintenance requires attention to three aspects: precautions for bearing disassembly, precautions for bearing cleaning, and precautions for bearing installation. When checking for bearing fault, attention must be paid to precautions for bearing disassembly; when checking the lubrication condition, attention must be paid to precautions for bearing installation. Motor bearings are generally shrink-fitted onto the shaft, with the inner ring fitting tightly on the shaft; during disassembly, a puller can be used to cold-draw the bearing off; if the wear is not severe, it is only necessary to clean and replace the grease, and the bearing usually does not need to be removed—the purpose of disassembly is to prevent damage to the bearing. In bearing maintenance, bearings with not severe wear generally do not need to be removed; it is only necessary to clean and replace the grease; bearings that are severely heated or whose grease is too dirty but can continue to be used need to be cleaned and maintained; the conventional cleaning process is to scrape off the dirty grease, soak in kerosene for 5–10 min, scrub with a brush, and perform a second cleaning with gasoline; bearings with hardened grease that is difficult to clean can be immersed in hot oil at 100–120°C to remove the oil contamination. When cleaning rolling bearings, they can be placed in kerosene and soaked for 5–10 min before brushing; when the grease is hardened, they can be immersed in hot oil at 100–120°C for cleaning. During cleaning, the hot oil temperature must not exceed 120°C; it is strictly forbidden to heat the oil with an open flame, and attention must be paid to fire prevention;

It is forbidden to use a sharp scraper to pick out oil contamination, to prevent damage to the bearing surface; after cleaning, if not used immediately, it must be wrapped in oil paper and stored in a clean place.

Before bearing installation, the shaft journal must be checked to ensure it is smooth and free of rust, cracks, burrs, or pitting; slight rust can be polished with fine sandpaper or an oilstone before installation. Installation commonly uses the driving-in method or the shrink-fit method: the driving-in method requires applying machine oil to the shaft journal and using a soft metal tube to press against the inner ring and tap it lightly to the specified position; the shrink-fit method heats the bearing in oil at 100°C, placing it on a wire mesh rack to avoid direct heating, then taking the bearing out after heating and immediately fitting it onto the shaft journal, and tapping it gently into place with a tube. The filling amount of bearing grease should be 1/3 to 1/2 of the bearing space volume; too much or too little will cause poor lubrication. When assembling and tightening the screws of the end cover and bearing cover, they should be tightened in sequence in the diagonal direction, to prevent damage to the fitting surface of the spigot and to prevent eccentricity.

Before disassembling the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover must first be removed; if the wear is not severe, the bearing generally does not need to be removed—it is only necessary to clean and replace the grease. When taking out the rotor, if there is a fan at one end of the rotor, it should be pulled out from the fan end to prevent jamming; for marine pole-changing variable-speed asynchronous motors such as cargo winches, it should be pulled out from the end with the larger outer diameter, because there are two cores with different outer diameters on the shaft, and it must be pulled out from the large-outer-diameter end. During the pulling process, it is strictly forbidden to damage the winding and core; the objects to be protected from damage include the winding end portions, commutator, or collector ring. The requirements for correctly placing the rotor are: the removed rotor should be placed on a support or wooden board to prevent rolling; when the ship is swaying, the placed rotor should be tied down securely; if the rotor is too heavy, a steel pipe can be fitted over the shaft and it can be pulled out manually or with an electric hoist. The requirements for correctly placing the rotor and the anti-damage requirements during rotor removal work together to ensure that the winding end portions, commutator, or collector ring are not damaged.

Precautions for pole disassembly include: before disassembly, the distance between the main poles should be recorded; during disassembly, the number of shims under each pole must be counted; if the shim thicknesses are different, they must also be marked, and attention should be paid to whether there are non-magnetic shims and to which pole they belong, in order to avoid incorrect reassembly.

Marine motors operate for long periods in harsh environments such as high marine humidity, salt spray, vibration, and confined spaces, which imposes special requirements on insulation, mechanical structure, and electrical performance. China's standards specify an ambient temperature of 45°C and require normal operation at a relative air humidity of 95%.

Insulation resistance is tested with an insulation resistance tester, also called a megohmmeter, which is a portable instrument composed of a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter, used to measure the insulation resistance of electrical equipment, lines, and cables, and often adopts a ratio meter structure. The insulation resistance tester includes a hand-cranked generator and a moving-coil ratio meter; its terminal posts are L, E, and G, and according to the highest voltage generated by the hand-cranked generator, it is classified into specifications such as 100V, 200V, 500V, 1000V, and 2500V.

When the insulation resistance of a marine motor winding is lower than 0.5MΩ, it must be tested with a 500V insulation resistance tester and dried. If the resistance decrease is caused by insulation aging, the insulation performance cannot be improved by drying. After seawater enters the motor, desalination must be carried out by boiling in fresh water with three water changes and boiling in distilled water. When drying cannot increase the insulation resistance, or when the winding has oil dirt and dust, the motor winding should be cleaned. Cleaning methods are divided into two types: cleaning with chemical agents and flushing with high-temperature high-pressure water: when the insulation resistance is high but the surface has dirt, a motor cleaner can be used with a brush or spray gun for cleaning; because the cleaner contains volatile gases, cleaning with motor cleaner should be carried out in a well-ventilated place; low insulation resistance indicates salt content, so only high-temperature high-pressure water flushing can be used, and only during maintenance; on board, the method of hot water soaking and boiling can be used to remove salt from the winding.

These requirements together constitute the precautions for cleaning motor windings and are also important content of motor winding maintenance.

During the drying process, the corresponding temperature and recording specifications must be observed. Marine motors are mostly Class E and Class B insulation, and the drying temperatures shall not exceed 110℃ and 120℃ respectively, that is, the hot-air drying temperature of Class E insulation marine motors shall not exceed 110℃, and the hot-air drying temperature of Class B insulation marine motors shall not exceed 120℃. Within 2h after the start of drying, record the temperature once every 30min; in the first 4h, raise the temperature by 15℃ per hour, and thereafter raise it by 30℃ per hour up to the maximum allowable value; during drying, measure the insulation resistance once every half hour or one hour, and when the insulation resistance reaches 5MΩ or more and no longer changes, drying can be stopped. Temperature rise monitoring requires attention to these drying precautions.

The maintenance focus of DC motors lies in the commutator and brush system, and commutator maintenance and brush grinding are the core work. When there is poor contact between brush and commutator and the contact area is less than 70%, it must be repaired by grinding the brush. The maintenance requirements for brushes and commutators are to ensure good contact between the brush and commutator, and that the commutator surface is smooth and clean with reliable insulation; regularly blow away brush powder and dust on the commutator with a hand blower or hair dryer, and wipe off dirt that cannot be blown away with a small amount of electrical cleaner; when the surface is found to be rough, the brush wears quickly, or there are black wear marks or burn marks, the commutator should be ground, first using 0# abrasive cloth to grind away the rough thin layer, then using old 00# abrasive cloth for rapid polishing. A rough commutator surface is manifested as rapid brush wear, formation of black wear marks or burn marks, and it is necessary to first use 0# abrasive cloth to grind away the rough thin layer, then use old abrasive cloth for polishing; after grinding, the surface roughness Ra should be controlled below 3.2μm, and normal maintenance requires the commutator surface to be smooth, clean and reliably insulated. Brush wear is a fault symptom of brush material loss during operation of DC motors and brushed generators, and the commutator needs to be cleaned regularly and worn brushes replaced; during daily maintenance of DC motors, a hand blower or blower must be used to remove brush powder and dust near the winding ends and the commutator;

When it is found that the brush wears quickly and the commutator surface is rough or has burn marks, the commutator surface should be ground; carbon powder produced by brush wear accumulated in the commutator grooves may cause short circuit between segments and must be cleaned regularly. For brushed motors, excessive brush wear is one of the common faults, alongside stator winding open circuit and short circuit; when the electric drill fails to start, if poor contact is caused by brush wear, the brush should be replaced directly. After replacing the brushes of a DC motor, if the contact area is less than 70%, the contact surface between the brush and commutator must be ground; when grinding newly replaced brushes, the brush must be placed in the brush holder, and 00# abrasive cloth wrapped around the commutator surface and pulled back and forth. The brush holder is the device that fixes the brush; when grinding the contact surface between the brush and commutator, the brush must be placed in the brush holder for the operation, and when checking the contact surface of a motor in operation, the brush can be taken out of the brush holder for observation. For marine motors under long-term 15° list, 7.5° trim and 22.5° roll, the connecting parts of the brush holder must be ensured not to loosen; too tight clearance fit between the brush and brush holder will cause jamming, resulting in excessive brush sparking; a loose brush holder causes the brushes to be arranged out of line, affecting commutation and increasing sparking. In DC motor maintenance, it must be ensured that the brush and commutator are in good contact and the surface is clean and smooth.

Before removing the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover must first be taken off; bearings are commonly installed by the driving-in method or the shrink-fit method, and the shrink-fit method requires heating the bearing in oil at about 100℃ and then fitting it onto the shaft journal. Checking bearing fault requires the use of bearings, and checking the lubrication condition likewise requires the use of bearings;

The precautions for assembly require that the assembly steps be the reverse of the disassembly steps, that is, what is removed last is installed first, and what is removed first is installed last. Do not tighten screws with excessive force to prevent twisting them off, and it is strictly forbidden to force screws of different pitch or size into place; the spring washers on the screws must be retained and must not be discarded. During assembly, the insulation at the winding ends must be protected, and after completion the rotor must be turned in both directions to check its flexibility and for abnormal noise; the screws of the end cover and bearing cover should be tightened in diagonal sequence to prevent damage to the spigot and eccentricity; at the start of assembly, the interior cavity of the motor should be blown with high-pressure air to ensure that no foreign matter or parts are left inside.

Protecting the winding during assembly requires that care be taken during assembly to protect the ends of the winding and not to damage the insulation; after assembly is completed, the rotor must be turned several turns in both directions to check flexibility and abnormal noise; at the start of assembly, the interior cavity of the motor is generally blown with high-pressure air to remove foreign matter; all removed parts must be reinstalled, and if any are missing or left over, the cause must be found and the work redone. The screw-tightening method applies to tightening the screws of the motor end cover and bearing cover; during operation they should be turned in diagonal sequence, the purpose being to prevent damage to the mating surface of the spigot and to avoid eccentricity, and during tightening the rotor should be turned while its flexibility is observed. Preventing foreign matter from being left behind requires that during motor assembly no foreign matter or parts be left forgotten in the motor; at the start of assembly the interior cavity of the motor is generally blown once with high-pressure air to remove foreign matter, and all removed parts must be reinstalled; if any are missing or left over, the cause must be found and the assembly redone.

Maintenance personnel are responsible for fault diagnosis and repair of marine electrical equipment and must be familiar with the principles and structure of the equipment and with repair materials; they are required to be familiar with the structure, working principle, functions of components (assemblies) and their locations of electrical equipment, and their methods can be summarized as asking, looking, touching, listening and smelling. In traditional fault diagnosis, the phenomena must be understood and a preliminary diagnosis made through asking, looking, touching, listening and smelling; one must be thoroughly familiar with the circuits, working principles and positions of all components of the ship's electrical equipment. Interviewing the operator is the step preceding observation, and observation in turn is the step preceding check the monitoring and indicating device. When measuring the resistance in a measuring circuit, at least one end of the resistor under measurement must be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply must be cut off; if capacitance exists in the circuit, it should be discharged before measuring the resistance, and never measure with power on. Measuring current requires an ammeter, connected in series after the circuit is opened. In the fault of generator no-load voltage high, an open shunt resistor will cause the voltage corrector to lose its main regulating action. Poor contact is a fault state in which the contact resistance at an electrical connection increases due to looseness, oxidation or foreign matter; loose fastening screws and terminal lugs will cause poor contact and increase the contact resistance; poor contact can cause local overheating, phase failure, phase-to-phase short circuit and other faults, and will cause random output action, corresponding to checking the terminal wiring.

In the daily maintenance of marine motors, general cleaning is a basic item, and its object includes both the motor itself and the installation environment in which the motor is located. Removing dirt from the exterior serves to ensure normal operation and heat dissipation of the motor. For enclosed motors, the ventilation ducts should be kept clean and the fan openings well ventilated; for protected motors, in addition to keeping the exterior clean, attention must also be paid to keeping the ventilation passages unobstructed. Without removing the end cover, the winding ends of a protected motor can be wiped or blown. A marine motor includes the maintenance item of general cleaning and also includes the check of the working environment. The check of the working environment is likewise not to be neglected; the environment must meet the requirements specified for use, for example, no water, no corrosive gases, etc., and the purpose of the check is to prevent damage to the insulation and other structural parts of the motor; this work falls within the scope of cleaning work in the daily maintenance and operation monitoring of marine motors. General cleaning requires attention to the precautions for cleaning motor windings; when wiping or blowing the winding ends, damage to the winding insulation should be avoided. A marine motor includes bearings and also includes bearing maintenance. The core work of bearing maintenance includes adding oil and changing oil, and at the same time the bearing temperature must be monitored to see whether it is normal, and the state judged by listening to the running sound.

Checking the bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition are both carried out directly with the bearing as the object. Carbon powder produced by brush wear accumulating in the grooves may likewise cause short circuit between segments and must be cleaned regularly. Checking the contact between the brush and the commutator and checking the commutator segments both take the commutator as the main inspection object. Checking the contact between the brush and the commutator requires attention to power supply voltage monitoring; sparks caused by poor contact are often associated with fluctuations in terminal voltage. The graphite brush is made of natural graphite with binders such as pitch and coal tar, is relatively soft in texture, contains more impurities when not heated at high temperature, easily damages the commutator, and is suitable for motors with general commutation conditions and uniform load. The electrographite brush is made of graphite, coke, carbon black and other raw materials, roasted at a high temperature above 2500℃, has good wear resistance and is easy to machine, and is suitable for various types of motors and motors with difficult commutation conditions;

During the major overhaul acceptance of the DC motor, its pressure is generally controlled at about 2.45MPa. Checking the brush holder condition and checking the brush position are both carried out around the brush. Checking the brush position requires attention to armature current monitoring; deviation of the brush position will cause abnormal changes in the armature current.

Almost all faults of the DC motor can be reflected in the commutation spark, and the color and size of the commutation spark best indicate the operating condition of the DC motor. The marine motor includes the maintenance item of commutation spark monitoring. The commutation spark of a normally operating motor should meet the specified grade; if the spark is too large, it indicates that the motor or load has some kind of fault, and the machine should be stopped for inspection. Maintenance management personnel must frequently observe the spark to become familiar with its grade, thereby judging faults. In terms of running sound monitoring, the marine motor includes running sound monitoring; a normally operating motor produces a uniform and continuous sound due to bearing friction, core magnetization, etc.; when there is a fault or abnormal mechanical parts, the motor sound is abnormal and vibration occurs. A screwdriver can be used to contact the bearing cover, with the handle against the ear to monitor the bearing running sound; if a continuous "grumbling sound" or other noise is heard, it indicates that the bearing is abnormal and needs inspection and treatment. A properly installed motor will not vibrate under normal conditions.

The contactor includes the core; in contactor maintenance, it is necessary to measure the insulation resistance between contacts, between the coil and the core, and between live parts and ground, and the voltage grade of the insulation resistance tester should be selected according to the rated voltage of the contactor during measurement.

In terms of operation monitoring, the marine motor includes power supply voltage monitoring, armature current monitoring and temperature rise monitoring. Power supply voltage monitoring is the primary item of ship motor operation monitoring; the motor terminal voltage must be maintained at the rated value, too high or too low voltage will cause changes in armature current, torque and temperature rise, the difference between the power supply voltage value and the rated value must not exceed ±5%, and the degree of three-phase voltage unbalance must not exceed ±5%. Power supply voltage monitoring requires attention to the various limits specified by power supply voltage monitoring itself, that is, both the difference between terminal voltage and rated value and the three-phase unbalance must be controlled within the above ranges.

Armature current monitoring requires that the armature current be kept within the rated value during motor operation, and the degree of current unbalance of the three-phase asynchronous motor must not exceed ±10%; the nameplate rated current corresponds to the rated working state when the ambient temperature is 45℃, and if the ambient temperature exceeds 45℃, the allowable current for long-term operation must be less than the nameplate data. Armature current monitoring requires attention to the rated value and unbalance requirements specified by armature current monitoring, and these must not be exceeded during operation. Temperature rise monitoring requires that the temperature rise of the motor under the rated working state must not exceed the allowable value; if the temperature rise exceeds the allowable value, it indicates that there is a problem with the motor or the control equipment and load, etc., and when the temperature rise is abnormal the cause must be ascertained, and operation can continue only after the fault is eliminated; temperature rise can be monitored with a thermometer or judged by experience, such as by hand feeling. Overvoltage is likewise one of the causes of motor overheating in AC electric drive systems.

Measuring insulation resistance is one of the mandatory inspection and test items for acceptance of a motor after new installation or major overhaul, used to verify the insulation performance of electrical equipment, and is often carried out after major overhaul of the equipment or after shutdown following operation. The objects of insulation testing before and after assembly include insulation between windings and insulation to ground; the test results before and after assembly need to be compared, and only when the results show no difference and meet the requirements may the power-on test be conducted; after power-on, the temperature rise, no-load current, noise and smoothness of rotation need to be observed. Regarding the appearance inspection, before power-on after major overhaul of the motor, the installation of components, the flexibility of the rotor, the deflection of the shaft extension and the contact surface of the brush should be checked; for a DC motor, the contact surface between the brush and the commutator, when observed in a bright place, should not be less than 70%.

During long-term operation of a marine motor, its internal components gradually deteriorate due to vibration, dampness, salt spray corrosion and normal wear, and maintenance work needs to be carried out item by item around observation, detection and testing. The marine motor itself is composed of several key components, including the bearing, winding, commutator and brush, and the working state of these components directly determines whether the motor can operate reliably. The insulation of the marine motor winding must undergo "three-proof" treatment against moisture, mildew and salt-oil mist, and must be oil-resistant. If the insulation resistance of the winding is low due to salt content, it needs to be washed with high-temperature and high-pressure water or desalinated by boiling in fresh water.

Overcurrent of the motor is the direct cause of overheating of the AC electric drive system.

If commutation sparking occurs during no-load operation of a DC motor, the step of checking the brush position should be carried out. When checking the brush position, it is necessary to confirm whether the brush jumps and its contact condition with the commutator, and at the same time attention should also be paid to monitoring the armature current, using the change in armature current to judge whether the brush position adjustment is appropriate. The greater the deviation of the brush position, the greater the sparking produced by the DC motor; the phenomenon of excessive sparking under brush corresponds to the corrective measure of checking the brush position. The brush contacts the collector ring and serves to transmit current. When checking the contact condition between the brush and the commutator, it is necessary to use the commutator to check whether its surface is clean and whether there is burning and uneven wear, and at the same time also use the brush to check its contact area, degree of wear and whether it moves freely in the brush holder; neither can be omitted. Checking the condition of the commutator segments is likewise inseparable from inspecting the commutator itself. Checking the condition of the brush holder needs to be centered on the brush, checking whether the brush holder is loose and whether the brushes are arranged in a straight line. After turning, the slots need to be undercut so that the mica is 1–2 mm lower than the commutator segments. Checking the bearing fault and checking the lubrication condition both need to be centered on the bearing. Before removing the end cover of a DC motor, the bearing outer cover needs to be removed first;

After all stator windings of the motor are replaced, a withstand voltage test needs to be carried out, the purpose of which is to determine the insulation strength of the windings to ground and between the windings. For a motor of 380 V and power ≥1 kW, the effective value of the test voltage is 1760 V at a frequency of 50 Hz; the winding should be able to withstand the test voltage for 1 minute continuously.

The no-load test is carried out after major overhaul or new installation of the motor, that is, no-load operation at rated voltage, to check electrical balance, rotation direction and mechanical state. Before the test, the three-phase winding resistance needs to be measured with a bridge, and the difference in resistance between phases should be less than ±5%. At the start, an inching test should be carried out first to check whether the rotation direction meets the requirements of the mechanical load; if the rotation direction of an AC motor is reversed, it is corrected by swapping the connections of two phases, while for a DC motor the excitation winding leads are swapped. Then the three-phase balanced rated voltage is applied to the stator winding to start, and it runs at no load for 30 min. The three-phase current is measured with a clamp meter, and the difference between phase currents should not exceed ±10%; the ratio of no-load current to rated current should conform to the value of normal operation of the motor before major overhaul.

When judging the nature of the noise, the power supply can be cut off under no load; if the noise disappears, it is electromagnetic noise, and if it disappears as the speed decreases, it is mechanical noise. In the commissioning of auxiliary machines, the no-load test needs to observe the rotation direction, speed and the starting and no-load current of each gear under step-by-step forward and reverse operation.

The load test and temperature rise measurement should be carried out after the no-load test is all normal. For every 15% increase in load, the armature current and speed need to be measured once, until rated load. When measuring the stable temperature rise, the load operation time must not be less than 4 hours. The average temperature rise of the winding can be measured by inserting a thermometer through the lifting hole, and must not exceed the allowable value for the insulation class. During load operation, the bearing temperature must not exceed 95°C; if too high, the bearing quality and the type of lubricating grease need to be checked; if the bearing temperature is abnormal, it should also be checked whether there is any abnormality in the motor and the driven load machinery.

Marine motors include many types, among which the marine asynchronous motor is the most widely used class, and the three-phase asynchronous motor used on most ships is in turn the cage-type asynchronous motor. When analyzing the motor internal fault, the fault tree (FTA) method is usually adopted, that is, fault tree analysis uses the fault tree as a tool to carry out diagnosis. A fault tree is a connected logic tree containing no closed loops, which uses graphical symbols to represent the logical combinations among various events that cause unwanted events of the system; it develops downward from the tree root of the top event, the branches represent accident events, and the nodes represent logical relationships. A fault tree contains the top event, intermediate events and basic events, among which the most commonly used logical relationships are the AND relationship and the OR relationship.

When constructing a fault tree, electrical equipment faults such as motor fails to start are often selected as the top event, and its boundary conditions are usually set as normal power supply and normal control circuit.

For the three-phase cage-type asynchronous motor failing to start, the main causes include no power supply, motor internal fault and mechanical fault. When analyzing its fault, the fault tree (FTA) method is usually adopted, covering eight categories of causes such as failure to start and motor speed low after starting. When checking this fault, the principle of from simple to complex and from the surface to the interior is followed: first check the power supply, then check whether the shaft is seized or the load is excessive, and finally check the interior of the motor. Specifically, power supply problems will cause the motor fails to start, mechanical problems will cause the motor fails to start, excessive load will likewise cause the motor fails to start, and motor internal fault will also cause the motor fails to start. The eight major causes of the asynchronous motor failing to start cover no power supply, winding short circuit or open circuit, shaft seizure and excessive load. In a single-speed non-reversible AC drive system, the direct causes of failure to start are motor fault, no power and mechanical seizure; the contactor KM not being closed will cause the motor to have no power, and its root cause may be coil fault, armature seizure or control circuit open circuit.

If a buzzing sound is heard when the motor fails to start, this indicates the presence of phase failure of the power supply or mechanical seizure; when phase failure causes locked-rotor, it should be stopped immediately to prevent the motor from being burned out after long-time operation.
