The installation of radar equipment is usually completed by technicians designated by the shipyard, manufacturer or supplier during construction, repair or while in port, and the electro-technical officer bears a certain responsibility for determining the equipment position and is responsible for the acceptance work after installation.

Before installation, a configuration scale diagram needs to be prepared, on which the antenna position, surrounding building obstructions and the range of turning objects are marked. The antenna should be installed on the wheelhouse top or on an independent radar mast, away from the funnel to avoid high heat and corrosive environments. The cabinets of each unit need to be well earthed, the cable shielding should be reliably earthed and the wiring should be as short as possible. After installation is completed, initialization settings need to be carried out, including tuning, reference point setting and error calibration. During acceptance, it is necessary to check whether the shadow sector meets the specification requirements and record the results in the radar log. Outdoor wiring needs attention to waterproofing, and sensor connections should conform to product standards and be connected to the specified interfaces.

Radar installation covers the steps of pre-installation preparation, antenna installation, transceiver installation, display installation, wiring and enabling initialization, and its applicable objects include the antenna, transceiver, display and waveguide. The installation and initialization setting process is completed by designated technicians, and the electro-technical officer is responsible for supervision and acceptance. Enabling initialization includes parameter setting, error calibration and shadow sector measurement, and the relevant results need to be recorded in the installation report. Radar installation is the preceding stage of radar acceptance; only after the installation work is completed and initialization has been carried out can the acceptance process be entered.

The installation of the antenna has several specific constraints. The radar antenna height should ensure that the horizontal distance from the line of sight at the bow touching the sea surface does not exceed 500m or twice the ship length, whichever is smaller. The antenna position should ensure that there is no shadow sector area within the range from dead ahead to 2 to 2.5° abaft the beam on both port and starboard sides. The antenna rotation plane should be parallel to the main deck, and a protective railing of not less than 0.9m should be provided around it. When two radars are installed on the ship, the elevation angle between the two radar antennas should be greater than 20°, and the vertical distance should not be less than 1m, to avoid electromagnetic interference. The lowest edge of the antenna radiation window should be more than 0.5m above the safety railing of the installation platform. In daily maintenance, the antenna metal gear transmission system needs to be cleaned of oil sludge and refilled with oil once a year; the maintenance links included in the antenna also include bearing lubrication of the antenna rotation link, cleaning and oiling of the antenna metal gear transmission system, and oil level inspection of the antenna worm gear reduction gearbox.

The precautions for radar antenna installation require that when installing the antenna base, it should be ensured that the antenna rotation plane is parallel to the main deck. If there is a forward mark, the mark line should be within ±5° on both sides of the bow line. In addition to sufficient space for antenna rotation around the antenna, there should also be a platform necessary for installation and maintenance work, and a protective railing of not less than 0.9m should be provided. These precautions directly target the antenna itself and are links that must be grasped in radar equipment installation.

The transceiver is usually installed in a well-ventilated equipment room near the bridge, the chart room or inside the bridge, and is located directly below the antenna as far as possible. The transceiver of a mast-below type radar is connected to the antenna through a waveguide, the effective length of the waveguide should not exceed 25m at maximum, and there should preferably be no more than five bent waveguides. The transceiver of a mast-above type radar is connected to the antenna using cables provided by the manufacturer, with a standard length of about 25m, and must not be shortened or lengthened at will.

When maintaining the transceiver, it is necessary to open the cover plate to clean the air filter intake pipe and the outlet filter; when there is a lot of dust in the intake filter, the filter element can be removed and washed. When maintaining high-voltage components, it is necessary to shut down and remove the protective cover that prevents high-voltage electric shock, clean dust with a brush and clean oil stains with alcohol. The maintenance items included in the transceiver are transmitter air filter cleaning and transmitter high-voltage component electrostatic dust removal, and its interior also contains the magnetron.

In mast-below type radar, the effective length of the waveguide shall not exceed 25m at maximum, and the number of bent waveguides should preferably not exceed five. The waveguide should preferably run in a straight line and be as short as possible, and the direction of travel should always keep the choke flange facing the transceiver. In mast-below type radar installation, the use of flexible waveguides should be avoided as much as possible. A special water-blocking film should be added to the waveguide surface at the transceiver outlet and the antenna inlet end.

The display should be installed in the wheelhouse in a place free from strong electromagnetic radiation, away from heat sources and dry, and fixed with a hardwood base. The main radar display should be oriented so that the observer faces the bow, installed on the starboard side of the bridge, and does not affect lookout. The height of the base should take into account the convenience of cable entry and bending, leave sufficient maintenance space around, and accommodate two observers standing. Display maintenance includes cleaning the air filter once a quarter, electrostatic dust removal cleaning of high-voltage components once every half year, and wiping the surface with a damp cotton cloth every day before departure and during navigation; cleaning agents are prohibited. The maintenance items included in the display are display air filter cleaning and display surface cleaning.

Radar wiring precautions require that the chassis of each radar unit be well earthed, and the cable shielding layer must be reliably earthed. Wiring should be as short as possible to avoid signal attenuation, and stay away from high-frequency radiation cables. Cables should be arranged to cross other equipment cables perpendicularly to avoid magnetic field coupling interference.

Enabling initialization includes parameter configuration such as tuning, common reference point setting and transmission sector suppression; initialization error calibration involves heading line azimuth error, ranging error and shadow sector determination.

Radar acceptance includes steps such as appearance inspection, power-on acceptance and performance testing. Acceptance of a new radar is implemented by the competent department of the shipowner or the electro-technical officer; the acceptance process must be truthfully recorded and the acceptance checklist provided by the manufacturer must be filled in, the installation engineering report form must be signed and the documents generated during installation must be archived. Appearance inspection includes the installation position and workmanship of the antenna, transceiver and display, with particular attention to whether the radar shadow sector meets the specification requirements, and also checks cable connection tightness, protection of vibration-prone parts and anti-corrosion treatment of corroded locations. Radar acceptance applies to radar equipment, and its results need to be recorded in the radar log. For radar equipment, attention should also be paid to radar repair acceptance precautions, that is, the repair and acceptance stages should follow the corresponding technical specifications and recording requirements to ensure that acceptance work has a basis. The content of observation includes abnormal phenomena, part status, wire status and equipment operating parameters; specifically, check whether parts are stuck or damaged, and whether wires are loose, broken, abraded or burnt. Observation belongs to the sub-step of fault analysis carried out under the condition of maintaining the site, which is the first step of traditional fault diagnosis.

The sensors are placed in the X-axis and Y-axis directions respectively in the ship station antenna control platform, and are used to send error signals to control compensation motion when the ship pitches and rolls; their function is to send error signals. The equipment to which the receiving antenna belongs is the weather facsimile receiver, and its installation position should maintain a safe distance from the radar antenna to avoid electromagnetic interference; in the marine weather facsimile receiver, the receiving antenna is used to receive radio signals, its performance is equivalent to that of an MF/HF single-sideband receiver, and together with the recording device it constitutes the complete machine.

Radar equipment consists of parts such as the antenna, transceiver, display and power supply, among which the antenna undertakes the task of radiating and receiving for target detection, the transceiver is responsible for transmitting and receiving radar signals, the display is used to present radar images, and the magnetron is the core component inside the transmitter.

Carrying out radar installation, radar acceptance and regular radar maintenance and servicing on radar equipment all belong to the basic work content in the whole life cycle of the equipment; radar range error correction and radar bearing error correction are likewise carried out on radar equipment. During installation and use of radar equipment, attention must be paid to radar antenna installation precautions, radar display installation precautions, radar wiring precautions and radar repair acceptance precautions, wherein radar antenna installation precautions put forward requirements for the antenna, radar display installation precautions put forward requirements for the display, radar wiring precautions put forward requirements for the radar equipment itself, and radar repair acceptance precautions put forward requirements for the magnetron. Wiring requires that the chassis be well earthed, that the cable shield be reliably earthed, and that the cable be as short as possible to avoid signal attenuation.

Radar installation takes radar acceptance as its preceding step, and its scope of application covers the antenna, transceiver, display and waveguide. The antenna base includes a reduction gearbox structure, and the reduction gearbox therein needs to be painted once every half year to prevent corrosion. During radar acceptance, the installation positions of the antenna and the like, the shadow sector, cable binding, and anti-corrosion and fire-prevention measures shall also be checked.

Regular radar maintenance and servicing belongs to the regular category in the classification of radar maintenance and servicing, and is parallel to unscheduled maintenance; a corresponding plan needs to be formulated, recording personnel, time, content and material consumption, etc., and it is one of the contents of the shift handover work of the electro-technical officer or the second officer; the shipowner shall provide the spare parts and spare components required by the plan, and the ship management company is responsible for supervising and reviewing the completion status and putting forward suggestions for improvement.

For bearing lubrication of the antenna rotation link, use an oil gun to add oil once every half year at the bearing lubrication nipple of the antenna rotation link; the execution frequency is oiling once per year; before operation it is necessary to shut down and place the antenna safety switch in the "OFF" position, and before oiling the dirt at the lubrication nipple hole should be cleaned. The execution period for cleaning and oiling of the antenna metal gear transmission system is once per year, and the main work content is to clean the oil sludge and re-oil; before operation it is likewise necessary to shut down and place the antenna safety switch in the "OFF" position. The frequency of oil level inspection of the antenna worm gear reduction gearbox is once per year, and oil needs to be topped up when necessary; before operation it is necessary to shut down and place the antenna safety switch in the "OFF" position; check the liquid level height through the oil level observation window, and when it is below the lower limit scale, top up with special gearbox oil from the oil filling hole, and the topped-up oil should reach an appropriate position between the lower limit and upper limit scales; if the gearbox oil has deteriorated, the oil change procedure needs to be carried out rather than merely topping up; during oil change, both the oil filling hole and the oil drain hole need to be opened, and a container should be used to hold the waste oil.

The transmitter air filter is cleaned once every quarter; before operation the equipment must be shut down and the transceiver cover plate opened; the air filter intake pipe and the outlet filter of the transceiver need to be cleaned; the intake filter usually accumulates more dust and is the key cleaning object; a filter with a filter element can be removed, washed clean with clean water and then reinstalled. The cleaning period for static-dust attraction on high-voltage components of the transmitter is once every half year; before operation it is necessary to shut down and open the transceiver cover plate; the transmitter and the high-voltage electric shock protection cover need to be removed; use a brush to gently clean the dust on the high-voltage components, and use alcohol to gently clean oil stains; after cleaning, assemble the protection cover and reinstall the transmitter.

The display section includes display air filter cleaning and display surface cleaning. The display air filter is cleaned once every quarter, and the cleaning method is similar to that for the transmitter air filter. The frequency of display surface cleaning is once per day before sailing and during navigation; during cleaning it is strictly forbidden to use any cleaning agent, and a damp cotton cloth should be used for wiping and cleaning. Radar equipment also includes power supply air filter cleaning, whose cleaning frequency is once per quarter, and the cleaning process is similar to the cleaning method for the transmitter and display air filters. The air filter is used to filter the air entering the equipment and prevent dust from entering; the air filters in the transmitter, display and power supply system all need to be cleaned every quarter.

Radar maintenance acceptance precautions requirements: each acceptance shall confirm that the radar responds correctly to the operation of each button, with clear echoes and stable images; after replacing the magnetron, the original working time shall be cleared and effective preheating shall be carried out according to technical requirements; verify the magnetron current and the working condition of the magnetron under various pulse widths; after repairing the azimuth sweep system or replacing the magnetron, the azimuth accuracy shall be verified; after repairing the range sweep system or changing the length of the signal cable, the ranging accuracy shall be verified; when system initialization or circuit adjustment is involved, the sensor information and radar image quality shall be carefully verified. As the core component of the radar transmitter, the magnetron has a service life limit: the service life of magnetrons below 10kW is about 20000 hours, and the service life of magnetrons above 25kW is about 4000 hours; after replacement, the original working time needs to be cleared and preheating shall be carried out according to technical requirements; after replacement, the radar azimuth accuracy shall be verified, the current and the working condition under various pulse widths need to be verified, and spare magnetrons shall be used alternately on a regular basis. After the radar works for
0.5h, the magnetron current needs to be detected and compared with the rated value.

The multimeter can be used to measure resistor, voltage and current, and the clamp-on ammeter is used to measure current. The measurable performance of voltage is the voltage value, and the measuring tool is the multimeter or voltmeter; the measurable performance of current is the current value, and the measuring tool is the multimeter, ammeter or clamp-on ammeter; the measurable performance of resistor is the resistance value, and the measuring tool is the multimeter. When measuring the resistor in the measuring circuit, at least one end of the resistor under test shall be completely disconnected from the circuit, and the power supply shall be cut off; if capacitance exists in the circuit, it shall be discharged before measuring the resistor, and never measure with power on. Poor contact is one of the causes of equipment failure: the contact resistance increases at electrical connections due to looseness, oxidation or foreign matter, and loose fastening screws and wiring terminals will cause poor contact and increase the contact resistance; poor contact can cause local overheating, phase failure, short circuit between phases and other faults.

The marine motor contains the bearing, and both the check of the bearing fault and the check of the lubrication condition are carried out on the bearing. The bearing is used to support the rotation of the rotor, and its fault will cause motor overheating, vibration and abnormal noise; bearing fault is one of the direct causes of motor overheating in the AC electric drive system, belonging to the branch of excessive mechanical resistance; when the upper bearing fault causes motor overheating, it is usually accompanied by very large uneven noise and the characteristic of overheating of the bearing end cover.

The radar equipment consists of two major parts: the antenna and the display. The antenna undertakes the task of target detection, while the display is responsible for presenting the radar image. As far as the installation stage is concerned, the requirements of radar installation apply to both the antenna and the display. The radar antenna installation precautions need attention to the antenna, that is, the installation position of the antenna, the rotation plane, the protective railing, the spacing between dual antennas and the height of the radiation window are all points that shall be checked item by item during antenna installation; the radar display installation precautions need attention to the display, that is, the placement environment of the display, the fixing method of the base, the orientation and the installation position are all points that shall be checked item by item during display installation. The reason why the check at the installation stage is important is that once the antenna and the display are fixed, subsequent error correction and daily maintenance can only be carried out under the established installation conditions, and installation deviations are often difficult to compensate by adjusting menus or replacing parts.

The antenna is a key component of the radar equipment, and its installation position needs to meet multiple conditions.

For the bearing lubrication of the antenna rotation link and the oil quantity check of the antenna worm gear reduction gearbox, the oil quantity and oil quality are checked according to the corresponding cycle, and when insufficiency or deterioration is found, it is replenished or replaced in time; the oil quantity can be checked with the aid of the oil gauge or oil dipstick, and the oil quality is checked by observation of its color, viscosity and whether water or metal chips are mixed in. The above three operations respectively correspond to the bearing lubrication of the antenna rotation link, the cleaning and lubrication of the antenna metal gear transmission system, and the oil quantity check of the antenna worm gear reduction gearbox, constituting the routine maintenance content of the mechanical part of the antenna.

The display is used to display the radar image, and its installation position shall be selected in the wheelhouse where there is no strong electromagnetic radiation, away from heat sources and dry, and it shall be equipped with a hardwood base for fixing, so as to reduce the influence of vibration and moisture on the display device. The air filter is cleaned once a quarter; during cleaning, take out the filter element, remove the accumulated dust and then put it back; high-voltage devices are cleaned once every half a year by electrostatic dust absorption; before cleaning high-voltage devices, the power shall be cut off first and they shall be fully discharged, so as to avoid residual charge damaging the devices or endangering the operator. The surface of the display shall be wiped with a damp cotton cloth every day before sailing and during navigation; cleaning agents are prohibited to avoid damaging the screen coating, and when wiping, the cotton cloth should preferably be wrung until it does not drip.

Radar range error correction applies to radar equipment, and its correction objects include timing error, common reference point error and variable range marker error. Pixel error and pulse width error are not within the scope of maintenance and correction required of the electro-technical officer; these two types of deviation shall be handled separately. Timing error correction shall be carried out when the weather and sea state are calm and the berthing or anchorage environment is suitable, usually with the north-up relative motion display mode selected and a range of not more than 0.25 nautical miles, so as to distinguish the echo positions of fixed targets at short range. For conventional PPI radar, correcting the timing error requires adjusting the delay line of the display system; modern radar can complete it by operating the display menu, and during operation each item is set one by one according to the menu prompts until the leading edge of the echo of the fixed target aligns with the range ring scale.

Radar range error correction also applies to the Sperry MK37 gyrocompass.

Radar bearing error correction also applies to radar equipment, and its correction scope covers only the heading line error, compass indication error and common reference point error that the electro-technical officer needs to pay attention to. Beam width error, pixel error, antenna main lobe deviation angle and beam asymmetry error are not part of the correction content of this step. The common reference point is the CCRP, and its deviation compensation setting shall be completed during installation and shall be carried out after calibrating the radar timing error; reversing the order will cause the compensation amount to lose its reference. An inaccurate CCRP deviation compensation amount will cause a range error relative to the CCRP when measuring target range on the radar display, so the compensation amount must be set according to the measured value. The CCRP position adjustment procedure is similar to the radar timing error adjustment, and it is necessary to set it according to the procedures specified in the technical manual, input each item and recheck. In terms of operation sequence, radar range error correction comes first, that is, complete the range error correction first, then carry out the radar bearing error correction; the two must not be reversed, otherwise the result of the bearing correction will lose meaning because the range reference has not been determined.

As for the installation position, the height of the radar antenna shall ensure that the horizontal distance from the bow line of sight to the sea surface does not exceed the smaller of 500 m or twice the ship's length; the antenna position shall also ensure that no shadow sector appears within the range from dead ahead to 2 to 2.5° abaft the beam on both sides.

Radar installation also applies to the antenna, and the antenna is an integral part of radar equipment.

As for ship station antennas, Inmarsat-B/M/Mini-M/F ship stations use a parabolic directional antenna with a diameter of about 0.8 m, while Inmarsat-C/E ship stations use an omnidirectional helical antenna, which does not require a satellite tracking system but has higher requirements for the satellite's transmission energy. The ship station directional antenna control system usually includes two motion axes, azimuth (AZ) and elevation (EL), to compensate for pointing deviation caused by ship rolling.

A directional antenna is a ship station satellite antenna that radiates electromagnetic waves in a certain direction and must work with the control system to always point at the satellite. Inmarsat-B/M/Mini-M/F ship stations all use directional antennas, mostly parabolic antennas with a diameter of about 0.8 m, using geometric characteristics to form strong directional radiation; in recent years, phased array antennas have begun to be used, which are small in size and fast in scanning, but costly and complex in control. During navigation, the directional antenna must always point at the satellite, and a four-axis control system is required to compensate for ship rolling and course change errors. During maintenance, it is necessary to regularly check whether the antenna base is desoldered and loose due to ship vibration. When the directional antenna is working, personnel are prohibited from staying within 5 m of the antenna to prevent microwave radiation injury, unless the radome is 2 m above the deck.

The directional antenna belongs to the parabolic antenna and also belongs to the phased array antenna. The maintenance and upkeep of Inmarsat ship station antennas apply to the directional antenna, and the directional antenna also requires attention to the antenna safety distance precautions.

The omnidirectional antenna, also known as a non-directional antenna, radiates electromagnetic waves uniformly in all directions, is used in Inmarsat-C/E ship stations, does not require a satellite tracking system, and has relatively high requirements for the satellite's transmission energy. The omnidirectional antenna shares transmission and reception, and due to reversibility its transmission and reception performance are the same; during maintenance, it is necessary to check whether the fixation is firm and the cable connection is good. The omnidirectional antenna belongs to the helical antenna, and the maintenance and upkeep of Inmarsat ship station antennas also apply to the omnidirectional antenna.

The parabolic antenna belongs to the directional antenna and is mainly used in Inmarsat-B, M, Mini-M and F ship stations, with a typical diameter of about

0.8 meters. Its working principle is to reflect the weakly directional radiation generated by the illuminator through a parabolic reflector to form strongly directional radiation, radiating electromagnetic waves in a specific direction. Parabolic antennas usually use mechanical tracking methods to drive the antenna movement to align with the satellite; in ship station applications, the step tracking method (hill-climbing method) is mostly used for control. Parabolic antennas use mechanical tracking.

Phased array antennas belong to directional antennas and use electronic tracking methods, controlling the beam direction by changing the phase shift value of the phase shifter to track the satellite. They have the advantages of flexible control, fast scanning speed, small antenna size, and the ability to conform to the carrier platform shape, while also having the disadvantages of high antenna cost and complex control. Phased array antennas are one of the types of directional antennas used in Inmarsat ship stations; phased array antennas use electronic tracking.

Helical antennas belong to omnidirectional antennas and are mainly used in Inmarsat-C and Inmarsat-E ship stations, radiating electromagnetic waves uniformly in all directions. When using helical antennas, no satellite tracking system is required, but the transmission energy requirements for the satellite are relatively high. Among the omnidirectional antennas of Inmarsat-C/E ship stations, helical antennas are the majority.

The equipment to which the receiving antenna belongs is the weather facsimile receiver, which is a component of the marine weather facsimile receiver and, together with the recording device, constitutes the complete machine; its performance is equivalent to that of an MF/HF single-sideband receiver. The receiving antenna belongs to the weather facsimile receiver.

The function of the antenna control system is to compensate for the pointing error of the ship's antenna caused by various factors. It obtains error signals through sensors that monitor the ship's motion, and controls the antenna pointing through a feedback system to compensate for the error. The antenna control system is usually established as a four-axis control system, including the X/Y axes that maintain level and the AZ/EL axes that compensate for heading position; the control platform formed by the X and Y axes maintains level in any weather, so that the AZ/EL axes specifically compensate for heading changes. Since the four axes are controlled independently and do not require mutual transformation, their control circuit structure is relatively simple.

The antenna needs to have two degrees of freedom of motion, azimuth and elevation, to track the satellite. The antenna control system includes a four-axis control system; the antenna control system also needs to pay attention to the precautions for starting the ship station.

The four-axis control system consists of the AZ axis, EL axis, X axis, and Y axis. The four axes are controlled separately, and the control circuit is relatively simple. Its control platform is composed of the X axis and Y axis, which are responsible for keeping the platform in a horizontal position under any weather conditions; the AZ axis and EL axis installed on the horizontal platform are specifically used to compensate for changes in the ship's heading and position. The four axes are controlled independently, and no coordinate transformation is required between them, so the control circuit structure is relatively simple. This system is designed to compensate for the problem of the antenna deviating from the satellite caused by ship swaying and pointing errors.

The four-axis control system includes the AZ axis, EL axis, and control platform.

The AZ axis, namely the azimuth axis, is one of the two degrees of freedom of motion of the ship station antenna control system, corresponding to the azimuth motion in the horizontal plane. Its control signal is provided by the ship's gyrocompass to obtain heading error information; when the ship's heading changes, the AZ axis is driven to rotate in the opposite direction by the same angle to compensate for the pointing deviation. The AZ axis is installed on the horizontal control platform composed of the X axis and Y axis, and is specifically used to compensate for changes in the ship's heading and position, and together with the EL axis forms part of the four-axis control system; they are controlled independently without transformation, simplifying the circuit. The AZ axis uses the gyrocompass.

The EL axis, namely the elevation axis, is responsible for elevation motion in the vertical plane and, together with the AZ axis, constitutes the two degrees of freedom of motion of the antenna relative to the ship hull. The EL axis is installed on the horizontal control platform composed of the X axis and Y axis, and is used to compensate for the antenna pointing error caused by changes in the ship's heading and position, and maintains continuous tracking of the satellite by automatically tracking the strongest received signal state. The control principle of the EL axis is the same as that of the AZ axis, both based on a feedback system for error compensation.

The control platform is composed of the X axis and the Y axis, keeps the platform in a horizontal position under any weather conditions, and serves as the mounting base for the AZ axis (azimuth) and the EL axis (elevation), specifically compensating for changes in the ship's heading and position. Sensors are placed in the directions of the two axes respectively, detecting the ship's pitch and roll and sending out error signals, which after processing control the X axis or the Y axis to perform compensating motion so as to keep the platform in a horizontal position as much as possible. In the four-axis control system based on this platform, the four axes are controlled separately, and no transformation is required between them. The control platform contains sensors.

In the ship station antenna control platform, the sensors are placed in the X-axis and Y-axis directions respectively, and are used to send out error signals to control the compensating motion when the ship pitches and rolls. In the engine room monitoring and alarm system, the analog sensor converts the parameter into a continuously varying electrical signal, which is suitable for scenarios where both the equipment status is monitored and the parameter value is displayed; the digital sensor converts the parameter out-of-limit condition into digital information of contact opening or closing, and is only used to monitor whether the equipment is normal.

The gyrocompass provides the AZ-axis control signal for the satellite communication antenna, so that the antenna rotates in the reverse direction by the same angle as the ship's heading changes. Before starting the Anschutz 4 type, it is necessary to check whether the follow-up switch on the switchboard inside the small door on the left side of the master gyrocompass is set to the "cut off" position; when starting the Sperry MK37 type, it is necessary to turn the changeover switch to the "rotate" position and adjust the heading to deviate 30° from the true heading.

The content of the precautions for starting the ship station is that after the ship station is started, the initial positioning of the antenna pointing requires satellite information and also ship position information.

Mechanical tracking is one of the two basic categories of automatic antenna tracking, and the other is electronic tracking. To implement mechanical tracking, a servo drive system must be provided; parabolic antennas generally adopt the mechanical tracking method. In ship station applications, the step tracking method is mostly adopted to meet the requirements of simple circuits and light equipment; its control principle is based on the principle of maximum received level, and the antenna movement direction is determined by comparing the levels before and after the movement. Each step of step tracking has a fixed angular displacement, generally
0.5°.

Mechanical tracking includes the step tracking method.

Electronic tracking is likewise one of the two overall divisions of automatic antenna tracking; it usually controls the antenna beam direction by changing the phase shift value of the phase shifter, and phased-array antennas adopt the electronic tracking method. Unlike mechanical tracking, which requires a servo drive system, electronic tracking relies on electronic control rather than mechanical motion.

The step tracking method, also called the hill-climbing method, belongs to the mechanical tracking method and is suitable for ship station antennas that do not require high precision and need simple circuits. Its control principle is to enable the antenna to obtain the maximum received level; when it deviates from the satellite, the received level decreases as the angle increases; if the level rises after movement, it continues to move in the same direction, and if it falls, it moves in the reverse direction, finally jumping back and forth near the peak value. Because changes in ship position cause the azimuth and elevation to change, the tracking process consists of alternating azimuth steps and elevation steps.

The C ship station belongs to the Inmarsat-C system and supports link testing (PV test) through menus. Some models use floppy disk operation, requiring the use of dedicated floppy disks and prevention of virus infection; some models have a remote alarm function, and the button needs to be tested regularly to ensure reliability. Maintenance requires ensuring registration in an ocean region with a relatively strong signal throughout the voyage; after the GPS is turned off and restarted, it must be checked and ensured that the ship station has an accurate ship position output; after a long period of non-use, a link test should be carried out, and this test is also part of the PSC inspection. For the C ship station, attention must be paid to the precautions for link testing, and also to the precautions for commissioning a new ship station.

The routine inspection and maintenance of the C ship station apply to the C ship station, and its content includes: ensuring that the ship station is registered in an ocean region with a relatively strong signal, checking or updating the ship position at any time, correct use and protection of the floppy disk, regular testing of the remote control button, regular internal testing, frequent checking of the ship position update function, and carrying out a link test after long periods of non-use. Specifically, during the voyage it is necessary to ensure that the C ship station completes registration in an ocean region with a relatively strong signal; the ship position should be checked or updated at any time to ensure the accuracy of the ship position information;

For a C ship station operated with floppy disks, the floppy disks should be stored away from magnetic objects, and the ambient temperature should preferably be 10–40°C; to prevent virus infection, the C ship station floppy disks should be dedicated and must not be run on other computers or replaced with other computers' floppy disks; for a C ship station with a remote alarm function, the remote control button should be tested periodically to ensure reliable function; using the menu provided by the C ship station, perform internal testing on it periodically.

The floppy disk belongs to the C ship station and also to the NBDP terminal. In the C ship station the floppy disk is used for operation, and a dedicated floppy disk should be used to prevent virus infection; the storage ambient temperature should preferably be 10–40°C, and it must be kept away from magnetic objects; running this floppy disk on other computers is prohibited to prevent faults caused by virus infection. In the NBDP terminal, the floppy disk is often used as a dedicated drive medium; if damaged, the equipment will fail to start, so during storage it must be kept away from radiation sources and heat sources.

Routine inspection and maintenance of the B/F ship station cover six aspects. During navigation, it is necessary to ensure that the ship station is synchronized to an ocean region satellite with a relatively strong signal, periodically check the distress confirmation ground station setting, ensure the parameters have been set and are known clearly, and use the menu to periodically perform internal testing of the B/F ship station, which must be carried out regardless of whether it is in use; frequently check the ship position update function, and after GPS restart it must be ensured that ship position output is available; the attached fax machine and printer should be cleaned periodically to ensure smooth communication; the telephone distress test requires RCC cooperation, must not be conducted frequently, and must be carried out strictly as required. The attached equipment of the B/F ship station includes the fax machine and printer; during navigation it is necessary to ensure synchronization to an ocean region satellite with a relatively strong signal, periodically check the setting status of the distress confirmation ground station, use the built-in menu to periodically perform internal testing, and regardless of whether it is in use, the attached fax machine, printer, etc. should be cleaned periodically to ensure smooth communication; after GPS restart, the ship position update function and output status need to be checked; the telephone distress test requires RCC cooperation and must not be conducted frequently.

The telephone distress test usually requires the cooperation of RCC personnel, so it must not be conducted frequently. Beijing Ground Station stipulates: to test equipment sending distress and urgency messages, a prior report must be made to the China Maritime Search and Rescue Center. Attention should be paid to understanding the specific requirements of the relevant ground station or RCC for distress tests, and they must be carried out strictly as required. Reference should be made to the operation manual to periodically perform the telephone distress test on the B/F ship station. For the B/F ship station, attention must be paid to the precautions for the telephone distress test, whose operating specifications require RCC cooperation and a prior report to the China Maritime Search and Rescue Center.

Within 24 h after a new ship station passes the commissioning test, only the coast station used for the commissioning test can be selected for continuing communication; during the 24 h restriction period the ship should navigate in the ocean region served by the coast station used for the commissioning test; after 24 h, communication may be carried out via coast stations of other Inmarsat systems; distress calls are not subject to the restriction of only a specific coast station within 24 h after the commissioning test. Both the C ship station and the B/F ship station need to pay attention to the precautions for commissioning a new ship station.

Regarding the link test, after the 2 min time limit has elapsed, the ship station operator does not need to manually send the distress alarm test message again. If it is still manually sent after the timeout, two distress alarm test messages will be sent consecutively, and the Inmarsat system will treat the retransmitted distress alarm test message as a real distress telegram; misoperation will cause the message to be sent to the search and rescue center (RCC) and start the distress rescue procedure, and this operating error will cause a serious false alarm accident. Some ship stations require the operator to send the distress alarm test message according to the screen prompt during the link test. The C ship station needs to pay attention to the precautions for the link test, namely the operating time limit and risk precautions for preventing retransmission of the distress alarm test message in the Inmarsat ship station link test.

The antenna is used for radar target detection; radar equipment includes the antenna, and the antenna belongs to radar equipment. Radar installation applies to the antenna; the radar antenna installation precautions require attention to the antenna. An omnidirectional antenna belongs to the helical antenna; the omnidirectional antenna is also called a non-directional antenna, radiating electromagnetic waves uniformly in all directions, and is mostly a helical antenna.

The satellite antenna radome is used to protect the antenna. Compared with ground system equipment, the ship station antenna equipped with a radome requires less maintenance. The satellite antenna radome should be kept clean, and spraying paint on the radome is strictly prohibited. When entering the radome for maintenance, the ship station power supply and the power switch inside the radome should be cut off. When the radome is more than 2m above the deck, personnel approaching are not subject to the 5m distance limit. When the RF transmitter is not turned off, the time personnel approach the antenna shall not exceed 1h per day.

The satellite antenna radome requires attention to the radome precautions; spraying paint on the Inmarsat ship station satellite antenna radome is strictly prohibited, and the Inmarsat ship station satellite antenna radome should be kept clean.

The maintenance and servicing of the Inmarsat ship station antenna applies to both the directional antenna and the omnidirectional antenna, and its content includes keeping the satellite antenna radome clean, regularly checking the antenna base, cutting off the power supply when entering the radome for maintenance, and regularly performing functional tests. The satellite antenna radome should be kept clean, and spraying paint on the radome is strictly prohibited. For the directional antenna, it is necessary to regularly check whether the base is loose due to desoldering caused by ship vibration. For the omnidirectional antenna, it is necessary to check the fastening firmness and the connection status between the cable and the antenna. When entering the radome for maintenance, the ship station power supply and the internal switch must be cut off. Under working conditions, personnel are prohibited from staying within 5m of the antenna to prevent microwave radiation. If the radome is more than 2m above the deck, it is not subject to the 5m safety distance limit.

Daily maintenance of the MF/HF transceiver The MF/HF transceiver is important shipborne equipment in the ground communication system, and whether its communication performance is normal is directly related to whether the ship can smoothly pass the PSC inspection.

The casing of this equipment has ventilation and heat dissipation holes, and this structure, while meeting the heat dissipation requirement, also becomes a passage for dust to enter the interior of the equipment. Once dust accumulates on the circuit board, it is very easy to cause faults such as discharge and short circuit under humid conditions. Therefore, in daily maintenance, tools such as a hand bellows (leather bellows) need to be used regularly for internal cleaning and dust removal, to remove dust accumulated on the circuit board and prevent discharge or short circuit faults in a humid environment. This is one of the basic maintenance measures to ensure normal communication performance of the equipment and smooth passage of the PSC inspection. The daily maintenance of the MF/HF transceiver carried out for the MF/HF transceiver includes timely internal cleaning and dust removal of the equipment, attention to moisture protection, attention to lightning protection, familiarity with the external power supply situation, prohibition of the equipment working with faults, reminding the operator not to press the keys too hard, timely detection of the equipment's service performance, and proper cleaning of the equipment panel and the microphone. The hand bellows is a cleaning tool used in the maintenance of the MF/HF transceiver; its other name is leather bellows, and its purpose is cleaning and dust removal, used for internal cleaning and dust removal work of communication equipment such as the MF/HF transceiver.

In terms of electrical connection, loose fastening screws and terminal lugs will cause poor contact and increase the contact resistance. Poor contact is one of the causes of equipment faults, referring to a fault state in which the contact resistance increases due to looseness, oxidation or foreign matter at the electrical connection, which can cause local overheating, phase failure, phase-to-phase short circuit and other faults, and lead to random output actions; the corresponding measure is to check the terminal wiring.

Daily maintenance of the DSC terminal The DSC terminal is the digital selective calling terminal, an independent terminal with automatic ship position update function and internal self-test function. The ship position parameters in the distress alert message are automatically extracted from the ship position memory; in addition to being used for alerts, the ship position parameters are also used for receiving area calls. If the ship position cannot be updated automatically, manual updating should be performed frequently.

Internal self-test includes watchkeeping receiver, DSC Modem, alarm and display tests. The certified officer on duty should perform a DSC self-test once a day during navigation. The independent DSC terminal needs frequent checks of its connections with other equipment to prevent looseness and detachment.

Routine maintenance of the DSC terminal includes frequently checking the connections with other equipment, frequently checking the automatic ship position update function, performing performance testing through the internal self-test function, and making test calls as required. The equipment panel and microphone must be kept clean, ensuring the function key markings are clear and the microphone is not covered with dust. For the independent DSC terminal, the connections with other equipment should be frequently checked to prevent loose or faulty connections caused by ship swaying and vibration. Ship position parameters are used not only for distress alerts but also for receiving area calls; their memory contents are usually located in the initial settings. In addition, the DSC communication function can be confirmed as normal by having the ship's two devices call each other.

The DSC terminal requires attention to test call precautions. Transmission testing is required once a week and is an important item of PSC inspection. In the message, the priority level should be selected as "Safety" and the communication instruction as "Test". Because the medium frequency band has only one distress and safety frequency, 2187.5kHz, its use should be avoided as far as possible. The message should be sent on the DSC distress and safety frequency, but it must be ensured that ongoing communications are not interfered with. During operation, the shore station MMSI must be entered and the appropriate transmission frequency selected to start transmission. The shore station's reply must be received to confirm that the terminal's reception, transmission and connection with the SSB are normal. In SSB communications, test calls are needed to confirm whether the terminal equipment and the SSB transceiver are receiving, transmitting and connected properly.

Routine maintenance of the NBDP terminal. The NBDP terminal is the narrow-band direct-printing telegraph terminal; its operating mode is ARQ and its drive mode is a dedicated floppy disk drive. As the terminal equipment of the combined radio station, it must ensure reliable communication performance. The "TEST+" command can be used to conduct a telex test with a shore station to determine its working status. Some equipment uses a dedicated floppy disk drive; damage to the floppy disk will prevent startup. Routine maintenance includes checking connections, performing self-tests in good time and protecting the floppy disk. The floppy disk must be stored away from radiation sources and heat sources, and must not be used in other computers to prevent viruses.

Routine maintenance of the NBDP terminal includes frequently checking the connections with other equipment, performing self-tests in good time, conducting telex tests through the "TEST+" command, and protecting the floppy disk well.

Perform self-tests in good time to confirm equipment status. In ARQ mode, with the cooperation of a shore station, use the "TEST+" command to conduct a telex test to determine the working status. If the floppy disk is damaged, the NBDP equipment will fail to start.

The floppy disk belongs to the C ship station and also to the NBDP terminal. In the NBDP terminal it is often used as a dedicated drive medium; damage will prevent the equipment from starting. When storing the NBDP terminal floppy disk, it must be kept away from radiation sources and heat sources. The magnetic medium used to store the inspection programs or data of the C ship station and NBDP terminal must be dedicated and kept away from magnetic fields and heat sources. For operation in the C ship station, a dedicated floppy disk should be used to prevent virus infection. The storage ambient temperature should preferably be 10–40°C, and it must be kept away from magnetic objects.

Maintenance of combined radio antenna. The content of combined radio antenna maintenance includes familiarizing with and mastering the antenna configuration and installation position, checking the stressed parts, insulation performance and corrosion condition of the antenna, checking the insulation and stability of the bottom of the mast-type vertical antenna, and checking the cable feeder connection of the automatic antenna tuner unit. It is necessary to be familiar with the antenna configuration and installation position of the ship's combined radio, conduct regular external inspections and promptly solve any problems found. Focus on checking the stressed parts, insulation performance and corrosion condition of the T-shaped and inverted-L-shaped multi-strand copper stranded wire antennas. Fasten, clean and apply anti-rust treatment to antennas that are prone to rust damage and breakage, ensuring their insulated erection state. Check the insulation and stability of the bottom of the mast-type vertical antenna to prevent loosening or failure due to strong wind. Check the cable feeder connection between the outdoor automatic antenna tuner unit and the antenna to prevent lightning damage caused by corroded connectors.

Combined radio antenna maintenance applies to T-shaped antennas, inverted-L-shaped antennas, mast-type vertical antennas and automatic antenna tuner units. T-shaped antennas and inverted-L-shaped antennas mostly use multi-strand copper stranded wire as material; due to strong winds at sea and material reasons, they are prone to rust damage and may break due to wind. Insulated erection is required during installation, and daily maintenance needs to focus on checking each stressed part, insulation performance and corrosion condition; for corrosion and loosening problems, fastening, cleaning and anti-rust treatment should be carried out promptly. The mast-type vertical antenna is relatively sturdy, but the insulation at the bottom needs to be checked, and the stability at the bottom also needs to be checked. The transmitter automatic antenna tuner unit of some equipment is installed outdoors, and the cable connection between the antenna and the automatic antenna tuner unit needs to be checked daily. There was once a case where corrosion of the feeder connector led to lightning strike, causing damage to the automatic antenna tuner unit. The automatic antenna tuner unit belongs to MF/HF equipment components and is threatened by the frequency bands below 20MHz that are concentratedly affected by lightning; there have been failures of automatic antenna tuner unit damage of MF/HF equipment caused by lightning strikes.

Corresponding relationship of radar equipment related maintenance. Radar equipment includes the antenna, transceiver and display; the antenna, transceiver and display all belong to radar equipment. Radar installation applies to the antenna, transceiver and display. Radar antenna installation precautions need to pay attention to the antenna; radar display installation precautions need to pay attention to the display. The transceiver includes transmitter air filter cleaning, transmitter high-voltage device electrostatic dust attraction and the magnetron. The display includes display air filter cleaning and display surface cleaning.

The antenna is the component in ship radar and communication equipment used to radiate or receive electromagnetic waves, and needs to meet specific installation height, field of view and anti-interference requirements. The radar antenna height should ensure that the horizontal distance from the bow line of sight to the sea surface does not exceed 500m or two times the ship's length, whichever is smaller. The radar antenna position should ensure that there is no shadow sector within the range from dead ahead to 2.5° abaft the beam on both port and starboard sides.

2
The transceiver is the core equipment unit of the radar system, responsible for signal transmission and reception, usually installed near the bridge or directly below the antenna, usually installed in a well-ventilated equipment room near the bridge, the chart room or inside the bridge, and as far as possible directly below the antenna. The mast-mounted radar transceiver connects to the antenna through a waveguide; the effective length of the waveguide should not exceed 25m at maximum, and there should preferably be no more than five bent waveguides. The display is the display terminal of ship radar and monitoring systems, used to present images, data and alarm information; it should be installed in the wheelhouse in a place free from strong electromagnetic radiation, away from heat sources and dry, fixed with a hardwood base, with the main radar display oriented so that the observer faces the bow, installed on the starboard side of the bridge.

Basic requirements for daily maintenance of VHF communication equipment. The bridge is equipped with two VHF communication equipment, and these two equipment have both communication and DSC terminal functions. In daily maintenance, these two equipment should be used alternately to avoid long-term use of only one of them, which may cause performance degradation or moisture and dust accumulation in the other. Daily maintenance of VHF communication equipment applies to the VHF communication equipment itself, and its content covers equipment rotation, cleaning, power supply inspection, and DSC function verification. Maintenance personnel need to regularly clean the microphone and panel to keep the transmission channel and operating surface clean; at the same time, they should frequently check the working condition of the equipment indicator lights and the regulated power supply to confirm that the power supply is normal and the indication status is consistent with the actual working status. The equipment wiring connectors should also be frequently checked and tightened to prevent poor contact caused by vibration.

DSC terminal and communication function check. The full name of the DSC terminal is the Digital Selective Calling terminal, which is an independent terminal with automatic ship position updating and internal self-test functions. Daily maintenance of the DSC terminal applies to the DSC terminal. Daily maintenance requires checking whether the DSC terminal ship position data is automatically updated, and frequently checking the working status of the DSC watchkeeping receiver. DSC self-test should be carried out daily, and at the same time, the DSC communication function can be confirmed as normal by mutual calling between the two equipment on board. The ship position parameters in the distress alert information are automatically extracted from the ship position memory. In addition to being used for alerts, the ship position parameters are also used for receiving area calls. Therefore, the automatic updating of ship position data is directly related to the accuracy of alert and call information. When making a test call to the DSC terminal, attention should be paid to the precautions for test calls to avoid mistakenly sending a distress alert or interfering with normal watchkeeping.

The antenna is used for radar target detection and, in ship radar and communication equipment, is used to radiate or receive electromagnetic waves, and must meet specific installation height, field of view, and anti-interference requirements. The precautions for radar antenna installation need to consider the installation conditions of the antenna itself; radar installation applies to the antenna. The height of the radar antenna should ensure that the horizontal distance from the bow line of sight to the sea surface does not exceed 500 m or twice the ship length, whichever is smaller; the position of the radar antenna should ensure that there is no shadow sector area within the range from dead ahead to 2 to 2.5° abaft the beam on both port and starboard sides. For VHF communication equipment, it is necessary to regularly check the outdoor antenna connections and waterproof performance to prevent contact corrosion or rainwater from entering the cable connectors. This is an important part of ensuring VHF communication distance and call quality.

Composition and maintenance focus of the weather facsimile receiver. Most models of marine weather facsimile receivers consist of two parts: an independent receiver and a recording device. The receiver is functionally equivalent to an MF/HF single-sideband receiver, while the recording device is mostly composed of precision mechanical components. The focus of daily maintenance is precisely around these two parts, the receiver and the recording device, so that through maintenance the equipment can still receive charts promptly and clearly under severe weather conditions such as typhoons.

The receiving antenna is part of the weather facsimile receiver. Together with the recording device, it forms the complete machine and is functionally equivalent to an MF/HF single-sideband receiver. Daily maintenance of the receiving antenna requires guarding against contact corrosion, loosening of fixing devices, and deterioration of insulation performance. During installation, protection against lightning damage is also required, and its installation position should maintain a safe distance from the radar antenna to avoid electromagnetic interference. The content of daily maintenance of the weather facsimile receiver includes: doing the maintenance work of the receiving antenna well, paying attention to preventing lightning strikes, performing thermal head testing and inspection, handling recording paper jams, replacing recording paper in a timely manner, checking the automatic reception function, and visually inspecting weather charts. The height of the radar antenna should ensure that the horizontal distance from the bow line of sight to the sea surface does not exceed 500 m or twice the ship length, whichever is smaller; the position of the radar antenna should ensure that there is no shadow sector area within the range from dead ahead to 2 to 2.5° abaft the beam on both port and starboard sides.

The precautions for radar installation of the radar antenna require attention to the antenna installation requirements; the radar installation likewise applies to the antenna.

The maintenance of the recording device components: the thermal head belongs to the recording device part of the marine weather facsimile receiver, and its function is to record weather charts. The thermal recording head is a precision component in the recording device of the marine weather facsimile receiver; the thermal head and the thermal recording head are different names for the same component. When the received weather chart is unclear, it is necessary to test the state of the thermal head and check whether the thermal recording head is damaged; if damage is detected, it should be replaced in time. Closing the paper compartment cover too forcefully may cause damage to the thermal head and may also cause damage to the thermal recording head.

The recording paper belongs to the weather facsimile receiver and is used to record weather charts. When the remaining length of the recording paper is less than 1 m, there will be an obvious mark to remind the user that it is about to run out. When a paper jam occurs, the equipment power should be switched off and the recording paper reinstalled. The weather facsimile receiver requires attention to the precautions for recording paper installation, that is, after installing the recording paper, the paper compartment cover should not be closed too forcefully, otherwise it will cause deformation of the paper compartment cover or damage to the thermal recording head.

In the daily maintenance of lightning protection and other related equipment, attention should be paid to preventing the influence of lightning strikes on the equipment. In thunderstorm weather, it is best not to use the weather facsimile receiver unless necessary; after use, the antenna should be disconnected and earthed.

The ship power station is the heart of the ship power system; the reliability and survivability of its operation are important indicators of the effectiveness of the system in achieving its prescribed tasks, and its basic responsibilities include ensuring reliable power supply, safe operation, and rapid elimination of faults after they occur. The ship power station includes the main switchboard, brushed synchronous generator, brushless synchronous generator, uncontrolled phase compounding voltage regulation system, controlled phase compounding voltage regulation system, thyristor excitation voltage regulation system, brushless excitation generator voltage regulation system, DW14 type circuit breaker, ship power network, and shore power box. The ship power network belongs to the ship power station; the precautions for connecting shore power require attention to the relevant requirements of the ship power station.

Composition and basic requirements of the ship power station: the ship power station is the heart of the ship power system, and the reliability and survivability of its operation are important indicators of the effectiveness of the system in achieving its prescribed tasks. Its basic responsibilities include ensuring reliable power supply, safe operation, and rapid elimination of faults after they occur. Around this responsibility, the equipment and systems included in the ship power station constitute a complete system for the generation, distribution, and conversion of electrical energy.

In the electrical energy distribution link, the main switchboard is the control center for the concentration and distribution of electrical energy in the ship power station; the ship power station includes the main switchboard, from which electrical energy is fed to the various power-consuming equipment throughout the ship. In the electrical energy generation link, the ship power station includes two types of generating devices, the brushed synchronous generator and the brushless synchronous generator, which respectively adapt to different excitation and maintenance conditions. In the voltage regulation link matched with the generator, the ship power station includes the uncontrolled phase compounding voltage regulation system, controlled phase compounding voltage regulation system, thyristor excitation voltage regulation system, and brushless excitation generator voltage regulation system; these voltage regulation systems respectively correspond to different types of generators and operating requirements. In the protection and switching link, the ship power station includes the DW14 type circuit breaker, used for closing and opening and fault removal of the generator main circuit. In the electrical energy output and external connection link, the ship power station includes the ship power network and the shore power box, wherein the ship power network belongs to the constituent parts of the ship power station and undertakes the function of transmitting power to the ship's loads; the shore power box is used for supplying power to the ship from the shore power source during berthing. The precautions for connecting shore power require attention to the relevant states and operating conditions of the ship power station, so as to ensure the safety of the ship power station when shore power is connected.

For AC generators operating in parallel, reverse power protection with a delay of 3 to 10 s should be provided to prevent the generator from continuing to operate in the reverse power state.

Key points of daily maintenance of the marine weather facsimile receiver: the daily maintenance of the marine weather facsimile receiver should be arranged comprehensively in combination with the power supply conditions and signal environment of the ship power station. The receiver is usually powered by the ship power network, so its operating state is directly related to the power supply reliability of the ship power station. In daily inspection, it should first be confirmed that the power supply of the ship power station is normal, the DW14 type circuit breaker of the corresponding branch of the main switchboard is in the closed position, and the voltage and frequency of the ship power network are stable, so as to avoid distortion of the recorded image or shutdown of the receiver caused by power supply fluctuations.

If the power supply part of the receiver is switched from the ship power station through the shore power box, when berthing and connecting shore power, the phase sequence and voltage should be checked in accordance with the precautions for connecting shore power, and it should be confirmed that the switching relationship between the ship power station and the shore power box is correct, so as to prevent the normal operation of the motor and recording mechanism in the receiver from being affected by a phase sequence mismatch. For ships powered by a brushed synchronous generator or a brushless synchronous generator, attention should also be paid to the voltage regulation characteristics of the uncontrolled phase compounding voltage regulation system, controlled phase compounding voltage regulation system, thyristor excitation voltage regulation system, and brushless excitation generator voltage regulation system when the load changes, so as to avoid excessive voltage deviation affecting the recording quality of the receiver.

Daily maintenance should also include inspection of the receiver antenna. The antenna should be kept away from strong electromagnetic interference sources such as the main switchboard, DW14 circuit breaker and high-power cables in the ship's power station, so as to reduce the influence of interference on the received signal. The connecting cable between the receiver and the ship's power network should be securely fixed, and the shielding layer should be well earthed. If the AC generators operating in parallel in the ship's power station are provided with reverse power protection acting with a delay of 3–10 s, important recording operations of the receiver should be avoided during generator changeover or paralleling operations, and the receiver should be put into operation only after the power supply of the ship's power station has recovered to stability. For ships supplied by the voltage regulation system of brushless excitation generators, since the voltage regulation link responds relatively quickly, the power supply section of the receiver generally requires no additional voltage stabilization, but the power supply voltage should still be measured periodically to check whether it is within the permissible range. When the receiver is re-energized after being out of service for a long time, first check whether the power supply of the ship's power station is normal, then confirm item by item the status of the main switchboard, the ship's power network, the shore power box and the DW14 circuit breaker, and only switch on after everything is confirmed correct.

Maintenance records should state the inspection date, the operating status of the ship's power station, the reception performance of the receiver and the handling performed, so as to facilitate subsequent comparative analysis. By combining the daily maintenance of the receiver with the power supply management of the ship's power station, reception faults caused by power supply and interference factors can be reduced, and the weather facsimile charts can be kept clear and complete.

The ship's power station is the heart of the ship's electrical power system, and the reliability and survivability of its operation are important indicators of the effectiveness of the system in accomplishing its prescribed tasks. This equipment bears the basic responsibility of ensuring reliable power supply and safe operation, and of promptly eliminating faults after they occur. In terms of composition, the ship's power station includes the main switchboard, the ship's power network and the shore power box, and also includes brushed synchronous generators and brushless synchronous generators, as well as different forms of voltage regulation devices such as the uncontrolled phase compounding voltage regulation system, the controlled phase compounding voltage regulation system, the thyristor excitation voltage regulation system and the brushless excitation generator voltage regulation system, and further includes the DW14 circuit breaker. The ship's power network is a constituent part of the ship's power station, while the main switchboard is the control center for the concentration and distribution of electrical energy in the power station, having functions of circuit making and breaking, protection alarming, parameter detection and power regulation; it can make and break circuits, issue alarms when protective devices operate, detect and display various electrical parameters, and regulate the voltage and frequency of the power station as well as the active and reactive power of generator sets operating in parallel. The main switchboard contains the main switch and the switchboard-type insulation resistance meter.

The main switch is used in the power station to connect and disconnect the generator and the main busbar; it is an air circuit breaker having both switching and protection functions, and its components include the undervoltage release, the shunt release, the overcurrent protection device, the arc extinguishing device, auxiliary contacts and the control and signal indication circuit. The DW14 circuit breaker adopts Japanese Terasaki technology and is fitted with an AOJ-1s overcurrent trip unit, which is mounted on the upper right side of the front of the circuit breaker. The trip unit is the electrical assembly in a circuit breaker used to implement protection functions such as overload, short circuit and undervoltage and to drive the contacts to open; the main switch mainly consists of the undervoltage release, the shunt release and the overcurrent protection device. As a switching apparatus used in the ship's electrical power system to protect circuits, the circuit breaker is a low-voltage distribution apparatus and is divided into two types, the frame type (air type) and the molded-case type; it can maintain thermal stability and electrodynamic stability during short circuit faults; the air circuit breaker is mostly used as the generator main switch and can automatically disconnect the generator to protect the power network. When used for generator protection, the circuit breaker opens after a delay of less than 2 min at 10%–50% overload; when the overcurrent exceeds 50%, the short-time-delay trip unit is set to 200%–250% of rated current with a delay ≤0.6 s; the undervoltage trip unit acts instantaneously when the voltage drops to 35% of rated value and acts with a delay at 35%–70%.

Circuit breaker maintenance applies to the equipment, the circuit breaker.

Both brushed synchronous generators and brushless synchronous generators include the generator prime mover, the generator stator winding and the excitation system. The generator prime mover is the power source of the generator; the generator stator winding is the stator part of the generator, used to generate induced electromotive force; in the brushless synchronous generator, three-phase AC power is induced in the stator winding of the main generator and output; the excitation system provides excitation current for the generator and belongs to the voltage regulation system of the synchronous generator, including brushed, brushless and thyristor forms, with common forms being the uncontrolled phase compounding, controlled phase compounding, thyristor excitation and brushless excitation voltage regulation systems. Maintenance of the excitation system applies to the excitation system, with a maintenance period of once every half year, and the insulation resistance value is required to be not less than 1 MΩ. The insulation of marine motor windings must undergo "three-proof" treatment against moisture, mould and salt/oil mist, and must be oil-resistant. The general alarm device consists of the shutter, alarm bell, alarm lamp and junction box, that is, the general alarm device includes the junction box. The junction box is the component in the ship's electrical system used to connect cables, protect wiring points and accommodate electrical elements; the solenoid valve of the paint room zone is not connected to an external junction box but is connected directly into the local control box.

In terms of fault symptom, a single-phase earthing fault of the power system is manifested as the insulation indicator lamp of one phase going out while the insulation indicator lamps of the other two phases are abnormally bright; its typical appearance feature is exactly that the insulation indicator lamp of one phase goes out and the insulation indicator lamps of the remaining two phases are abnormally bright. The fault causes of this fault include an earthing fault caused by single-phase insulation breakdown of an electrical load, including loose wiring or shell contact in the junction box of a load motor, including a breakdown fault of a power distribution switch or other electrical equipment in the main switchboard, and also including earthing occurring inside the generator. This fault belongs to the fault category caused by harsh environmental conditions reducing the electrical insulation capability. The low insulation resistance fault of the power system is manifested as low insulation resistance that has already reached the alarm value, and is divided into two types, 400V and 220V. 400V system faults mostly occur at the load end, on open-deck equipment or inside the main switchboard; 220V system faults mostly occur in the lighting distribution systems of each deck, in kitchen electrical equipment or in deck lighting.

If such a fault is not solved in time, another fault in another phase will form a short circuit current, and the consequence of the short circuit may cause some load switches to trip or even the main switchboard to trip. Harsh environmental conditions reducing the electrical insulation capability is one of the main causes.

As far as fault cause is concerned, common faults of the equipment itself include: damage to the generator prime mover, such as failure of the prime mover governor, overheating of the cylinder block, etc.; burning out or open circuit of the generator stator winding; damage to the excitation system; insulation damage of the cable junction box.
